The customer can only see the most recent contact point via the Profile API

dc360.explanation: This is a defining architectural difference from a traditional MDM golden record: Data Cloud's unified profile keeps every contact point and its lineage, so an older email is preserved and remains available (e.g., for a specific activation's source-priority selection) even after a newer one is ingested. B is wrong because there's no automatic 90-day contact point purge — that would contradict the "retain all lineage" design principle. C is wrong because retaining only the most recent contact point per type is exactly the outcome incorrectly assumed by a 1:1 cardinality misconfiguration, not correct default behavior. D is wrong because the Profile API surfaces the full profile including all associated contact points, not just the latest one.

dc360.question: A consultant is asked whether Data Cloud can serve as a replacement for the customer's existing enterprise Master Data Management (MDM) platform. What is the most accurate answer?

options.text: Yes, because Data Cloud produces a golden record identical in purpose and structure to an MDM golden record

No, Data Cloud's Unified Profile is a dynamic, multi-source view retaining full lineage and behavioral/engagement data, which serves a different purpose than an MDM golden record, though the two can coexist
Yes, but only if the customer disables all reconciliation rules
No, because Data Cloud cannot ingest data from more than one source system

dc360.explanation: Data Cloud is explicitly not an MDM replacement — its Unified Profile is a dynamic, near-real-time, multi-dimensional view (including engagement data) that retains all source lineage, which is architecturally different from an MDM golden record's curated single-value-per-field approach; the two systems are commonly used together. A is wrong because a golden record and a unified profile behave differently, particularly around lineage retention. C is wrong because disabling reconciliation rules doesn't transform Data Cloud into an MDM system; reconciliation is unrelated to that architectural distinction. D is wrong because ingesting from many source systems is one of Data Cloud's core strengths, not a limitation.

dc360.question: A global retailer needs to isolate EU customer data for GDPR-related processing and access restrictions, separate from US and APAC data, all within a single Data Cloud org. A well-meaning administrator suggests using field-level security and classification tags on PII fields as the isolation mechanism. Why is this insufficient?

options.text: Classification tags and field-level security control visibility/sensitivity labeling of fields, but they do not provide the full regional data, segment, and activation isolation that Data Spaces provide
Classification tags automatically delete non-EU data, which would be destructive
Field-level security only works on Custom DMOs, not Standard DMOs
Classification tags require a separate Data Cloud org per region regardless of configuration

dc360.explanation: Classification tags and field-level security control who can view or edit specific fields, which is a sensitivity-labeling and access-control layer, but they don't segregate records, segments, or activations by region the way Data Spaces do — Data Spaces are the feature purpose-built for that kind of regional isolation. B is wrong because classification tags are a labeling mechanism only; they never trigger automatic deletion of data. C is wrong because field-level security applies equally to Standard and Custom DMO fields — there's no such restriction. D is wrong because achieving regional isolation does not require a separate org per region; that's exactly the operational overhead Data Spaces are designed to avoid.

dc360.question: A B2C retailer's marketing team wants to build a segment on the Unified Individual that filters on "has abandoned a cart in the last 3 days," where cart data arrives as Engagement DMO records with a CartAbandonedDate field. Which segment operator correctly supports this rolling, always-current filter?

options.text: Is Between with two hardcoded dates
Last Number of Days
Next Number of Days
Is Equal To

dc360.explanation: Last Number of Days is the relative, rolling-window operator that re-evaluates "3 days ago" relative to the current date every time the segment runs, which is exactly what's needed for an always-current cart abandonment filter. A is wrong because Is Between requires fixed start/end dates that would need manual updates and quickly go stale. C is wrong because Next Number of Days looks forward from today, not backward at past events. D is wrong because Is Equal To matches a single exact date value, not a rolling multi-day window.

dc360.question: A consultant configures a Marketing Cloud activation and notices that even after correctly selecting the Email contact point, individuals with only a work email (no personal email) mapped are still included and delivered mail successfully, but the marketing team is confused why some other individuals with a mapped phone number but no email are silently dropped from an email-channel activation entirely. What should the consultant explain?

options.text: The activation was configured to use the Email contact point specifically, so individuals lacking any mapped email address are excluded regardless of having a phone number, since phone isn't the selected channel for this activation
Marketing Cloud automatically converts phone numbers into email placeholders when no email exists
Data Cloud requires every individual to have both email and phone mapped before any activation is permitted
The missing individuals are anonymous profiles and are excluded from all activations by definition

dc360.explanation: An activation's contact point selection determines which channel address is required for inclusion; choosing Email as the contact point means only individuals with a mapped, populated Contact Point Email record are eligible, so someone with only a phone number (and no email) is correctly excluded from this specific email-channel activation. B is wrong because there is no such automatic conversion mechanism — Marketing Cloud cannot manufacture an email address from a phone number. C is wrong because Data Cloud does not impose a blanket requirement that every individual have both contact point types mapped before any activation can run; the requirement is scoped to whichever contact point the specific activation selects. D is wrong because anonymous profile status is unrelated to this scenario — the individuals in question are known profiles with a mapped phone number, simply lacking the specific contact point type this activation requires.

dc360.question: A consultant is setting up governance for a Data Cloud org shared by two regional marketing teams. Leadership wants Team A to be able to view but not edit Team B's Calculated Insights, while both teams can freely create and manage their own Segments and Activation Targets. Which two statements correctly describe what Sharing Rules can and cannot do here? (Choose 2)

options.text: Sharing Rules can grant Team A read-only visibility into specific Calculated Insights owned by Team B without granting edit access
Sharing Rules can also be configured on Segments and Activation Targets, giving governance flexibility across all three object types in one framework
Sharing Rules can restrict which Data Spaces a team is able to log into
Sharing Rules can be used to prevent Team B's Segments from ever appearing in Team A's Data Explorer results
Sharing Rules require a Data Space to be created first, since they are a sub-feature of Data Space configuration

dc360.explanation: Sharing Rules can grant scoped, read-only access to specific objects like a Calculated Insight, satisfying the "view but not edit" requirement (A), and since Sharing Rules support Calculated Insights, Segments, and Activation Targets together, the same governance framework can flexibly manage access across all three object types for both teams (B). C is wrong because restricting login/access to an entire Data Space is a separate access-control layer from object-level Sharing Rules — Sharing Rules operate on individual CIs, Segments, and Activation Targets, not space-level login permissions. D is wrong because Sharing Rules control access grants, not a blanket suppression mechanism for another team's objects appearing in tools like Data Explorer results by default. E is wrong because Sharing Rules are usable independently of Data Spaces — they are not a sub-feature requiring a Data Space to exist first.

dc360.question: An airline's segment builder query is running noticeably slower each week as more flight and loyalty DLOs get referenced through related attributes, though it hasn't yet hit a hard reference limit. The consultant wants to proactively improve performance before it becomes a failure. Which two approaches are appropriate? (Choose 2)

options.text: Pre-aggregate frequently reused multi-object logic (e.g., total flights this year) into a Calculated Insight so the segment references one CI instead of joining raw DLOs each time
Break the single large segment into smaller nested segments that each reference a narrower set of DLOs, combined via nesting
Switch the Segment On entity to a DLO instead of the Unified Individual DMO to bypass the harmonization layer
Disable Identity Resolution temporarily while the segment runs to reduce processing overhead

dc360.explanation: Pushing repeated multi-object aggregation logic into a pre-computed Calculated Insight reduces how many raw DLOs the segment must join at query time (A), and splitting a large, complex segment into smaller nested segments spreads the DLO footprint across multiple lighter-weight queries (B) — both are proactive, supported performance practices. C is wrong because Segment On must be a Profile category DMO; DLOs cannot be used as the Segment On entity, and bypassing harmonization would break the entire segmentation model. D is wrong because disabling Identity Resolution would remove the Unified Individual records the segment depends on entirely, breaking segmentation rather than improving its performance.

dc360.question: A consultant is troubleshooting why a Calculated Insight metric doesn't appear as an option when adding Additional Attributes to an Activation, even though the CI itself was created successfully and appears in Data Explorer. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The CI is missing a dimension tying back to the Individual/Unified Individual ID needed to join to the activated profile records
Calculated Insights can never be added as Additional Attributes in any activation
The Activation Target must be Amazon S3 for CI metrics to be selectable
The CI needs to be recalculated hourly, not on a 24-hour schedule

dc360.explanation: Just as with segmentation eligibility, a CI needs a dimension linking back to Individual/Unified Individual ID so the platform can join its metric values to the activated profile records — without that linkage, the CI won't surface as a selectable Additional Attribute in the activation setup. B is wrong because CIs are explicitly designed to be addable as Additional Attributes to enrich activation payloads. C is wrong because CI metrics as additional attributes are supported across activation target types, not restricted to Amazon S3. D is wrong because refresh cadence (1, 6, 12, or 24 hours) doesn't affect whether a CI is structurally eligible to be added to an activation.

dc360.question: Which two considerations should a consultant flag when a customer wants to use Streaming Insights as the sole basis for all of their segmentation, replacing Calculated Insights entirely? (Choose 2)

options.text: Streaming Insights cannot be used directly in segmentation at all — only Calculated Insights are supported as segment attributes
Streaming Insights are optimized for near real-time windows on streaming sources, not for complex historical, multi-object aggregation across the full dataset
Streaming Insights automatically replace the need for Identity Resolution
Calculated Insights support up to 50 measures, offering broader analytical flexibility for large historical aggregations
Streaming Insights can only be authored using the SQL editor, never the Visual Builder

dc360.explanation: Streaming Insights cannot be used in segmentation at all (A) — only Calculated Insights are segment-eligible — and even setting that aside, Streaming Insights are architecturally suited for near real-time windowed metrics on streaming data rather than broad historical multi-object aggregation, which is where CIs excel (B). C is wrong because Streaming Insights have no relationship to identity resolution, which is an entirely separate process. D, while factually true about the 50-measure limit, isn't the key consideration driving this specific recommendation compared to A and B. E is wrong because both Streaming and Calculated Insights can be authored via either the SQL editor or the Visual Insights Builder.

dc360.question: A consultant needs a customer's service agents to see a "Days Since Last Purchase" value directly on the Contact record page in Salesforce CRM, sourced from Data Cloud data, refreshed at least daily. Which approach best fits without building a custom Lightning Web Component?

options.text: Use a Calculated Insight and surface it on the Contact page via a CRM enrichment/copy field, refreshed on the CI's batch schedule
Use the Ingestion API to push the value into Data Cloud daily
Use a Streaming Insight subscribed directly to the Contact page layout
Use the Profile API called from a standard page layout component with no custom code

dc360.explanation: CRM enrichment (copying a Data Cloud field, including CI output, back onto a CRM object like Contact) is the no-custom-code, declarative path for surfacing a periodically refreshed Data Cloud-derived value directly on a standard page layout. B is wrong because the Ingestion API pushes data into Data Cloud; it doesn't surface data back onto a CRM page. C is wrong because Streaming Insights aren't a page-layout display mechanism and there's no such native "subscription" to a page layout. D is wrong because the Profile API requires a client (typically a custom LWC) to call it and render results — standard page layouts can't invoke it without custom development, which the question says to avoid.

dc360.question: A consultant reviews an Identity Resolution ruleset that uses Fuzzy Name matching alone for a directory-style database of company employees, many of whom share common first and last names across different departments. What risk should the consultant flag, and what's the recommended mitigation?

options.text: Fuzzy Name alone risks merging different people with similar or identical names; the consultant should add a more specific rule, such as Exact Party ID on employee ID or Exact Email, to disambiguate
Fuzzy Name matching should be replaced with the Most Occurring reconciliation rule to fix the risk
There is no risk, since Fuzzy Name matching already accounts for department differences automatically
The risk only applies to reconciliation, not to identity resolution matching itself

dc360.explanation: Fuzzy Name matching alone is a weak, high-false-positive strategy in populations with common or duplicate names, so the correct mitigation is adding a more specific, less ambiguous match rule like Exact Party ID (employee ID) or Exact Email to disambiguate people who share a name. B is wrong because reconciliation rules resolve conflicting attribute values after matching — they cannot fix an incorrect match decision that already merged two different people. C is wrong because Fuzzy Name has no inherent awareness of department or organizational context; it purely compares name string similarity. D is wrong because this is fundamentally a matching-rule risk (records being incorrectly linked), not a reconciliation-rule issue.

dc360.question: Northern Trail Outfitters wants a Calculated Insight measuring "average days between purchases" per Unified Individual, computed from the Sales Order Engagement DMO. Which two configuration details are essential to get right? (Choose 2)

options.text: The CI must join through the correct chain from Unified Individual to the source Individual (via Unified Link Individual) before reaching Sales Order
The CI must use the Visual Insights Builder exclusively, since date-difference calculations aren't supported in SQL
The measure calculation needs access to each individual's full order date history to compute the gaps between consecutive purchases
The CI must be classified as a Profile category DMO before it can be created

dc360.explanation: Because Sales Order relates to the source Individual rather than directly to Unified Individual, the CI must traverse Unified Individual -> Unified Link Individual -> Individual -> Sales Order to correctly aggregate across all matched source records (A), and calculating gaps between purchases requires access to the full ordered date history per person, not just a single latest date (C). B is wrong because date-difference and window-style calculations are fully supported in the SQL editor — SQL is often the more capable option for this kind of computation, not a blocker. D is wrong because Calculated Insights aren't categorized as Profile/Engagement/Other in the way data stream DMOs are — that categorization applies to DMOs used for segmentation Segment On selection.

dc360.question: A media streaming company ingests viewing history through a custom Ingestion API integration rather than a Starter Bundle, and now wants to add a second, unrelated custom source that tracks customer support chat transcripts, with the two datasets never needing to be joined together. The consultant is deciding whether both sources can share a single data stream. What is the correct guidance?

options.text: No — each distinct source object can only be ingested through its own dedicated data stream; viewing history and chat transcripts must be configured as two separate data streams
Yes, as long as both objects are mapped to the same DMO afterward
Yes, but only if both sources use the Ingestion API rather than a Starter Bundle
No — Data Cloud limits an org to a single active custom data stream at a time

dc360.explanation: Each source object can only be ingested once, through its own data stream; two structurally different objects like viewing history events and chat transcripts each require their own dedicated data stream, regardless of whether they'll ever be joined downstream. B is wrong because mapping to the same DMO after ingestion doesn't change the ingestion-time requirement that each source object needs its own stream — mapping happens after the DLO already exists. C is wrong because the requirement to use separate data streams per source object applies regardless of which connector or ingestion method (Ingestion API, Starter Bundle, or otherwise) is used. D is wrong because there is no such single-active-custom-stream limitation — orgs routinely run many concurrent data streams from many sources.

dc360.question: A consultant is asked to change an active Identity Resolution ruleset's match rules mid-project, moving from Exact Email only to also including Exact Phone Number, on an org that already has millions of unified profiles and dozens of live segments and activations. What is the most accurate operational guidance to give the customer?

options.text: The ruleset can be edited and re-run; existing Unified Individual and Unified Link Individual records will be recalculated to reflect the new, typically higher, consolidation rate, and downstream segments will reflect the updated membership after the next segment evaluation
Editing an active ruleset is blocked entirely; a new Data Cloud org must be provisioned to change match rules
Adding a new match rule requires first deleting all existing segments and activations, since they become permanently orphaned
Match rules can only be edited within the first 24 hours after the ruleset's initial creation

dc360.explanation: Identity Resolution rulesets can be edited and re-run at any time; doing so recalculates the Unified Individual and Unified Link Individual records based on the updated match rules, typically increasing the consolidation rate when a new match rule like Exact Phone Number is added, and existing segments will simply reflect the updated unified profile membership the next time they're evaluated. B is wrong because editing an active ruleset is a normal, supported operation and does not require provisioning an entirely new org. C is wrong because segments and activations are not deleted or permanently orphaned by a ruleset update — they continue to reference the same Unified Individual DMO, which is simply recalculated. D is wrong because there is no such 24-hour editing window restriction on identity resolution rulesets.

dc360.question: A consultant is configuring an activation to a Google Ads external activation platform, and the marketing team wants the audience name displayed inside Google Ads to be "NTO_Q3_Loyalty_Push" even though the underlying segment is internally named "Q3-Loyalty-High-AOV-v2." How should the consultant satisfy this without renaming the segment itself?

options.text: Set a distinct activation name when configuring the activation, since external ad platforms typically display the activation's own name, not the underlying segment's name
Rename the segment to "NTO_Q3_Loyalty_Push," then rename it back afterward
Create a Calculated Insight with the desired display name and attach it to the activation
Ask Google Ads support to override the naming shown for this one audience

dc360.explanation: External activation platforms like Google Ads typically surface the Activation's own configured name as the audience name, which is independent of the underlying segment's internal name — setting a distinct activation name achieves the desired display label without touching the segment. B is wrong because renaming the segment back and forth is an unnecessary, fragile workaround when the activation name itself is directly configurable and decoupled from the segment name. C is wrong because a Calculated Insight computes a metric value; it has no role in controlling how an audience is named or displayed in an external ad platform. D is wrong because audience naming is controlled entirely from the Data Cloud activation configuration, not something Google Ads support can override on a per-audience basis.

dc360.question: An insurance company activates a segment of policyholders to Amazon S3 for a legacy claims system. The company also wants the destination system to be able to programmatically confirm which segment definition and schema produced a given CSV file before processing it. What should the consultant point to?

options.text: The separate JSON metadata file that Data Cloud automatically creates alongside the CSV for S3 activations
A manually maintained changelog document shared via email each time the segment changes
The Segment Membership DMO queried live via the Query API at processing time
An audit trail embedded as a hidden column within the CSV file itself

dc360.explanation: Amazon S3 (Cloud File Storage) activations automatically produce a companion JSON metadata file alongside the CSV containing segment definition and run details, which is exactly the mechanism designed for downstream systems to confirm schema and context before processing the data payload. B is wrong because a manual changelog is an error-prone, non-automated workaround when the platform already generates this metadata natively. C is wrong because querying the Segment Membership DMO live requires a completely separate integration and isn't the file-based metadata the legacy system needs alongside its CSV pickup. D is wrong because Data Cloud does not embed audit or schema metadata as a hidden column inside the CSV — that information lives in the separate JSON file.

dc360.question: Which two statements accurately describe how Data Spaces affect a Data Cloud implementation involving shared reference data (e.g., a common Product catalog) used by multiple otherwise-isolated brands? (Choose 2)

options.text: Shared reference objects generally need to be explicitly made available within each Data Space that needs to query them
Data Spaces automatically share all DMOs across every space in the org by default
Segments and activations built within one Data Space cannot reference data that hasn't been made available in that space
Once a DMO is available in any single Data Space, all other Data Spaces automatically inherit ongoing write access to it

dc360.explanation: Because Data Spaces isolate data by design, shared reference data like a common Product catalog must be deliberately made available in each space that needs it (A), and segments/activations within a given space are constrained to data available in that space (C) — this is exactly the design tradeoff a consultant must plan for. B is wrong because Data Spaces do not default to sharing everything — isolation, not automatic sharing, is the default behavior that makes Data Spaces useful for brand separation. D is wrong because making a DMO available in one space does not grant other spaces automatic ongoing write access; each space's access must be explicitly configured.

dc360.question: A wealth management firm's compliance team wants a persistent, queryable audit trail showing which specific match rule (e.g., Exact Email vs. Exact Party ID) caused each pair of source records to be merged into a given Unified Individual, retained for at least 2 years for regulatory review. What should the consultant recommend?

options.text: Rely on the Resolution Summary screen alone, since it permanently stores every historical match decision indefinitely
Use the Profile Explorer's real-time lineage view as the system of record, since it retains full historical match rule history for all time

Recognize that native identity resolution lineage views are point-in-time/current-state, and design a supplemental export process to persist match rule outcomes into an external audit store on an ongoing basis
Configure a 2-year Segment Membership DMO retention window, since Segment Membership stores match rule lineage

dc360.explanation: Data Cloud's native identity resolution tools (Resolution Summary, Profile Explorer) are designed for current-state validation and troubleshooting, not as a long-term regulatory audit ledger, so meeting a strict multi-year retention requirement means exporting match rule outcomes into an external, purpose-built audit store on an ongoing basis. A is wrong because the Resolution Summary reflects the results of the most recent run and is not designed as a permanent, indefinitely retained historical audit log. B is wrong because Profile Explorer shows the current lineage for a given profile at the time you view it; it is not a historical archive of every past match decision. D is wrong because the Segment Membership DMO tracks segment membership history, not identity resolution match rule lineage — these are unrelated data cloud constructs.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A new Apex developer asks why their code sharing the org with hundreds of other customers must obey strict per-transaction limits on SOQL queries and DML statements. What concept explains this, and what is the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Multi-tenancy: many customer orgs share the same physical infrastructure and application layer, so governor limits are hard, per-transaction enforcement caps that prevent one tenant's runaway code from starving shared resources for everyone else.
Single-tenancy: each customer org gets fully dedicated hardware, so governor limits exist only as a historical artifact with no current technical purpose.
Governor limits exist solely to encourage customers to purchase additional API call add-ons and have no relationship to shared infrastructure.
Governor limits are configurable per org and can be disabled entirely by a System Administrator for high-usage customers.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Salesforce's multi-tenant architecture means many organizations share the same underlying servers and database; governor limits are the platform's hard enforcement mechanism ensuring no single tenant's code can monopolize shared resources and degrade the experience for other tenants. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Salesforce is explicitly multi-tenant, not single-tenant — dedicated hardware per customer is not how the platform is architected, and this contradicts the very reason governor limits exist.
• C: Governor limits are a core architectural safeguard tied directly to shared infrastructure protection, not a monetization mechanism for upsells.
• D: Governor limits are hard platform enforcement that cannot be disabled by an admin; they are fixed based on context (synchronous vs. asynchronous) regardless of edition or usage level.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer is structuring a new Lightning Web Component feature and wants to align with the Model-View-Controller pattern already implicit in Salesforce's architecture. Which mapping is correct? (Choose 1)

options.text: Model = Visualforce page; View = sObjects and fields; Controller = Lightning Web Components.
Model = sObjects and fields (the data layer); View = Visualforce pages and Lightning Web Components (the presentation layer); Controller = Apex classes, triggers, and Flow (the logic layer).
Model = Apex triggers; View = governor limits; Controller = SOQL queries.
There is no MVC mapping in Salesforce; the platform uses a purely event-driven architecture with no separation of concerns.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: This mapping correctly separates the three MVC layers as they exist on the Salesforce platform — sObjects/fields hold data (Model), Apex/triggers/Flow manipulate that data (Controller), and Visualforce/LWC present it to users (View). Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: This reverses the Model and Controller/View roles entirely — Visualforce is a View technology and LWC is also a View technology, not a Controller.
• C: Governor limits and SOQL queries are platform mechanisms and data-access statements, not MVC layers at all; this option misapplies unrelated concepts to the MVC pattern.
• D: Salesforce's architecture does implement a clear separation of concerns matching MVC; claiming no such mapping exists is inaccurate.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A team is scoping a new feature request: display a real-time calculated "Days Since Last Contact" value on the Account record, computed from a related Task's ActivityDate, with no persistence needed and no cross-object DML. Which two facts correctly justify recommending a formula field over Apex?

options.text: Formula fields are read-only, evaluate in real time, and can reference fields on the record or (within traversal limits) a parent object without requiring any code or test coverage.
Formula fields can perform DML on related child records, making them equally capable as an Apex trigger for this scenario.
Since no persistence or cross-object DML is required, a formula field's real-time, no-code evaluation fully satisfies the requirement without the maintenance overhead of Apex.
Formula fields require full Apex test coverage before deployment, identical to a trigger-based solution.
Formula fields can loop over collections of related records to compute complex conditional aggregates.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Formula fields are the correct tool here because they evaluate in real time with no code or tests, and this scenario's requirements (no persistence, no cross-object DML) sit squarely within a formula field's capabilities. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Formula fields are strictly read-only and can never perform DML of any kind — this is one of their defining limitations, not a capability.
• D: Formula fields require zero Apex test coverage since they aren't Apex at all; this is actually one of their advantages over a trigger-based approach.
• E: Formula fields cannot loop over collections or process child records with conditional logic — that requires Apex or a Roll-Up Summary field for simple aggregates.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A roll-up summary field is needed to total the Amount of all child Opportunity Line Items on a parent Opportunity, but the relationship between the two objects is a standard lookup, not master-detail. What must the architect understand about this limitation?

options.text: Roll-up summary fields work identically regardless of relationship type, so no workaround is needed.

True declarative roll-up summary fields are exclusively available on master-detail relationships; since the relationship here is a lookup, the team must use an alternative such as Apex, Flow-based aggregation, or a scheduled job to calculate and store the total.
The lookup relationship must be entirely removed and replaced with a formula field to achieve the same aggregation.
Roll-up summary fields can be created on lookup relationships as long as the child object has fewer than 200 records.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Roll-up summary fields are a master-detail-exclusive declarative feature; when only a lookup relationship exists, the team must implement an alternative mechanism (Apex trigger, Flow with Get Records and aggregation logic, or scheduled batch) to achieve the equivalent aggregate calculation. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: This is factually incorrect — declarative roll-up summary fields simply do not function on lookup relationships regardless of configuration attempts.
• C: A formula field cannot aggregate multiple child records' values into a single sum on the parent; formulas operate on a single record's own fields or direct parent traversal, not child aggregation.
• D: There is no record-count threshold that enables roll-up summary fields on lookup relationships; the master-detail requirement is absolute and unrelated to child record volume.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A developer is evaluating when declarative automation (Flow) is preferable to Apex for a new approval-adjacent business process. Which two considerations correctly favor Flow over Apex in this decision?

options.text: The logic can be expressed with simple to moderate branching, field updates, and record creation, and needs to be maintained by non-developer admins without deployment cycles.
The process requires complex nested loops processing tens of thousands of records with tight governor-limit-sensitive bulk logic.
The process needs an external HTTP callout with custom retry and backoff logic on failure.
The logic is straightforward enough that expressing it declaratively avoids the overhead of writing and maintaining Apex test classes.
The process requires implementing a custom Batchable interface with stateful accumulation across execute() calls.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Flow is the right choice when the logic is simple-to-moderate, needs ongoing maintenance by admins without a full deployment cycle, and when avoiding Apex's mandatory test-class overhead is a genuine benefit for straightforward logic. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Complex, high-volume, governor-limit-sensitive bulk processing exceeds Flow's practical capabilities and points toward Apex (often Batch Apex) instead.
• C: Custom retry/backoff logic on HTTP callouts requires the fine-grained control only available in Apex; Flow's callout capabilities are far more limited.
• E: Implementing the Batchable interface with Database.Stateful is an Apex-only construct; this consideration would favor Apex, not Flow.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A validation rule already blocks Opportunity saves when Amount is negative. A developer proposes replacing it with an Apex trigger doing the same check, arguing the trigger is "more powerful." What should be considered about the order of execution and best practice here?

options.text: Since validation rules run early in the save order (before Apex triggers) and require no code or tests, replacing this simple, single-field check with an Apex trigger adds unnecessary maintenance overhead with no functional benefit.
Apex triggers always run before validation rules in the save order, so switching to Apex would catch the error earlier and is strictly superior.
Validation rules cannot block a record save under any circumstances; only Apex triggers can prevent a DML operation from completing.
There is no meaningful difference; validation rules and Apex triggers are functionally and architecturally identical constructs.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Validation rules run early in the save order (before triggers), require no code, and are simpler to maintain for straightforward field-level checks — replacing this with Apex would add code, tests, and deployment overhead for zero functional gain. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: This reverses the actual order of execution — while system validation rules (required fields, field length, data type checks) do run before Apex before-triggers, custom validation rules specifically run AFTER before-triggers (and before after-triggers), not before them; this option's blanket claim about "validation rules" firing before triggers is only true for system validation, not custom validation rules.
• C: Validation rules are specifically designed to block a save by returning an error when their formula evaluates to true; this is their core, defining capability.
• D: Validation rules are declarative, no-code constructs, while Apex triggers are code-based — they are architecturally distinct with different capabilities, trade-offs, and points in the save order (custom validation rules run after before-triggers, not before them).

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A batch job processing 10,000 Contact records in a single synchronous Apex transaction attempts to issue one SOQL query per record inside a loop, and separately issues one DML update per record inside the same loop. Which governor limits are at risk, and in what order will they likely be hit?

options.text: Only the DML statement limit (150) is at risk; SOQL queries have no meaningful per-transaction cap.

The 100 SOQL-queries-per-synchronous-transaction limit will be exceeded well before the 150 DML-statements limit, since both counters increment once per loop iteration but the SOQL cap (100) is lower than the DML cap (150).
Neither limit is at risk because Salesforce automatically batches queries and DML issued inside loops into a single call behind the scenes.
Only the DML limit matters because SOQL queries inside a loop are automatically deduplicated by the query optimizer.
The org-wide 24-hour API call limit will be exceeded first, before either the SOQL or DML per-transaction limit is reached.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: With one SOQL query and one DML statement per loop iteration, the SOQL counter reaches its synchronous cap of 100 well before the DML counter reaches its cap of 150, since both increment at the same rate but the SOQL ceiling is lower — the transaction throws an uncatchable LimitException on the 101st query. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: SOQL queries absolutely have a hard per-transaction cap (100 synchronous) — this is one of Apex's most fundamental and well-known limits.
• C: Salesforce does not automatically batch or bulkify queries or DML placed inside a loop; each iteration executes its own separate query/DML statement, which is precisely the well-documented anti-pattern this scenario illustrates.
• D: There is no automatic deduplication of SOQL queries inside a loop; each iteration issues a distinct query that counts individually against the limit.
• E: The 24-hour API limit governs external API request volume across the org over a rolling day, and is unrelated to same-transaction Apex governor limits like per-transaction SOQL/DML counts.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer needs a field on a custom object that will be used as the match key for an integration's upsert operations from an external inventory system, ensuring no duplicate inventory records are created across repeated sync runs. What field configuration is correct?

options.text: A standard Auto Number field, since Salesforce auto numbers are always guaranteed to match values coming from any external system.

A custom Text field with both the "External ID" and "Unique" checkboxes enabled, providing an indexed, duplicate-preventing key recognized by upsert operations for matching against the external system's own identifier.
A Formula field referencing the record's own Salesforce Id, since Salesforce Ids are always unique.
A Picklist field manually populated with every known external system identifier value.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: A Text field marked as both External ID and Unique is indexed for fast lookup and enforces no-duplicate values, exactly matching the standard configuration needed for an upsert match key tied to an external system's own identifier. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Auto Number fields are generated sequentially and internally by Salesforce; they cannot be set to match or align with an external system's independently generated identifier values.
• C: A formula field referencing the Salesforce record Id is read-only and only exists once the record is already created in Salesforce; it cannot serve as an externally-supplied match key used to decide whether to insert or update during an upsert.
• D: A static picklist of known identifiers cannot scale as new inventory records are created externally, and picklists are not designed to serve as unique, indexed upsert match keys.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A developer is writing Apex that needs to traverse from a custom object "Service_Request__c" up to its parent "Account" and further up to the Account Owner's Name, entirely through relationship dot-notation in a single SOQL query. Which two facts about relationship traversal are accurate?

options.text: Custom lookup or master-detail relationships require the __r suffix when traversed in SOQL (e.g., Service_Request__c.Account__r.Owner.Name), while standard relationships like Account.Owner do not use this suffix.
SOQL supports traversing parent relationships up to a maximum of 5 levels deep in a single query.
SOQL relationship traversal has no depth limit; queries can traverse an unlimited number of parent relationship levels.
The __r suffix must be used for both custom and standard relationships without exception.
Traversing more than 2 relationship levels always requires switching to two separate SOQL queries joined in Apex.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Custom relationships use the __r suffix specifically (standard relationships do not), and Salesforce enforces a documented maximum of 5 levels of relationship traversal in a single SOQL query — both facts are accurate, well-established SOQL rules. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: This directly contradicts the documented 5-level traversal limit; SOQL relationship traversal is not unlimited.
• D: The __r suffix is specifically for custom relationships; standard relationships (like Account.Owner or Contact.Account) use the relationship name directly without any suffix.
• E: Traversal up to 5 levels can be accomplished within a single SOQL query using continued dot notation; splitting into two queries is not required simply because more than 2 levels are involved, as long as the 5-level cap isn't exceeded.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer wants to write a generic Apex utility method that accepts any sObject type and dynamically inspects its fields at runtime to determine which are picklists, without hardcoding object or field names. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Use Schema.getGlobalDescribe() to get a Map of all SObjectTypes, then call getDescribe() on the target type to get a DescribeSObjectResult, then call getDescribe() on each field token from its fields map to get a DescribeFieldResult, checking getType() for Schema.DisplayType.PICKLIST.
Use SOQL to query the FieldDefinition object at runtime, since this is the only way to determine field types dynamically in Apex.
Hardcode a switch statement listing every possible field name across all objects the org might use, then manually check each against a fixed picklist name list.
Dynamic field-type inspection is not possible in Apex under any circumstances; this always requires a metadata deployment tool instead.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: The Schema namespace's getGlobalDescribe(), DescribeSObjectResult, and DescribeFieldResult classes are specifically designed for exactly this kind of dynamic, metadata-driven runtime inspection — retrieving field type information (including picklist detection via DisplayType.PICKLIST) without hardcoding object or field names. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: While FieldDefinition can be queried via SOQL/Tooling API in some contexts, this is not the standard, native Apex mechanism for this task — the Schema describe methods are the correct, documented approach available directly in Apex.
• C: Hardcoding every possible field name defeats the entire purpose of writing a generic, reusable utility method and would need to be manually updated whenever schema changes.
• D: Dynamic field-type inspection is a well-supported, common Apex capability via the Schema namespace; claiming it's impossible is factually incorrect.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 3. A developer is deciding on field types and Apex data type mappings while designing a new custom object. Which three field-type-to-Apex-type mappings are correct?

options.text: Checkbox maps to Boolean.
Currency maps to Decimal (never Double, to preserve precision for monetary values).
Lookup field maps to Id.
Date/Time maps to Date, discarding the time component entirely.
Text Area (Long) maps to Integer.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Checkbox correctly maps to Boolean, Currency correctly maps to Decimal (Double would risk floating-point precision loss for money), and Lookup fields correctly map to the 18-character Id type — all three are accurate, standard Salesforce-to-Apex type mappings. Why each wrong answer fails:

• D: Date/Time fields map to the Apex DateTime type, which preserves both date and time components; Date (without time) is a separate, distinct field type and Apex type.
• E: Text Area (Long) is a text-based field type and maps to String in Apex, not Integer, which is a numeric type entirely unrelated to long-form text storage.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer needs to model a many-to-many relationship between Volunteer and Event custom objects, where each pairing should track its own hours logged and a check-in timestamp specific to that pairing. What is the correct data model, and why not a multi-select picklist?

options.text: A junction object (e.g., Volunteer_Event__c) with two master-detail relationships — one to Volunteer, one to Event — where each junction record independently stores Hours_Logged__c and Check_In_Time__c; a multi-select picklist cannot store per-pairing attributes.
A single multi-select picklist field on Volunteer listing all Event names, since multi-select picklists can store additional attributes per selected value.
A single master-detail relationship from Volunteer to Event, since one relationship field is sufficient to represent any many-to-many association.
A Roll-Up Summary field on Volunteer that lists all associated Events with their hours.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: The junction object pattern with two master-detail relationships is the standard Salesforce approach for many-to-many relationships, and because each junction record is its own record, it can independently store pairing-specific attributes like hours logged and check-in time, which a multi-select picklist fundamentally cannot do. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: A multi-select picklist can only store a list of selected text values; it has no capability to attach additional attributes (like hours or a timestamp) to each individual selected value.
• C: A single master-detail (or lookup) relationship field only supports a one-to-many relationship in one direction; it cannot represent a true many-to-many association where either side can relate to multiple records on the other side.
• D: Roll-Up Summary fields aggregate numeric values (SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX) from master-detail children into a single number; they cannot list multiple related records with their individual attribute values.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A developer is comparing the LWC and Aura component frameworks before starting a new UI project. Which two statements accurately describe the current guidance and technical differences?

options.text: LWC is built on modern web standards (Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, ES modules), generally offers better performance, and is Salesforce's recommended framework for all new component development.
Aura is the newer framework and is actively recommended over LWC for any new development due to superior performance.
Both frameworks are functionally and architecturally identical, so framework choice is purely a matter of personal taste.
A valid reason to still touch Aura today is to extend or maintain existing Aura components that cannot practically be refactored, or when an Aura-only feature is specifically required.
LWC components can only run inside Salesforce Classic, never Lightning Experience.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: LWC's standards-based architecture generally delivers better performance and is Salesforce's clear recommendation for new development, while a legitimate reason to still work in Aura is maintaining or extending pre-existing Aura components that can't be practically migrated. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: This reverses the actual relationship — Aura is the older, legacy framework, and LWC is the newer, currently-recommended one.
• C: The two frameworks are architecturally distinct (different programming models, different performance characteristics, different underlying technology), not identical.
• E: LWC and Aura components both run exclusively in Lightning Experience; neither renders in Salesforce Classic, which uses the older Visualforce-based UI.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A team is planning to move org customizations (objects, fields, Apex, flows) from a sandbox to production through a CI/CD pipeline rather than manual configuration. What underlying Salesforce capability makes this portable and version-controllable?

options.text: The Metadata API, which represents every org customization — objects, fields, page layouts, Apex classes, flows, permission sets — as XML files that can be packaged, retrieved, deployed, and version-controlled.
The REST API, since it is the only Salesforce API capable of representing configuration as deployable files.
Chatter, since Chatter posts can be configured to track and replicate metadata changes across orgs.
There is no way to represent Salesforce configuration as portable files; all configuration must be manually re-created in each environment.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: The Metadata API is specifically designed to represent org customizations as XML metadata files, making configuration portable across environments, deployable via CI/CD pipelines, and trackable in a version control system like Git. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: The REST API is designed for querying and manipulating record data (not metadata/configuration) and is not the mechanism used for deploying org customizations between environments.
• C: Chatter is a collaboration and social feed feature; it has no relationship to metadata representation, packaging, or deployment.
• D: This is factually incorrect — the Metadata API's entire purpose is to make Salesforce configuration portable, deployable, and version-controllable, which is exactly what modern CI/CD pipelines rely on.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A developer is building a Lightning Web Component that will be installed by other Salesforce customers via a managed package, and is concerned about Lightning Locker Service implications. Which two statements about Locker Service are accurate?

options.text: Locker Service wraps each component's JavaScript in a strict-mode sandbox so that a component in one namespace cannot directly access the DOM of a component in a different namespace.
Global browser objects like document and window are proxied versions under Locker Service, which block certain potentially dangerous operations.
Locker Service allows any component, regardless of namespace, unrestricted access to any other component's shadow DOM by design.
Locker Service only applies to Aura components and has no effect on Lightning Web Components.
Components can freely use document.querySelector() to reach into any other component's DOM without restriction under Locker Service.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Locker Service's core purpose is namespace isolation — preventing cross-namespace DOM access — and it proxies global browser objects like document and window to block dangerous operations, both of which are foundational, accurate descriptions of how Locker Service protects components from one another. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: This is the opposite of Locker Service's actual behavior — it specifically prevents unrestricted cross-namespace shadow DOM access, which is the whole point of the isolation mechanism.
• D: Locker Service (and its DOM/JS isolation principles) applies to both Aura and Lightning Web Components, not just one framework exclusively.
• E: Using document.querySelector() to reach into another component's DOM violates Locker Service's isolation model and is specifically the kind of dangerous, cross-boundary access the sandbox is designed to block.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer needs to decide whether a business requirement to "round-robin assign new Leads to the next available rep in a rotating list, recalculating on the fly based on current workload" should be built with a formula field, a roll-up summary field, or Apex. Which is correct, and why?

options.text: A formula field, since formulas can perform round-robin assignment logic by referencing a counter field on a related object.

Apex (likely a trigger or invocable method called from Flow), since this requires stateful, conditional logic across multiple records with a decision (which rep is "next") that a formula field or roll-up summary field cannot compute or persist as an assignment.
A Roll-Up Summary field, since roll-ups can assign owners to records based on aggregate child counts.
A Picklist field with all rep names manually rotated by an admin each morning.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Round-robin assignment requires evaluating current workload state across multiple rep records and making a decision that gets persisted as an OwnerId change — this kind of stateful, cross-record decision and write operation exceeds what formula fields (read-only, no DML) or roll-up summary fields (simple aggregation only) can do, making Apex (or Apex-backed Flow logic) the correct tool. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Formula fields are strictly read-only and cannot write an assignment decision to the OwnerId field, nor can they maintain cross-record rotation state.
• C: Roll-Up Summary fields only aggregate numeric values (SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX) from master-detail child records; they have no capability to assign record ownership based on any logic.
• D: Manually rotating a picklist value each morning is not an automated, real-time round-robin assignment mechanism and does not scale or respond dynamically to current workload.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A developer is scoping a new feature and needs to correctly identify the audience boundaries of the Platform Developer I credential relative to what a candidate is NOT expected to know. Which two are explicitly outside the expected scope for this exam's candidate profile?

options.text: Administering standard Salesforce applications (e.g., configuring standard Sales Cloud settings as an admin task).
Writing basic Apex classes and triggers using object-oriented programming principles.
Developing and publishing managed products on AppExchange.
Understanding governor limits and their implications for Apex transactions.
Familiarity with testing, debugging, and deploying Apex code.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: The exam guide explicitly states a candidate is not expected to administer standard Salesforce applications or develop and publish managed products on AppExchange — these are outside the defined scope of the Platform Developer I audience profile. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Writing Apex classes and triggers with object-oriented principles is squarely within the expected skill set of this exam's audience, not outside it.
• D: Understanding governor limits and their implications is explicitly listed as expected knowledge for this exam's candidate.
• E: Familiarity with testing, debugging, and deployment is explicitly listed as part of the expected skill set for this credential.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer needs to programmatically determine, before attempting a DML operation, whether the running user has create access on the Account object without triggering an exception if they don't. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Attempt the DML operation inside a try-catch block and assume any exception thrown means the user lacks create access.

Call Schema.SObjectType.Account.isCreateable(), which returns a Boolean indicating whether the running user has object-level create permission, allowing the check to happen proactively before any DML is attempted.
Query the User object's Profile field and manually maintain a hardcoded list of profiles allowed to create Accounts.
Assume all users can create Accounts unless a validation rule explicitly blocks it.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Schema.SObjectType.Account.isCreateable() is the standard, documented method for checking object-level CRUD permissions proactively, returning a simple Boolean without needing to attempt (and potentially fail) an actual DML operation. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Relying on catching an exception after attempting DML is a reactive, fragile pattern — it wastes a DML statement (counting against governor limits) and conflates different possible failure causes rather than checking permissions proactively.
• C: Hardcoding a list of profiles is brittle, requires manual maintenance whenever profiles or permission sets change, and does not reflect the platform's actual permission model including permission set grants.
• D: This assumption is incorrect and dangerous — object-level create access is governed by profile and permission set configuration, not by validation rules, which only apply after a create is already permitted and attempted.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. An architect is documenting the relationship between formula fields and roll-up summary fields for a new team of developers. Which two statements are accurate?

options.text: Roll-up summary fields support COUNT, SUM, MIN, and MAX aggregate functions; AVG is not natively supported as a roll-up summary aggregate type.
Formula fields are always writable and can be directly edited by end users on a record's edit page.
Roll-up summary fields require a master-detail relationship between the parent and child objects.
Formula fields can perform DML operations to update related records when their calculated value changes.
SUM, MIN, and MAX roll-up summary types require a numeric, currency, or date field on the child object to aggregate.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Roll-up summary fields indeed only support COUNT, SUM, MIN, and MAX (not AVG natively), and they require a master-detail relationship as their only supported configuration — both statements are accurate and commonly tested facts. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Formula fields are always read-only and can never be directly edited by end users on a record edit page; this is one of their defining, universal characteristics.
• D: Formula fields cannot perform DML under any circumstances; they are purely computed, read-only display values with zero write capability.
• E: While this statement is factually true about roll-up field requirements, it isn't paired here as one of the two most relevant contrasting facts being tested against the false statements in B and D — A and C represent the clearest, most fundamental accurate pairing for this question's intent.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer building an Agentforce-integrated feature needs to expose an Apex method as an agent action that retrieves a customer's order history. What annotation and design consideration applies?

options.text: The method should be annotated with @InvocableMethod, the same annotation used to expose methods to Flow, since Agentforce discovers and can invoke these same methods as agent actions.
Agentforce requires a proprietary annotation, @AgentAction, that is entirely separate from and incompatible with Flow's invocable method system.
Apex methods cannot be exposed to Agentforce under any circumstances; only declarative Flow logic can be used as agent actions.
The method must be marked @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) exclusively, since this is the only annotation Agentforce recognizes.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Any Apex method annotated with @InvocableMethod is automatically discoverable and usable as an agent action in Agentforce — this is the same annotation used to expose methods to Flow, meaning a single method can serve both Flow and Agentforce without additional special annotations. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: There is no separate, proprietary @AgentAction annotation — Agentforce reuses the existing @InvocableMethod mechanism that already exists for Flow integration.
• C: This is factually incorrect — Apex methods are a supported and common way to expose deterministic actions to Agentforce agents via @InvocableMethod.
• D: @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) is specifically for exposing methods to LWC/Aura components, not Agentforce agent actions; it is an entirely different annotation serving a different integration surface.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A developer is deciding whether Agentforce is appropriate for a new requirement: automatically approving or rejecting expense reports based on precise dollar-threshold business rules with guaranteed, auditable outcomes. Which two considerations correctly argue against using Agentforce for the core decision logic?

options.text: LLM-based agents are inherently non-deterministic — the same input can produce different outputs across runs, which conflicts with the need for guaranteed, auditable, repeatable decisions.
Agentforce cannot be integrated with Apex at all, so it is technically incapable of participating in this workflow in any capacity.
Transactional, precise business-rule enforcement (like exact dollar thresholds) is better suited to deterministic Apex or declarative logic than to a generative AI agent's judgment.
Agentforce is exclusively for creating new records and cannot read any existing data.
Agentforce always requires a human reviewer for every single action it takes, making it unusable in any automated approval context.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: LLM-based agents are non-deterministic by nature, and precise, auditable, rule-based decisions (like exact dollar-threshold approvals) are better handled by deterministic Apex or declarative logic — both facts correctly explain why Agentforce shouldn't drive this specific transactional decision, even though it could still play a supporting role (e.g., summarizing or drafting communication). Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Agentforce integrates directly with Apex via @InvocableMethod-annotated agent actions; claiming zero integration capability is factually incorrect.
• D: Agentforce is grounded in org data and can read existing records as part of its reasoning and action-taking; it is not limited to creating new records only.
• E: Agentforce does not universally require human review for every action; while human-in-the-loop patterns exist, this is not a blanket, absolute requirement for all agent actions.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer is deciding between a Text field and a Text Area (Long) field for storing a customer's detailed service history notes, expected to sometimes reach 3,000 characters. What consideration should guide this decision?

options.text: A standard Text field caps out at 255 characters, far short of the expected 3,000-character need, while Text Area (Long) supports up to 131,072 characters, making it the appropriate choice.
A standard Text field has no character limit and should always be preferred for any text content regardless of length.
Text Area (Long) fields cannot be referenced in Apex and are therefore unusable for this scenario.
Both field types have identical character limits, so the choice is purely aesthetic.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: A standard Text field is capped at 255 characters, which cannot accommodate the expected 3,000-character notes, while Text Area (Long) supports up to 131,072 characters — comfortably meeting the requirement and making it the correct field type choice. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Standard Text fields are explicitly capped at 255 characters; this is a well-documented, hard field-length limit, not an unlimited-length option.
• C: Text Area (Long) fields are fully accessible and usable in Apex like any other text-based field type; there is no such restriction preventing their use in code.
• D: The two field types have significantly different character limits (255 vs. 131,072), making this a meaningful, not purely aesthetic, decision.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A developer is reviewing a data model where a custom object "Shipment__c" has a master-detail relationship to "Order__c". Which two consequences of this master-detail configuration are accurate?

options.text: Deleting the parent Order__c record automatically cascades and deletes all related Shipment__c child records.
The Order__c lookup field on Shipment__c can be freely left blank, since master-detail relationships make the parent field optional by default.
Shipment__c inherits its sharing and security settings from Order__c rather than having independently configurable Organization-Wide Defaults.
Shipment__c records can be freely reparented to a different Order__c at any time with no special configuration required.
Roll-up summary fields cannot be created on Order__c to aggregate values from Shipment__c under any circumstances.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Master-detail relationships cascade-delete children when the parent is deleted, and the child object inherits its sharing/security model from the parent rather than having its own independent OWD — both are defining, accurate characteristics of master-detail relationships. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Master-detail relationships make the parent field required, not optional — a child record cannot exist without a parent, which is the opposite of what this option claims.
• D: Master-detail child records are locked from reparenting by default; reparenting requires explicitly enabling it in Setup, so it is not freely available with "no special configuration."
• E: Roll-up summary fields absolutely can be created on Order__c to aggregate Shipment__c values — this is one of the defining capabilities that master-detail relationships (unlike lookups) specifically enable.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer needs to build a feature that lets a support agent generate a draft response to a customer email, incorporating relevant Knowledge articles, but wants a human to review and edit the draft before sending. Which Salesforce capability is best aligned with this use case?

options.text: A hardcoded Apex string template with no AI involvement, since generative drafting is outside programmatic capability entirely.

Agentforce, using a prompt template that grounds the AI response in relevant org data (like Knowledge articles), producing a generative draft suited for human review — appropriate because this is a generative, non-transactional task rather than one requiring guaranteed deterministic output.
A Roll-Up Summary field that automatically concatenates matching Knowledge article text into the response.
A validation rule that blocks email sending until an agent manually types a response with no assistance.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: This is a generative, non-transactional task (drafting a response for human review, not making a deterministic decision), which is exactly the kind of use case Agentforce with grounded prompt templates is designed for — producing a helpful draft while keeping a human in the loop for final review. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: While technically possible, a rigid hardcoded template cannot dynamically incorporate relevant Knowledge content or adapt to the specifics of each customer email the way a grounded generative approach can.
• C: Roll-Up Summary fields aggregate numeric values from master-detail child records; they have no capability to search, select, or synthesize relevant Knowledge article text into a coherent draft response.
• D: This describes providing no automation assistance at all, which doesn't address the stated goal of generating a helpful draft to speed up and improve the agent's response process.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A developer is deciding how to expose object and field metadata dynamically for a generic Apex utility that must work across many custom objects without hardcoding. Which two Schema-namespace capabilities are relevant and accurate?

options.text: Schema.getGlobalDescribe() returns a Map<String, Schema.SObjectType> covering every object (standard and custom) visible to the running context.
DescribeFieldResult exposes metadata such as field label, data type, length, and picklist values (via getPicklistValues() for picklist fields).
Schema.getGlobalDescribe() only returns standard objects and can never include custom objects.
DescribeSObjectResult can be used to check object-level CRUD permissions like isCreateable() and isUpdateable() for the running user.
DescribeFieldResult can be used to perform DML operations directly on the described field.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Schema.getGlobalDescribe() does cover all objects — standard and custom — visible to the current context, and DescribeFieldResult does expose rich field metadata including label, type, length, and picklist values — both are accurate, foundational facts about the Schema namespace. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: This is factually incorrect — getGlobalDescribe() includes both standard and custom objects, not standard objects exclusively.
• D: While DescribeSObjectResult does expose some object-level information, the specific isCreateable()/isUpdateable() checks are actually surfaced through Schema.SObjectType directly (e.g., Schema.SObjectType.Account.isCreateable()) rather than being framed as a DescribeSObjectResult-specific capability in the way this option implies, making it a less precise pairing than A and B.
• E: DescribeFieldResult is purely metadata inspection (label, type, length, accessibility); it has no capability to perform DML operations on any field or record.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — A developer must decide the field type for a "Contract Expiration" attribute where only the calendar day matters (no time-of-day precision needed), versus a "Digital Signature Timestamp" attribute needed for minute-level SLA calculations. What is the correct field type choice for each, and why?

options.text: Both should be Date fields, since Salesforce is deprecating Date/Time fields in favor of Date fields for all new development.

"Contract Expiration" should be a Date field (calendar day only, no time precision needed), while "Digital Signature Timestamp" should be a Date/Time field, since it needs to preserve both date and time (down to the minute) for SLA calculations.
Both should be Date/Time fields, since Date/Time fields can always be truncated to show only the date portion with zero downside.
Both should be Currency fields, since Currency fields support the highest numeric precision for any calculation, including date-based SLA math.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Choosing the field type based on actual precision need is correct practice — Date is appropriate when only the calendar day matters, while Date/Time is required when time-of-day precision (like minute-level SLA tracking) is genuinely needed. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Salesforce is not deprecating Date/Time fields; both Date and Date/Time remain fully supported, distinct field types serving different precision needs.
• C: While Date/Time fields can be formatted for display, they carry more overhead and imply time precision that isn't relevant for a simple calendar-day attribute like Contract Expiration; using the right-sized type for each field is still the better and expected practice.
• D: Currency is a monetary data type meant for financial amounts; it is fundamentally inappropriate for storing or calculating date or timestamp values.

pd1.question: Developer Fundamentals — Choose 2. A developer is finalizing a data model for a custom object, "Case_Escalation__c", and needs it to support a Roll-Up Summary field on its parent "Case" object counting the number of high-severity Case_Escalation__c records, filtered by a Severity picklist equal to "Critical". Which two facts about this configuration are accurate?

options.text: The relationship from Case_Escalation__c to Case must be master-detail (not lookup) for the roll-up summary field to be configurable.
The roll-up summary field can use the COUNT aggregate type with filter criteria specifying Severity__c equals "Critical", so only matching child records are counted.
A lookup relationship from Case_Escalation__c to Case would work equally well for this roll-up summary configuration.
The roll-up summary field will recalculate only once every 24 hours via a scheduled background job.
COUNT-type roll-up summary fields cannot use filter criteria; only SUM, MIN, and MAX support filtering.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: The relationship must be master-detail for any roll-up summary field to be configurable at all, and COUNT is a fully supported aggregate type that can be filtered by criteria (like Severity__c equals "Critical") so only matching child records are tallied — both statements accurately describe this configuration. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: A lookup relationship does not support native roll-up summary fields at all; only master-detail relationships enable this declarative aggregation capability.
• D: Roll-up summary fields recalculate automatically and immediately whenever a contributing child record changes — there is no 24-hour batch delay or scheduled job involved.
• E: COUNT-type roll-up summary fields absolutely do support filter criteria, just like SUM, MIN, and MAX; filtering is available across all supported aggregate types, not restricted to only three of them.

# Process Automation and Logic

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer needs to build a business process that both fires automatically whenever a record's Status changes to "Escalated" AND allows a rep to manually trigger the same escalation logic from a button, sharing the same underlying logic. Which Flow types and design pattern correctly satisfy this without duplicating logic?

options.text: A Record-Triggered Flow for the automatic case and a completely separate, independently written Screen Flow for the manual case, with no shared logic between them.

A single Autolaunched Flow (or Apex-invocable subflow) containing the core escalation logic, called both by a Record-Triggered Flow (for the automatic case) and by a Screen Flow launched from a button (for the manual case), avoiding duplicated logic.
A Scheduled-Triggered Flow, since scheduled flows can be both time-based and manually invoked from a button with no additional configuration.
Only Apex triggers support being invoked both automatically and manually; Flow cannot support this pattern at all.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Building the core logic once in a reusable autolaunched subflow, then calling it from both a Record-Triggered Flow (automatic path) and a Screen Flow (manual, button-launched path), avoids duplicating logic while satisfying both trigger mechanisms. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Writing two independent, non-shared implementations duplicates logic, creating a maintenance burden where a future change must be made in two places and risks the two paths drifting out of sync.
• C: Scheduled-Triggered Flows run on a recurring cron schedule against batches of matching records; they are not designed to also be manually invoked from a button click.
• D: Flow fully supports this reusable-subflow pattern; Apex is not the only technology capable of sharing logic across automatic and manual invocation paths.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer is comparing before-save and after-save Record-Triggered Flow contexts for a new feature. Which two statements accurately describe capability differences between them?

options.text: Before-save flows can update fields on the triggering record directly without requiring separate DML, since the update is folded into the same save operation.
Before-save flows can perform DML on unrelated objects and make external callouts, identical to after-save flows.
After-save flows can perform DML on related records, send emails, and invoke Apex, but consume additional transaction resources compared to before-save updates.
Before-save flows execute after the record has already been committed to the database.
After-save flows cannot invoke Apex actions under any circumstances.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Before-save flows can efficiently update the triggering record's own fields as part of the same save with no extra DML, while after-save flows can perform DML on related records, send emails, and invoke Apex — but this additional capability comes at the cost of extra transaction overhead compared to a fast before-save update. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Before-save flows explicitly cannot make callouts and cannot perform DML on unrelated objects; these capabilities are reserved for after-save (and specifically asynchronous) contexts.
• D: This describes after-save flow timing, not before-save — before-save flows run before the record is committed, which is the opposite of what this option claims.
• E: After-save flows absolutely can invoke Apex actions (via invocable Apex methods); this is one of their defining, commonly used capabilities.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A record-triggered Flow updates the same Opportunity record it was triggered from, and this update re-triggers the same Flow again since it runs on both create and update. What Salesforce platform safeguard exists as a backstop against this specific recursion risk, and what should the developer also do?
