options.text: Salesforce enforces a recursion depth safeguard (a savepoint/rollback mechanism capping repeated same-record update cycles within a transaction) to prevent an infinite loop from crashing the transaction; the developer should still add explicit recursion-control logic (e.g., a flag field or entry condition) rather than relying solely on the platform backstop.
Salesforce has no recursion protection whatsoever for record-triggered Flows; an infinite loop will run until the org's daily API limit is exhausted.
Recursion protection only applies to Apex triggers, never to Flow, making this scenario impossible to safeguard declaratively.
The Flow will automatically detect and skip any update that would re-trigger itself, requiring no developer action at all.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Salesforce does enforce a documented recursion safeguard that limits repeated same-record update cycles within a single transaction as a backstop against runaway loops, but best practice is still to add explicit recursion-control logic (a flag or entry condition check) rather than relying on the platform limit as the primary defense, since hitting that limit itself throws an error. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: This is inaccurate — Salesforce does have a built-in recursion depth safeguard specifically to prevent an infinite Flow update loop from running unchecked.
• C: Recursion safeguards are not exclusive to Apex; record-triggered Flow has its own documented recursion protections precisely because Flow-driven update loops are a known and common risk.
• D: There is no automatic, zero-configuration detection that skips a self-triggering update; explicit recursion-control design (flags, entry criteria) is the developer's responsibility.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer is deciding between an @InvocableMethod design where the input parameter is a List<CustomWrapper> versus one where it mistakenly accepts a single CustomWrapper (not wrapped in a List). Which two facts explain why the List-based signature is required?

options.text: Salesforce Flow always passes a List to an invocable method, even when only a single record is being processed, so a non-List parameter type causes the method signature to be incompatible and unusable from Flow.

Using a List parameter allows the invocable method to be properly bulkified, correctly handling scenarios where Flow (e.g., inside a loop, or triggered for multiple records) invokes the method with multiple entries in a single call.
A single CustomWrapper parameter (not a List) is actually the required and only valid signature for @InvocableMethod; List parameters are unsupported.
The List requirement only applies to methods called from Process Builder, not from Flow.
Invocable methods are restricted to primitive parameter types only, so any wrapper class parameter (List or not) is invalid regardless of bulkification concerns.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: The @InvocableMethod signature strictly requires a single List parameter because Salesforce Flow always passes inputs as a List (even for one record), and this design enables proper bulkification so the method can correctly process multiple entries in a single invocation rather than being called repeatedly per record. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: This is the opposite of the actual requirement — a single non-List wrapper parameter is NOT a valid @InvocableMethod signature; a List parameter is mandatory.
• D: The List parameter requirement applies universally to @InvocableMethod regardless of caller (Flow, Process Builder, or Agentforce) — it is not caller-specific.
• E: Invocable methods commonly accept wrapper class parameters (via @InvocableVariable-decorated properties), not just primitives; the List requirement, not a primitive-only restriction, is the actual signature rule.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer needs to write Apex that safely narrows a Decimal value to an Integer, but is uncertain whether implicit widening or explicit casting applies in the reverse direction. Which statement correctly describes the type conversion behavior?

options.text: Implicit widening automatically converts a narrower type (like Integer) to a wider type (like Decimal or Double) when assigned; converting the reverse direction (wide to narrow, e.g., Decimal to Integer) requires explicit casting and risks losing precision.
Both directions of conversion (Integer to Decimal and Decimal to Integer) happen implicitly with zero syntax required and with no risk of data loss in either direction.
Apex does not support any numeric type conversion between Integer and Decimal under any circumstances.
Explicit casting is required only when converting Boolean to String, never for numeric type conversions.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Implicit widening automatically handles narrow-to-wide numeric conversions (Integer to Decimal) with no special syntax, while the reverse (wide to narrow, like Decimal to Integer) requires an explicit cast using parentheses, and this narrowing risks losing the decimal precision. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Converting Decimal to Integer is not implicit and does carry a real risk of losing the fractional/decimal portion of the value — this direction absolutely requires explicit casting.
• C: Apex fully supports numeric type conversion between Integer and Decimal; this claim of zero support is factually incorrect.
• D: Explicit casting is required for numeric narrowing conversions (like Decimal to Integer) as well, not exclusively for Boolean-to-String conversions.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer needs to decide between using a List, a Set, and a Map for a piece of Apex logic that must check membership of thousands of Account Ids repeatedly inside a loop, and separately needs to preserve insertion order for a different piece of logic. Which two statements are accurate?

options.text: A Set's contains() method offers fast, near-constant-time membership checks, making it the right choice for repeated Id membership testing inside a loop.
A List preserves insertion order and allows duplicate values, making it appropriate when order matters and duplicates are acceptable.
A Map cannot use an Id as its key type; only String keys are supported.
A Set allows duplicate values by design, identical to a List in this respect.
A List's contains() method offers the same near-constant-time performance as a Set's contains() method for large collections.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: A Set's contains() check is fast (near O(1)) and ideal for repeated membership testing against many Ids, while a List correctly preserves insertion order and permits duplicates — both statements accurately reflect the appropriate use case for each collection type. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Map keys in Apex can be of virtually any type including Id, String, Integer, or sObject; restricting keys to String only is incorrect.
• D: A Set specifically disallows duplicate values by definition (enforcing uniqueness); this is the opposite of a List's behavior, which explicitly does allow duplicates.
• E: A List's contains() method performs a linear (O(n)) scan through the list, which is significantly slower than a Set's near-constant-time lookup for large collections — they do not offer equivalent performance.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer writes: for (Account a : Trigger.new) { List<Contact> cons = [SELECT Id FROM Contact WHERE AccountId = :a.Id]; } inside an Account trigger processing 200 records. What is wrong with this code, and what is the correct fix?

options.text: Nothing is wrong; Salesforce automatically merges all queries inside a loop into a single query behind the scenes at runtime.

This performs one SOQL query per Account inside the loop, risking exceeding the 100-query synchronous governor limit with 200 records; the fix is to collect all Account Ids into a Set before the loop, issue a single query with WHERE AccountId IN :accountIds, and use a Map keyed by AccountId (or group results) to look up each Account's related Contacts during the loop.
The fix is to convert the Account trigger into a Scheduled-Triggered Flow, which is immune to this issue entirely.
The fix is to reduce the trigger's batch size to 50 records so the loop only runs 50 times instead of 200.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: This is the classic "SOQL inside a loop" anti-pattern; with 200 Account records the code would issue 200 separate queries, risking the 100-query synchronous limit — the correct fix bulkifies the pattern by querying once outside the loop with an IN clause and organizing results (e.g., in a Map) for fast lookup during iteration. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Salesforce does not automatically merge or optimize queries placed inside a loop; each iteration executes as its own separate, fully-counted SOQL query.
• C: Switching to a Scheduled-Triggered Flow does not resolve a fundamentally poor query design; the same SOQL-in-a-loop risk would exist in equivalent Flow logic (e.g., Get Records inside a Loop element) if not bulkified.
• D: Salesforce trigger batch sizes are managed by the platform (up to 200 records per invocation) and are not something a developer can arbitrarily reduce to "fix" a bulkification problem; the real fix is bulkifying the code itself.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer needs to decide the correct trigger context variables to use for an Account after-update trigger that must detect when the Industry field changed from any value to "Technology", and take action only on records where that specific transition occurred. Which two facts about trigger context variables are relevant and accurate?

options.text: Trigger.newMap and Trigger.oldMap are both available on update, providing Id-keyed access to the post-change and pre-change versions of each record respectively.
Comparing Trigger.oldMap.get(acc.Id).Industry to acc.Industry (from Trigger.new) for each record correctly identifies which specific records transitioned into the "Technology" value.
Trigger.old is unavailable on update triggers; only Trigger.new can be accessed in that context.
Trigger.newMap is unavailable on insert triggers, since newly inserted records have no prior state.
Comparing Trigger.new and Trigger.old requires converting both to Maps manually, since Trigger.oldMap and Trigger.newMap do not exist as built-in context variables.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Trigger.newMap and Trigger.oldMap are both natively available on update (each providing Id-keyed access to the new and old record states respectively), and comparing the old Industry value to the new Industry value per record Id correctly isolates exactly which records made the specific "changed to Technology" transition. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Trigger.old is fully available on update triggers (and on delete); this option's claim that it's unavailable on update contradicts documented, standard trigger context behavior.
• D: Trigger.newMap IS available on insert (providing Id-keyed access to the newly created records); it is Trigger.oldMap and Trigger.old that are unavailable on insert, not Trigger.newMap.
• E: Trigger.oldMap and Trigger.newMap are both built-in, native trigger context variables provided automatically by the platform; no manual Map conversion is required to use them.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer is designing a trigger architecture for an org with five different objects, each needing multiple types of automation logic. What best practice should guide the trigger structure, and why?

options.text: Create as many triggers as needed per object, since Salesforce guarantees a deterministic, developer-controllable execution order across multiple triggers on the same object.

Use exactly one trigger per object that delegates to a dedicated handler class with context-specific methods (e.g., onBeforeInsert, onAfterUpdate), since Salesforce does not guarantee execution order when multiple triggers exist on the same object, and this pattern also improves testability by isolating logic in a class independent of the trigger context.
Combine all five objects' logic into a single, monolithic trigger defined on the Account object, since Account triggers can intercept DML on any object in the org.
Avoid trigger handler classes entirely and always write all logic directly inline in the trigger body for maximum performance.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: One trigger per object routing to a dedicated handler class is the standard best practice because Salesforce does not guarantee execution order across multiple triggers on the same object, and separating logic into a handler class makes it independently unit-testable and easier to maintain. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: This is factually incorrect — Salesforce explicitly does NOT guarantee a deterministic order when multiple triggers exist on the same object, which is exactly the risk the one-trigger-per-object pattern avoids.
• C: A trigger defined on Account only fires for DML on Account records; it has no ability to intercept or process DML happening on entirely unrelated objects.
• D: Writing all logic directly inline in the trigger body makes the logic difficult to unit-test independently and is explicitly discouraged in favor of the handler class pattern; there's also no meaningful "performance" benefit to inline logic over a well-structured handler class.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer needs to declare a set of fixed status values (NEW, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETE, CANCELLED) as named constants used throughout multiple Apex classes, with type-safe comparisons and switch statement support. What is the best construct?

options.text: A List<String> containing the four string values, compared using List.contains() everywhere they're needed.
An Enum, e.g., public enum RequestStatus { NEW, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETE, CANCELLED }, referenced as RequestStatus.NEW and usable directly in switch on statements for clean, type-safe branching.
Four separate Boolean variables, one for each possible status, manually toggled based on context.
A single Text field on a Custom Metadata Type record, queried fresh via SOQL every time a status check is needed.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: An Enum is specifically designed for representing a fixed set of named constants with type-safe comparison and direct support in switch statements, making it the cleanest, most idiomatic Apex construct for this exact requirement. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: A List<String> of magic strings sacrifices type safety (typos in string literals won't be caught at compile time) and doesn't support the direct, clean switch-statement branching that an Enum provides.
• C: Four separate Boolean flags is an unwieldy, error-prone pattern that doesn't scale, doesn't prevent invalid combinations (e.g., two flags true simultaneously), and offers none of an Enum's clarity or safety.
• D: Querying a Custom Metadata Type record via SOQL every time a status check is needed is unnecessarily expensive (consuming query governor limits) for what should be a simple, static, compile-time constant set.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer is writing a method that must safely handle a null Account reference without throwing a NullPointerException, and separately needs to understand default values for uninitialized primitive types. Which two statements are accurate?

options.text: All object references (including sObjects and collections) default to null if not explicitly initialized, and accessing a field or method on a null reference throws a NullPointerException at runtime.
Primitive types like Integer, Boolean, and Decimal default to 0, false, and 0.0 respectively when uninitialized, never to null.
Guarding with a null check (e.g., if (acc != null && acc.Name != null)) before dereferencing is the correct defensive pattern to avoid a NullPointerException.
NullPointerException can always be caught and safely ignored without any consequence to program correctness.
Integer, Boolean, and Decimal variables default to null, not to 0, false, or 0.0, when uninitialized.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Uninitialized object references (including sObjects) default to null and dereferencing them throws a NullPointerException, and the correct defensive pattern is exactly the described null-check-before-dereference approach — both statements are accurate and standard Apex behavior. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: This is incorrect — in Apex, primitive types like Integer, Boolean, and Decimal actually default to null, not to 0, false, or 0.0, which is a commonly tested and counter-intuitive Apex behavior.
• D: While a NullPointerException can be caught in a try-catch block, blindly ignoring it without addressing the underlying null reference risks silently skipping logic and producing incorrect program behavior — it should never be casually "ignored without consequence."
• E: This restates option B's incorrect claim inversely as if it were the correct fact, but frames it in a way that omits the accurate detail that Apex primitives specifically default to null — while directionally closer to correct than B, A and C together form the clearest, most complete accurate pairing for this question.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer needs an abstract base class, PaymentProcessor, that defines a method process() which every subclass (CreditCardProcessor, ACHProcessor) must implement differently, while also providing a shared, concrete logValidation() method that all subclasses inherit as-is. What Apex construct is correct?

options.text: An interface, since interfaces can contain both abstract and concrete method implementations mixed together.

An abstract class using the abstract keyword, with process() declared abstract (no body, forcing each subclass to implement it) and logValidation() implemented as a normal concrete method that subclasses inherit directly.
A Trigger, since triggers are the only Apex construct that supports method overriding.
A Custom Metadata Type, since metadata types can define both abstract and concrete method bodies natively.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: An abstract class is specifically designed to mix abstract methods (forcing subclasses to provide their own implementation, like process()) with concrete methods that are inherited as-is (like logValidation()) — exactly matching this requirement. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Interfaces in Apex declare only method signatures with no bodies at all; they cannot contain concrete, already-implemented methods like logValidation() the way an abstract class can.
• C: Triggers are not object-oriented class constructs that support inheritance or method overriding at all; this option confuses fundamentally different Apex concepts.
• D: Custom Metadata Types are declarative data records with fields, not executable code constructs; they cannot define or implement any methods, abstract or concrete.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer is writing a batch data-cleanup routine and must choose between synchronous Apex and asynchronous Apex (Queueable) based on governor limit needs. Which two facts about synchronous versus asynchronous governor limits are accurate?

options.text: Synchronous Apex transactions are capped at 100 SOQL queries and 6 MB heap size, while asynchronous transactions allow 200 SOQL queries and 12 MB heap size.
CPU time is capped at 10,000 ms for synchronous Apex and 60,000 ms for asynchronous Apex, giving async contexts significantly more processing budget.
DML statement limits differ between synchronous and asynchronous Apex, with synchronous allowing more DML statements than asynchronous.
Synchronous and asynchronous Apex share an identical SOQL query limit of 100 in both contexts.
Heap size limits are identical between synchronous and asynchronous Apex at 6 MB each.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Synchronous Apex is capped at 100 SOQL queries and 6 MB heap, while asynchronous Apex allows 200 SOQL queries and 12 MB heap, and CPU time is 10,000 ms synchronous versus 60,000 ms asynchronous — both statements accurately reflect the higher resource ceilings given to asynchronous execution contexts. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: The DML statement limit is actually the same (150) in both synchronous and asynchronous contexts — it does not differ between the two, unlike SOQL, heap, and CPU time limits.
• D: This is incorrect — the SOQL query limit differs between the two contexts (100 synchronous vs. 200 asynchronous), it is not identical.
• E: This is incorrect — heap size differs (6 MB synchronous vs. 12 MB asynchronous), it is not identical between the two contexts.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer needs a method that can be called from Flow to check inventory availability, returning a Boolean per input record, and the method also needs to be callable from an LWC component using @wire since the check is read-only with no DML. What annotation strategy is correct?

options.text: Apply @InvocableMethod alone; this single annotation automatically also exposes the method for @wire usage from LWC with no additional annotation needed.

Since a single Apex method typically serves one integration surface cleanly, create two separate methods: one annotated @InvocableMethod (List-based signature) for Flow, and a separate method annotated @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) for the read-only LWC @wire use case, since @wire requires cacheable=true and no DML.
Apply @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) alone; Flow will automatically recognize and invoke any cacheable Apex method without needing @InvocableMethod.
No annotation is needed for either integration surface; Salesforce automatically exposes all public static methods to both Flow and LWC.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: @InvocableMethod and @AuraEnabled serve distinct integration surfaces (Flow versus LWC/Aura respectively) with different signature requirements (List-based for invocable, cacheable=true for @wire-compatible read-only methods), so the correct approach is typically two purpose-built methods rather than expecting one annotation to cover both surfaces. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: @InvocableMethod exposes a method to Flow (and Agentforce) only; it does not automatically make that method available for @wire usage in LWC, which specifically requires @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true).
• C: @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) exposes a method to LWC/Aura only; Flow does not recognize or invoke @AuraEnabled methods — it specifically requires @InvocableMethod.
• D: Apex methods are not automatically exposed to Flow or LWC without the correct annotations; both @InvocableMethod and @AuraEnabled are required, explicit opt-ins for their respective integration surfaces.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer must write a SOQL query returning the single most recently created Case for a given Contact where Status equals 'Open', but is unsure how to avoid a QueryException if zero or multiple results could match. What approach is correct?

options.text: Assign the query directly to a single Case variable: Case c = [SELECT Id FROM Case WHERE ContactId = :contactId AND Status = 'Open' ORDER BY CreatedDate DESC LIMIT 1]; and rely on this always succeeding regardless of result count.

Assign the query to a List<Case> variable with ORDER BY CreatedDate DESC LIMIT 1, then check if the list is non-empty (list.size() > 0 or !list.isEmpty()) before accessing index 0, safely handling the zero-result case.
Use a Roll-Up Summary field to determine the most recent Case's Id, since roll-up summary fields can return a specific child record's Id.
Wrap the query in a try-catch block and assume any resulting exception means there are no matching Cases, then default to a hardcoded Id.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Assigning to a List (even when expecting at most one result) followed by an explicit empty-check before accessing index 0 is the correct, safe pattern that avoids a QueryException entirely, since a single-sObject assignment throws when the result count isn't exactly one. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Assigning a query directly to a single sObject variable throws a QueryException if the result set has zero rows or more than one row; even with LIMIT 1, a zero-result scenario (no open Cases for the Contact) would throw "List has no rows for assignment."
• C: Roll-Up Summary fields only support aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX) on numeric/date fields; they cannot return a specific child record's Id value.
• D: Relying on catching an exception to infer "no results" is a fragile anti-pattern; it conflates all possible exception causes into one assumption and doesn't represent proper defensive query handling.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer is writing a dynamic SOQL query where an object name and a user-supplied filter value are both determined at runtime. Which two practices correctly mitigate SOQL injection risk in this scenario?

options.text: Wrap any user-supplied string used in the dynamic query with String.escapeSingleQuotes() before concatenating it into the query string, escaping single quotes so they cannot be interpreted as SOQL syntax.
Use bind variables (the colon-prefixed syntax) wherever possible instead of raw string concatenation, since bind variables are resolved safely at query parse time.
Concatenate user input directly into the dynamic query string with no escaping, since Database.query() automatically sanitizes all inputs internally.
SOQL injection is not a real risk in Apex; only traditional SQL databases are vulnerable to injection attacks.
Avoid Database.query(String) entirely in all cases and always use only static, hardcoded inline SOQL regardless of the requirement for dynamic object/field names.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Escaping user-supplied strings with String.escapeSingleQuotes() and preferring bind variables over raw concatenation are both standard, documented mitigations against SOQL injection when building dynamic queries with runtime-determined values. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Database.query() does not automatically sanitize concatenated input; unescaped user input concatenated directly into a dynamic query string is exactly the vulnerability that leads to SOQL injection.
• D: SOQL injection is a real, well-documented risk specific to Apex's dynamic SOQL capability; the general SQL injection concept fully applies here despite SOQL not being traditional SQL.
• E: When a genuine requirement exists for dynamic object or field names determined at runtime, Database.query(String) is the only mechanism that supports this; avoiding it entirely isn't a practical option in that scenario — proper sanitization is the correct response instead.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer's Apex trigger performs an update DML on the same records currently being processed in an after-update trigger context, and needs to understand how this interacts with the save order of execution and potential re-entrancy. What is accurate about this scenario?

options.text: Performing DML inside an after-update trigger on the same records being processed can cause the trigger to fire again for that same update, and this re-entrant execution shares the same transaction and its governor limit counters with the original invocation.
DML performed inside an after-update trigger always executes in a brand new, separate transaction with its own independent governor limits.
Triggers can never perform DML on the records currently being processed within their own context; this is blocked by the platform entirely.
Re-triggering from an after-update trigger's DML has no risk of infinite recursion since Salesforce silently discards any DML that would cause a trigger to re-fire.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: An after-update trigger performing DML on its own triggering records can cause that trigger to fire again, and this re-entrant execution remains within the same overall transaction, meaning all governor limit counters (SOQL, DML, CPU) continue accumulating from the original invocation rather than resetting. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: DML performed within a trigger's execution stays within the same Apex transaction; it does not spawn a separate transaction with independent governor limits.
• C: Triggers absolutely can perform DML on records within their own context (this is a common pattern, e.g., updating a different field on the same records); it is not blocked by the platform.
• D: Salesforce does not silently discard such DML; instead, without proper recursion-control logic, this scenario risks genuine infinite recursion, mitigated only by the platform's recursion depth safeguard as a backstop, not automatic silent discarding.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer needs to implement error handling for a service method that validates loan applications, where specific business rule violations (e.g., "credit score too low") should be distinguishable from generic system errors by calling code. Which two practices are correct?

options.text: Create a custom exception class extending Exception (e.g., public class LoanValidationException extends Exception {}), throw it for specific business rule violations, and catch it specifically in calling code to distinguish it from generic Exception types.
Use only the generic System Exception type for all error conditions, since custom exception classes are not supported in Apex.

Order catch blocks from most specific exception type to most generic, so a specific custom exception is caught by its dedicated catch block rather than falling through to a generic catch (Exception e) block.
Custom exceptions must always extend DmlException specifically, never the base Exception class.
Since Apex catch blocks execute in a random order at runtime, the order in which catch blocks are written has no effect on which one handles a given exception.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Extending the base Exception class to create a custom, named exception type lets calling code distinguish specific business rule violations from generic errors, and ordering catch blocks from most specific to most generic ensures the intended, specific handler actually catches the custom exception rather than being masked by a broader catch. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Custom exception classes are fully supported in Apex via the extends Exception syntax; this is a standard, well-documented capability, not an unsupported one.
• D: Custom exceptions can extend the base Exception class directly; there is no requirement to extend DmlException specifically unless you specifically want DML-related exception behavior.
• E: Catch blocks execute in the exact order they are written, from top to bottom, evaluated against the actual exception type thrown — order is deterministic and meaningful, not random.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer's @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) method, intended to be called via @wire from LWC, attempts to perform an update DML operation inside its body. What happens, and what is the correct fix?

options.text: The method executes normally with no restriction; cacheable=true has no effect on DML capability.

The method throws a runtime exception because cacheable=true methods are strictly read-only and cannot perform DML; the fix is to split the logic into a separate, non-cacheable @AuraEnabled method for the DML operation, called imperatively rather than via @wire.
The DML silently succeeds but is automatically rolled back at the end of the transaction with no error surfaced.
cacheable=true only restricts DML on custom objects, never on standard objects like Account or Contact.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Methods marked @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) are strictly read-only by design (enabling client-side caching and @wire compatibility), so any DML attempt inside them throws a runtime exception; the correct fix is separating read (cacheable) and write (non-cacheable, imperatively called) concerns into distinct methods. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: cacheable=true absolutely does restrict DML — this is one of its most important and commonly tested constraints, not a no-op setting.
• C: The DML does not silently succeed and roll back; it throws an explicit exception at the DML statement itself, immediately surfacing the error rather than silently failing.
• D: The read-only restriction on cacheable=true methods applies universally to DML on any object, standard or custom — there is no object-type-based exception to this rule.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer needs to expose an Apex method as a Flow action that accepts a Contact record Id and a discount percentage, then returns a calculated final price as output. Which two implementation details are required for a correctly structured @InvocableMethod?

options.text: The input wrapper class properties (Contact Id and discount percentage) must be annotated with @InvocableVariable so Flow Builder recognizes them as configurable input fields.

The method signature must accept a List of the input wrapper type and return a List of the output wrapper type (or void), since Flow always passes and expects collections even for single-record invocations.
The method must be annotated with @AuraEnabled instead of @InvocableMethod, since @InvocableMethod is deprecated in favor of @AuraEnabled for all new development.
The output wrapper class does not need any special annotation, since Flow automatically detects public properties as outputs without any decoration.
The method must return a single, non-List instance of the output wrapper class directly, since returning a List would confuse Flow Builder's output mapping.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: @InvocableVariable is required on wrapper class properties for Flow Builder to recognize them as configurable inputs/outputs, and the method signature must use List-based input and output types because Flow always passes and expects collections, even for a single record — both are core, accurate requirements for a correctly structured invocable method. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: @InvocableMethod is not deprecated and remains the correct, required annotation for exposing Apex methods to Flow; @AuraEnabled serves an entirely different purpose (LWC/Aura exposure).
• D: Output wrapper class properties still require @InvocableVariable annotation to be recognized and mapped correctly by Flow Builder; there is no automatic detection of plain public properties without it.
• E: The correct signature returns a List of the output wrapper type (matching the List-based convention), not a single non-List instance; Flow's convention consistently uses Lists for both directions.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer needs to implement a class that will be run on a recurring nightly schedule to archive old records, using System.schedule(). Which interface must the class implement, and what is the required method signature?

options.text: The class must implement Queueable, with a method named run() that takes no parameters.
The class must implement Schedulable, with a public void execute(SchedulableContext sc) method, then be scheduled using System.schedule('Job Name', cronExpression, new MyScheduledClass()).
The class must implement Database.Batchable<SObject>, since only Batchable classes can be run on a schedule.
The class must extend the base Trigger class and override its onSchedule() method.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: A class intended to run on a recurring schedule via System.schedule() must implement the Schedulable interface with the exact required method signature public void execute(SchedulableContext sc), which the platform calls at the scheduled time defined by the cron expression. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Queueable is used for asynchronous jobs enqueued via System.enqueueJob(), not for time-based recurring scheduling; its required method is execute(QueueableContext ctx), and it has no run() method requirement.
• C: Database.Batchable defines start(), execute(), and finish() for processing large record sets in chunks; a Batchable class doesn't run on a schedule by itself — it is commonly invoked FROM within a Schedulable class's execute() method, but Schedulable is still the required scheduling interface.
• D: There is no such thing as extending a base Trigger class with an onSchedule() override in Apex; this describes a nonexistent construct.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer needs to process 2 million records nightly with complex per-record logic, chunked automatically by the platform, with the ability to preserve a running total across all chunks. Which two Batch Apex design elements are required?

options.text: Implementing Database.Batchable<SObject> with a start() method returning a Database.QueryLocator (supporting up to 50 million records, well beyond the 50,000-record SOQL limit), and execute()/finish() methods to process each chunk and finalize results.

Additionally implementing Database.Stateful alongside Database.Batchable, so instance variables (like a running total) persist their values across every execute() call rather than resetting with each new chunk.
A List<SObject> passed directly as the start() return type instead of a QueryLocator, since Lists support unlimited record volume without any SOQL row limit.
Instance variables in a Batchable class persist across execute() calls by default with no additional interface needed.
Batch Apex chunk size defaults to 2,000 records and cannot be configured to any other value.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: A Database.QueryLocator supports up to 50 million records (bypassing the standard 50,000-record SOQL limit) making it correct for processing 2 million records, and Database.Stateful is specifically required to preserve instance variable values (like a running total) across all execute() calls rather than resetting with each chunk. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: A List<SObject> return type from start() is still bound by normal SOQL query limits (50,000 records) since it must be populated via a query first; it does not support unlimited volume the way QueryLocator does.
• D: This is the opposite of actual behavior — by default, each execute() call gets a fresh instance with reset instance variables; Database.Stateful is specifically required to preserve state across calls.
• E: The default batch size is 200 records, not 2,000, and it can be explicitly configured (up to a maximum of 2,000) via the optional scope parameter in Database.executeBatch().

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer's @future(callout=true) method is failing to compile because it accepts an Account sObject as a parameter. What is the issue, and what is the correct fix?

options.text: @future methods cannot accept sObject parameters at all; only primitive types (String, Integer, Boolean, etc.) or collections of primitives are allowed, since the record's state could change between when the method is invoked and when it actually executes asynchronously — the fix is to pass the record's Id (or a Set/List of Ids) instead and re-query fresh data inside the method.
@future methods can accept any parameter type including sObjects; the compile error must be caused by an unrelated syntax issue.
The fix is to mark the Account parameter with @InvocableVariable to make it compatible with @future.
@future methods require all parameters to be marked transient to be valid, regardless of type.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: @future methods have a hard platform restriction disallowing sObject parameters (and non-primitive collections) specifically because the record's state in the database could change between the synchronous call and the later asynchronous execution; the standard fix is passing Ids and re-querying fresh data inside the future method. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: This restriction is a real, well-documented, and strictly enforced compile-time rule for @future methods — it is not an unrelated issue masking a different syntax error.
• C: @InvocableVariable is specifically for annotating properties within @InvocableMethod input/output wrapper classes for Flow; it has no relevance to or effect on @future method parameter type restrictions.
• D: There is no requirement that @future method parameters be marked transient; the actual restriction is specifically about disallowing sObject types (and non-primitive collections), unrelated to the transient keyword.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer needs to chain multiple asynchronous jobs together, where Job B should only start after Job A fully completes, and wants to pass state or context between them. Which two facts about Queueable Apex chaining are accurate?

options.text: A Queueable job can enqueue another Queueable job from within its own execute() method, and this chaining is a documented, supported pattern for sequential asynchronous processing.

From a synchronous context (e.g., a standard UI save or trigger), up to 50 Queueable jobs can be enqueued via System.enqueueJob() in a single transaction; but from within an already-executing asynchronous Queueable job's execute() method, only 1 child Queueable job can be enqueued — this is the limit that governs chaining depth.
@future methods support the exact same chaining capability as Queueable, since both are asynchronous Apex mechanisms with identical constraints.
Queueable Apex cannot accept sObject or other complex object parameters in its constructor, only primitives, identical to @future method restrictions.
Chained Queueable jobs execute simultaneously in parallel with the job that enqueued them, never sequentially.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Queueable Apex explicitly supports chaining — enqueuing a new Queueable job from within an already-running Queueable's execute() method — and the governor limit that actually constrains this is 50 jobs enqueued per synchronous transaction versus only 1 job enqueued per asynchronous transaction, which is what limits how deep a chain of Queueable jobs launched from within other async jobs can go. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: @future methods do not support chaining at all — you cannot call another @future method from within an executing @future method; this is a key differentiator that makes Queueable more powerful for sequential workflows.
• D: Unlike @future methods, Queueable Apex constructors CAN accept complex object parameters including sObjects, since the Queueable instance itself is serialized and its state preserved until execution — this is a major advantage over @future's primitive-only restriction.
• E: Chained Queueable jobs execute sequentially, not in parallel — the second job is only enqueued and begins execution after the first job's execute() method completes, which is the entire point of the chaining pattern.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer needs to understand precisely where in Salesforce's save order of execution a workflow rule's field update sits relative to validation rules and triggers, since a workflow field update is causing validation rules to seemingly re-run. What is accurate about this behavior?

options.text: When a workflow rule's field update fires, Salesforce re-runs the system validation and custom validation rules (along with before/after triggers) against the updated field value, as part of the documented save order — this is why validation appears to "re-run" after the workflow field update.
Workflow field updates never cause any re-evaluation of validation rules or triggers; the described behavior must be caused by an unrelated bug.
Validation rules only ever run once per save operation under all circumstances, with zero exceptions, regardless of what automation fires afterward.
Workflow rules execute entirely outside of and unrelated to the documented save order of execution.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Salesforce's documented save order of execution specifies that when a workflow rule's field update occurs, the platform re-runs validation (system and custom) and before/after triggers against the newly updated value — this re-evaluation is expected, documented platform behavior, not a bug. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: This directly contradicts the documented save order of execution, which explicitly describes workflow field updates triggering a re-run of validation and trigger logic.
• C: Validation rules can indeed be re-evaluated more than once in a single save operation specifically when a workflow field update causes the documented re-run behavior; the "only ever once, zero exceptions" claim is inaccurate.
• D: Workflow rules are explicitly part of the documented save order of execution, occurring at a specific point in that sequence — they do not operate entirely outside or unrelated to it.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer needs to implement a partial rollback within a single Apex transaction: attempt a risky secondary operation, and if it fails, undo only that operation's changes while preserving earlier, already-successful work in the same transaction. Which two facts about savepoints are accurate?

options.text: Savepoint sp = Database.setSavepoint(); captures the transaction's state at that point, and Database.rollback(sp); later undoes all DML performed after that savepoint was set, without rolling back the entire transaction.
Governor limit counts (such as the number of SOQL queries or DML statements already consumed) are restored to their pre-savepoint values when Database.rollback(sp) is called.
Database.rollback(sp) only undoes DML on the specific object type that caused the failure, leaving DML on other object types intact even if performed after the savepoint.
A savepoint can be used to roll back a portion of a transaction's DML changes while keeping earlier DML changes (made before the savepoint) intact.
Only one savepoint can ever be set per transaction; attempting to set a second savepoint throws a runtime exception.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Database.setSavepoint() and Database.rollback(sp) work exactly as described — capturing a point-in-time state and later undoing all DML after that point while preserving earlier, pre-savepoint DML — giving developers precise, partial rollback control within a single transaction. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Governor limit counts (SOQL queries, DML statements, etc.) are NOT restored after a rollback; the resource consumption incurred before the rollback still counts against the transaction's overall limits.
• C: Database.rollback(sp) undoes ALL DML performed after the savepoint was set, regardless of which object type it affected — it is not selective by object type.
• E: Multiple savepoints can be set within a single transaction (each call to Database.setSavepoint() creates a new one); there is no hard one-savepoint-per-transaction restriction.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — A developer needs a method that logs debug information at the FINEST level only during a specific troubleshooting scenario, without affecting standard DEBUG-level logging used throughout the rest of the org's Apex code. What is the correct approach to writing this log statement?

options.text: System.debug(LoggingLevel.FINEST, 'Detailed troubleshooting info: ' + someVariable); explicitly specifies the FINEST log level for this specific statement, independent of other System.debug() calls using the default DEBUG level.
System.debug() statements always log at the FINEST level automatically; no level specification is possible or necessary.
Logging levels can only be set org-wide and cannot be specified on a per-statement basis within Apex code.
FINEST is not a valid logging level in Salesforce; only ERROR, WARN, and INFO are supported.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: System.debug() accepts an optional LoggingLevel parameter, allowing a specific statement to log at a chosen level (like FINEST) independently of other calls using the default DEBUG level, giving fine-grained control per log statement. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: System.debug() defaults to the DEBUG level when no level is specified; it does not automatically log at FINEST unless explicitly told to do so.
• C: Logging level can absolutely be specified per individual System.debug() statement in code, in addition to the trace flag's overall log level configuration in Setup — it is not solely an org-wide setting.
• D: FINEST is indeed a valid, documented Salesforce logging level (part of the full sequence: NONE, ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG, FINE, FINER, FINEST); claiming it doesn't exist is factually incorrect.

pd1.question: Process Automation and Logic — Choose 2. A developer needs to decide how to automate a business process requiring: simple conditional field updates on save (no DML on other objects), AND a separate requirement needing complex algorithmic logic with tight, governor-limit-sensitive bulk processing across 50,000 records nightly. Which two tool choices correctly match each sub-requirement?

options.text: The simple conditional field-update requirement (no DML on other objects) is well-suited to a before-save Record-Triggered Flow, requiring no code or tests.

The complex, high-volume, governor-limit-sensitive nightly bulk processing requirement is well-suited to Batch Apex, which is specifically designed for processing large record volumes in governor-limit-safe chunks.
Both requirements should use the same single before-save Flow, since before-save Flows can handle any volume of records with any complexity level.
The nightly bulk processing requirement should use a before-save Record-Triggered Flow instead of Batch Apex, since before-save Flows have no governor limit constraints whatsoever.
The simple conditional field-update requirement should use Batch Apex exclusively, since Batch Apex is required for any automation touching more than one record.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: A before-save Record-Triggered Flow is the right, code-free tool for simple same-record conditional field updates, while Batch Apex is specifically designed for complex, high-volume, governor-limit-sensitive nightly processing across tens of thousands of records — correctly matching each sub-requirement to its appropriate tool. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Before-save Flows are not suited to complex, high-volume, governor-limit-sensitive bulk processing; that scenario specifically exceeds Flow's practical capabilities and requires Batch Apex.
• D: Before-save Flows are absolutely subject to governor limits like any other Salesforce automation; claiming no constraints whatsoever is factually incorrect, and they are not designed for large-scale nightly batch processing.
• E: Batch Apex is not "required" for any multi-record automation — it is specifically suited to large-volume, chunked processing; a simple conditional field update on a single record's save is far better handled by a lightweight before-save Flow.

# User Interface

pd1.question: User Interface — A developer needs to build an Apex web service method that safely returns Account data to an LWC component, ensuring the running user's field-level security and object permissions are respected before the data leaves the server. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Query the data normally with a plain SOQL statement and return it directly with no additional security check, since @AuraEnabled automatically enforces FLS on every returned field.

Use WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED in the SOQL query (or Security.stripInaccessible(AccessType.READABLE, records)) to enforce field- and object-level security before the data is returned, since with sharing alone only enforces row-level (record) sharing, not FLS.
Declare the class without sharing, since without sharing automatically applies stricter FLS enforcement than with sharing.
Rely solely on the Visualforce page's escape='true' attribute to enforce field-level security on returned Apex data.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: with/without sharing controls only row-level (record) access; field-level security must be enforced separately using WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED in SOQL or Security.stripInaccessible(), which is exactly the correct, documented approach for ensuring FLS compliance before returning data to a client component. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: @AuraEnabled does not automatically enforce FLS on returned fields; this is a common misconception, and explicit enforcement (SECURITY_ENFORCED or stripInaccessible) is required.
• C: without sharing ignores the running user's record-level sharing rules entirely (running in system mode for sharing purposes) and has no relationship to field-level security enforcement, let alone "stricter" enforcement.
• D: The escape='true' attribute in Visualforce controls HTML output encoding (XSS prevention) for displayed text; it has no relationship to field-level security enforcement on Apex-returned data.

pd1.question: User Interface — Choose 2. A developer is reviewing a class for XSS (cross-site scripting) risk in Visualforce and separately reviewing SOQL injection risk in a related Apex controller. Which two mitigations are correctly matched to their respective vulnerability type?

options.text: In Visualforce, the {! expression } merge syntax automatically HTML-encodes output by default, converting characters like < and > to prevent script injection; explicit HTMLENCODE() calls are needed for manually constructed strings or specific contexts requiring explicit encoding.
In Apex dynamic SOQL, wrapping user-supplied input with String.escapeSingleQuotes() before concatenation is the documented mitigation against SOQL injection.
HTMLENCODE() is the correct mitigation against SOQL injection, while String.escapeSingleQuotes() is the correct mitigation against XSS.
Visualforce's {! expression } syntax never encodes output; all encoding must always be added manually with HTMLENCODE() regardless of context.
SOQL injection and XSS are the same vulnerability with identical mitigation techniques, since both involve unsanitized user input.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Visualforce's default merge syntax auto-encodes output to guard against XSS (with HTMLENCODE() available for extra explicit cases), while String.escapeSingleQuotes() is the documented, standard mitigation specifically for SOQL injection in dynamic queries — both statements correctly match mitigation to vulnerability type. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: This swaps the mitigations backward — HTMLENCODE() addresses XSS (HTML/script injection), while String.escapeSingleQuotes() addresses SOQL injection, not the reverse.
• D: Visualforce's {! expression } syntax does auto-encode output by default; claiming it never encodes anything contradicts well-documented, standard Visualforce behavior.
• E: XSS (malicious script injection into rendered HTML) and SOQL injection (malicious alteration of query logic) are distinct vulnerability types with different attack vectors and different, non-interchangeable mitigation techniques.

pd1.question: User Interface — A developer needs to check, before performing an insert DML in Apex, whether the running user has create permission on the Opportunity object, and separately needs to check field-level access to the Amount field before returning it in a response. What are the correct method calls for each check?

options.text: Schema.SObjectType.Opportunity.isCreateable() for the object-level create check, and Schema.SObjectType.Opportunity.fields.Amount.getDescribe().isAccessible() for the field-level read-access check.
Schema.SObjectType.Opportunity.isAccessible() for both checks, since isAccessible() covers both object-level and field-level permissions simultaneously.
Security.stripInaccessible(AccessType.CREATABLE, records) is the only valid way to check object-level create permission; Schema-based describe methods cannot check CRUD.
FLS and object CRUD checks are automatically enforced by every with sharing class with no explicit method calls required.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: isCreateable() on the SObjectType is the correct, standard method for the object-level create permission check, while calling getDescribe().isAccessible() on the specific field token is the correct method for checking field-level read access — these are two distinct checks at two distinct levels, each with its own dedicated method. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: isAccessible() at the object level checks object-level read permission specifically, not create permission, and it does not simultaneously cover field-level checks — field-level checks require calling getDescribe() on the specific field.
• C: Security.stripInaccessible() is one valid, bulk-oriented approach for filtering records by access, but Schema.SObjectType's isCreateable(), isAccessible(), isUpdateable(), and isDeletable() methods are equally valid, commonly used, and explicitly documented ways to check CRUD permissions.
• D: with sharing only enforces row-level (record) sharing rules; it does not automatically enforce object-level CRUD or field-level security — those require the explicit checks described in this scenario.

pd1.question: User Interface — Choose 2. A developer is building a Visualforce page and needs to decide between a Custom Controller and a Controller Extension for a new requirement: display an Account record with all standard save/cancel/edit behavior preserved, plus one additional custom method for a specialized calculation. Which two facts correctly support choosing a Controller Extension here?

options.text: A Controller Extension augments the Standard Controller (standardController='Account' with extensions='MyExtension'), preserving standard actions like save, cancel, and edit while adding custom methods and properties.
The extension's constructor receives the Standard Controller as a parameter, allowing the extension to access the record via stdController.getRecord() while still benefiting from standard behavior.
A Custom Controller is required whenever any additional custom method is needed beyond what the Standard Controller natively provides.
Using extensions='MyExtension' completely replaces and disables all standard controller actions, requiring the developer to reimplement save and cancel manually.
Controller Extensions cannot access the underlying record; only Custom Controllers can query and manipulate record data.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: A Controller Extension is specifically designed to add custom methods/properties while preserving all standard controller behavior (save, cancel, edit), and its constructor receiving the Standard Controller as a parameter (accessed via getRecord()) is exactly the mechanism that enables this augmentation — both facts directly support choosing an extension for this scenario. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: A Custom Controller (fully replacing the Standard Controller) is only needed when standard behavior doesn't fit at all or there's no single-record context; adding one additional custom method while keeping standard actions is exactly the Controller Extension use case, not a reason to require a full custom controller.
• D: Using extensions does not disable standard actions — save, cancel, and edit remain fully functional and available; that preservation is precisely the point of using an extension over a full custom controller.
• E: Controller Extensions absolutely can access the underlying record, specifically via the Standard Controller reference passed into their constructor (stdController.getRecord()); this is a core, defining capability of extensions.

pd1.question: User Interface — A Visualforce page is throwing a view state size error after a developer added several instance variables holding full query results used only during page load, never referenced again after initial rendering. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Mark those instance variables as transient, excluding them from the serialized view state sent between requests, since they are not needed for subsequent partial page refreshes.
Increase the org's view state limit setting from 170 KB to a higher custom value in Setup.
Convert the Visualforce page into a Lightning Web Component, since LWC has no equivalent capacity constraint of any kind.
Remove the Standard Controller entirely, since only Custom Controllers are subject to view state limits.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Marking instance variables that are only needed during initial load (and never referenced in subsequent partial-page-refresh requests) as transient excludes them from the serialized view state, directly reducing its size and resolving the view state limit error. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: The 170 KB view state limit is a fixed platform constraint; there is no Setup option to increase it to a custom, higher value.
• C: While LWC does not use the Visualforce view state mechanism, it has its own distinct performance and resource considerations; claiming "no equivalent capacity constraint of any kind" overstates this, and rewriting the page is a far larger change than the targeted, appropriate transient fix.
• D: View state limits apply to Visualforce pages regardless of whether they use a Standard Controller or Custom Controller; removing the Standard Controller does not exempt a page from this limit.

pd1.question: User Interface — Choose 2. A developer is deciding how to expose an LWC component so it appears as an option in Lightning App Builder for both Record Pages and App Pages, and separately wants a component usable inside a Flow screen. Which two target configuration facts are accurate?

options.text: The .js-meta.xml file's <targets> section must declare lightning__RecordPage and lightning__AppPage for the component to appear as a placement option for those respective page types in Lightning App Builder.
Declaring lightning__FlowScreen as a target makes the component usable as a screen component inside a Flow's Screen element.
Components with no declared targets at all are automatically available in every possible placement context by default.
lightning__RecordPage automatically grants the component the current record's Id without any additional @api property declaration.
A single component's .js-meta.xml file can declare only one target at a time; declaring multiple targets requires separate component bundles.
targetConfigs are mandatory for every target and cannot be omitted under any circumstances.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Declaring lightning__RecordPage and lightning__AppPage in the targets section makes the component available for those specific page-builder placement contexts, and declaring lightning__FlowScreen specifically enables the component to be used inside a Flow's Screen element — both are accurate, standard target configuration facts. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Components with no declared targets are NOT automatically available everywhere; without an explicit target declaration, a component will not appear as a placement option in App Builder or Flow at all.
• D: While lightning__RecordPage does provide record context, the component must still explicitly declare an @api recordId property to receive and use that Id — it is not automatically granted with zero property declaration.
• E: A single .js-meta.xml file can declare multiple targets simultaneously (e.g., both lightning__RecordPage and lightning__AppPage together) within one component bundle; separate bundles are not required for multiple targets.

pd1.question: User Interface — A developer needs an LWC child component to expose a public property that a parent component sets declaratively via an HTML attribute, and this property must trigger reactive re-rendering in the child whenever the parent updates it. What decorator and pattern is correct?

options.text: @api on the child's property (e.g., @api title;), set from the parent's template as an HTML attribute (<c-child title={parentTitle}>), which is reactive — when parentTitle changes in the parent, the child's title updates and re-renders automatically.
@wire on the child's property, since @wire is required for any property set by a parent component via HTML attributes.
@track on the child's property is mandatory in all modern LWC (API 45+) for any property to be settable from a parent, since @api alone is insufficient.
The property must be set using a custom event dispatched from the parent to the child, since HTML attributes cannot pass data from parent to child in LWC.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: @api is specifically the decorator that exposes a component property as public-facing, settable via an HTML attribute from a parent template, and @api properties are reactive by default — exactly matching the described requirement with no additional decorators needed. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: @wire connects a property or function to a data source (like an Apex method or a UI API wire adapter); it has no role in exposing a property for parent-to-child attribute binding — that is @api's specific purpose.
• C: @track is largely redundant in modern LWC since all properties are reactive by default for primitive reassignment; it is not a mandatory requirement layered on top of @api for parent-to-child data flow.
• D: HTML attributes are precisely how parent-to-child data flow works in LWC via @api properties; custom events are the mechanism for the opposite direction (child-to-parent communication), not parent-to-child.

pd1.question: User Interface — Choose 2. A developer is deciding between calling an Apex method imperatively versus using @wire in an LWC component that needs to: (1) load a list of records automatically when the component first renders, and (2) save a user's edited record only when they click a Save button. Which two tool choices correctly match each need?

options.text: Use @wire for need (1), since @wire is designed for data that should load automatically and reactively refresh when its reactive parameters change.
Use an imperative Apex call for need (2), since the save action is user-triggered (on a button click) and involves DML, which is incompatible with a cacheable=true wired method.
Use @wire for need (2) as well, since @wire methods can perform DML as long as the button click passes the correct parameters.
Use an imperative Apex call for need (1), since imperative calls are always required for any data that loads when a component renders.
Both needs should use the exact same @wire property, since a single wire adapter can serve both automatic loading and user-triggered saving.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: @wire is the correct fit for automatically loading data on render (reactive, declarative), while an imperative call is required for the user-triggered save action since DML cannot be performed inside a cacheable=true wired method — correctly matching each need to the appropriate mechanism. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: @wire methods used with cacheable=true (required for @wire) are strictly read-only and cannot perform DML regardless of what parameters are passed; this option describes an impossible configuration.
• D: Imperative calls are not "always required" for data loaded on render — @wire is specifically designed for and commonly used for exactly this automatic, on-render loading scenario.
• E: A single @wire property cannot serve both an automatic reactive read and a user-triggered DML write; these are fundamentally different operations requiring separate methods (a cacheable wired method and a separate imperative method).

pd1.question: User Interface — A developer's LWC component needs to notify its parent that a specific item was selected by the user, passing the selected item's Id as data, without the parent needing to poll or manually check the child's state. What is the correct implementation pattern?

options.text: In the child, dispatch a custom event: this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('itemselected', { detail: { itemId: this.selectedId } })); in the parent's template, listen with onitemselected={handleItemSelected}, and read event.detail.itemId in the handler.
The parent should directly call a public method on the child via this.template.querySelector() every render cycle to poll for the current selection.
The child should mutate an @api property on the parent directly, since @api properties are writable in both directions by any connected component.
Use document.dispatchEvent() instead of this.dispatchEvent(), since document-level events are required for any parent-child LWC communication.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Dispatching a custom event from the child with a descriptive lowercase name and a detail payload, then listening for it in the parent's template via the on-prefixed attribute, is the standard, documented child-to-parent communication pattern in LWC — delivering the selected Id without any polling. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Polling via querySelector() on every render cycle is inefficient, fragile, and not the idiomatic LWC communication pattern; event dispatching provides immediate, push-based notification instead.
• C: @api properties are designed for one-way parent-to-child data flow; children should never directly mutate a parent's properties, and @api does not support that reverse-direction mutation pattern.
• D: this.dispatchEvent() dispatched from the component itself (not document) is the correct, standard mechanism; using document.dispatchEvent() would bypass the component's own event system and violate the intended encapsulated communication model.

pd1.question: User Interface — Choose 2. A developer needs two LWC components that are siblings (not directly nested) on the same Lightning Record Page to communicate: selecting a filter in Component A should update the displayed data in Component B, and neither component has a shared parent that both are children of within the same custom component tree. Which two approaches correctly solve this?

options.text: Use Lightning Message Service (LMS) with a defined MessageChannel: Component A publishes a message via publish(), and Component B subscribes via subscribe(), enabling communication across the page regardless of DOM hierarchy.
If both components happen to share a common ancestor container that manages state, that ancestor can catch an event from Component A and update an @api property passed down to Component B.
Use this.template.querySelector() from Component A to directly reach into Component B's shadow DOM and set its internal properties.
Custom events dispatched from Component A will automatically bubble across the entire Lightning page to reach any sibling component with zero configuration.
Use document.querySelector() to locate Component B's DOM node from Component A and call an internal method directly.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: Lightning Message Service is specifically designed for exactly this scenario — decoupled communication across any DOM hierarchy on the page — and if a genuine shared ancestor/container exists that can catch an event and pass data down via @api, that pattern also correctly solves the sibling communication problem. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: this.template.querySelector() can only reach within a component's OWN shadow DOM; it cannot reach into a sibling component's internal shadow DOM to set properties, due to Shadow DOM/Locker Service isolation.
• D: Custom events do not automatically bubble across the entire page to arbitrary siblings by default; achieving broader propagation requires explicit bubbles/composed configuration and even then depends on actual DOM ancestry, not just page presence.
• E: document.querySelector() violates Locker Service's shadow DOM isolation model and is explicitly the kind of dangerous, boundary-crossing access the sandbox is designed to prevent; it is not a valid or supported communication pattern.

pd1.question: User Interface — A developer's LWC component uses @wire(getRecord, {recordId: '$recordId', fields: [NAME_FIELD]}) but the wire never re-fires when recordId changes after the initial render. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The $ prefix is missing from the actual property reference in code (it should reference the reactive property, e.g., '$recordId', exactly as shown) — without the $ prefix, Salesforce treats the value as a static literal rather than a reactive reference, so changes to recordId never trigger a re-fetch.
@wire adapters can never be reactive under any circumstances; a full manual re-render trigger is always required.
getRecord specifically does not support reactive parameters, unlike all other wire adapters.
The fields array must also use the $ prefix on every field reference for reactivity to work.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: The $ prefix is what marks a property reference as reactive in a @wire configuration; if recordId is referenced without the $ prefix (as a static value instead), the wire will never detect changes to it and will not automatically re-fetch data when it changes. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: @wire adapters absolutely can be reactive — this is one of their core, defining features when properties are correctly referenced with the $ prefix; claiming no reactivity is possible is factually incorrect.
• C: getRecord fully supports reactive parameters like recordId via the $ prefix; this is a standard, common, documented usage pattern, not an exception.
• D: The $ prefix is applied to reactive property references used as parameter values (like recordId); field API name imports (like NAME_FIELD) in the fields array are static schema references and do not use or need the $ prefix.

pd1.question: User Interface — Choose 2. A developer building an LWC component needs to navigate programmatically to a specific Account record's detail page after a successful save action. Which two facts about NavigationMixin are accurate?

options.text: The component class must extend NavigationMixin(LightningElement) after importing NavigationMixin from 'lightning/navigation'.
Navigation is triggered by calling thisNavigationMixin.Navigate.
NavigationMixin can only navigate to standard object pages; it has no support for navigating to a specific record's detail page.
Hardcoding the record's URL as a string (e.g., '/lightning/r/Account/' + accountId + '/view') is the Salesforce-recommended best practice over using NavigationMixin.
NavigationMixin.Navigate is a standalone function that can be called directly without extending the component class with NavigationMixin.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: NavigationMixin must be imported and used to extend the component class, and navigation is triggered by calling thisNavigationMixin.Navigate with a page reference object specifying the type (standard__recordPage) and attributes (recordId, actionName) — both are accurate, standard implementation facts. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: NavigationMixin fully supports navigating to a specific record's detail page via the standard__recordPage page type with a recordId attribute; this is one of its most common use cases, not an unsupported one.
• D: Salesforce explicitly recommends using NavigationMixin over hardcoded URL strings, since hardcoded URLs are fragile, environment-dependent, and bypass the platform's navigation service.
• E: thisNavigationMixin.Navigate must be called on a component instance that has extended NavigationMixin(LightningElement); it is not a standalone function usable without that extension.

pd1.question: User Interface — A developer needs to read a URL query parameter (e.g., a campaign source code) when an LWC component loads on a standalone App Page, reactively responding if the parameter changes without a full page reload. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Use @wire(CurrentPageReference) from 'lightning/navigation', then extract the value via a getter reading this.pageRef?.state?.myParam, since CurrentPageReference's state property holds URL query parameters and the wire is reactive to URL changes.
Use window.location.search directly in connectedCallback(), since this is the Salesforce-recommended, Locker Service-compliant approach for reading URL parameters in LWC.
URL query parameters cannot be read in LWC under any circumstances; this requires a Visualforce page instead.
Use @api urlParams; and Salesforce will automatically populate it with all URL query parameters with no additional configuration.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: @wire(CurrentPageReference) is the correct, reactive, Locker Service-compliant mechanism for reading page reference data including URL state (query parameters) in LWC, and since it's a wire adapter, it reactively updates the component if the underlying page reference changes. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Directly accessing window.location is discouraged and can conflict with Locker Service's sandboxing model; CurrentPageReference is the Salesforce-recommended, supported approach specifically for this purpose.
• C: LWC fully supports reading URL parameters via the CurrentPageReference wire adapter; claiming it's impossible and requires Visualforce is factually incorrect.
• D: There is no @api urlParams magic property that Salesforce automatically populates; developers must explicitly wire CurrentPageReference and extract values from its state property themselves.

pd1.question: User Interface — Choose 2. A developer is deciding between lightning-record-form, lightning-record-edit-form, and lightning-record-view-form for a new feature requiring highly customized field layout with conditional field visibility logic driven by component JavaScript. Which two facts correctly inform this decision?

options.text: lightning-record-form is the simplest option, auto-generating a view or edit form based on page layout or a field list, but offers the least layout customization control.

lightning-record-edit-form paired with lightning-input-field components gives the developer full control over field layout and submission logic, making it suitable for conditional field visibility driven by custom JavaScript.
lightning-record-view-form is the only option that supports any form of field-level customization; both other form types render every field identically with zero flexibility.
lightning-record-form always provides more granular layout control than lightning-record-edit-form, making it the better choice for this specific requirement.
All three form components require an explicit Apex controller method to load record data; none of them use the UI API directly.

pd1.explanation:
Why correct: lightning-record-form is indeed the simplest but least customizable option, while lightning-record-edit-form with lightning-input-field components provides the fine-grained layout control and custom submission logic needed for conditional field visibility — correctly informing the choice toward the edit-form approach for this requirement. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: lightning-record-edit-form (using lightning-input-field) also supports meaningful field-level customization and conditional rendering; view-form is not uniquely capable of this among the three options.
