• C: Package-based development requires source control, CLI tooling, and team discipline that don't yet exist — skipping straight there ignores the maturity gap.
• D: A formal CAB for every change is disproportionate governance overhead for a single-admin org and will simply be bypassed under delivery pressure.

pdlda.question: Application Lifecycle Management — A mid-sized insurer has version control and a defined branching strategy, and CI runs on every pull request, but release frequency is inconsistent and nobody tracks deployment lead time or defect escape rate. Which maturity level best characterizes this organization, and what is the appropriate next investment?

options.text: This is "ad hoc" maturity; the next investment is introducing source control.
This is "defined" maturity; the next investment is adding metrics and KPIs such as deployment frequency and lead time to move toward "managed."
This is "optimizing" maturity; the next investment is chaos engineering.
This is "repeatable" maturity; the next investment is a documented deployment runbook.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Standardized, enforced processes (CI on every PR, defined branching) without measurement is the "defined" level; advancing to "managed" requires instrumenting the pipeline with KPIs like lead time and deployment frequency. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Ad hoc implies no consistent process at all, which contradicts the enforced CI and branching strategy already in place.
• C: Optimizing-level practices like chaos engineering presume measured, controlled processes already exist — this org hasn't yet added metrics, so it's not there.
• D: A documented runbook is a "repeatable" level action; this org has already moved past that with enforced CI and branching.

pdlda.question: Application Lifecycle Management — A healthcare customer operating under HIPAA wants to adopt agile delivery for faster releases but is worried about losing the audit trail their compliance team requires. As the architect, what governance recommendation best balances agile speed with regulatory requirements?

options.text: Revert to waterfall exclusively, since HIPAA compliance is incompatible with agile delivery.
Skip formal CAB review entirely and rely solely on developer self-certification of compliance for every deployment.

Keep agile development in lower environments, but add lightweight sprint-boundary approval checkpoints and a formal CAB gate before any production deployment, with automated testing as the primary quality gate.
Require every commit, including work-in-progress commits to feature branches, to go through full CAB approval before merging.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: This preserves auditability (who changed what, when, why) and regulatory sign-off at the point that matters — production — while letting agile iteration happen without being throttled by governance at every commit. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Waterfall is not a HIPAA requirement; many regulated organizations run agile delivery successfully with compensating governance controls.
• B: Self-certification without any independent review removes the audit trail and accountability HIPAA-style compliance requires.
• D: Gating every commit (not just production releases) with full CAB approval defeats the purpose of agile iteration and creates unsustainable bottleneck at the wrong level.

pdlda.question: Application Lifecycle Management — Three business units at a manufacturing company each independently built Salesforce customizations over several years. Technical debt is accumulating, coding standards differ wildly between teams, and duplicate custom objects have appeared. Leadership asks what structural governance mechanism would best address the root cause. What should you recommend?

options.text: Hire more developers on each business unit's team to work through the technical debt backlog faster.
Merge all three orgs into one immediately without any deduplication assessment.
Mandate that all three teams adopt the exact same CI/CD vendor tooling within 30 days.
Establish a Center of Excellence that owns coding standards, metadata architecture guidelines, an approved tooling list, and governance policies shared across all three teams.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A CoE directly addresses the root cause — lack of centralized standards and shared practices across independently operating teams — without requiring an immediate, high-risk org merge. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Adding headcount without addressing standards accelerates the accumulation of inconsistent, duplicated customizations rather than resolving it.
• B: Merging orgs without a feasibility study and deduplication plan is exactly the kind of high-risk, unplanned action a CoE is meant to prevent.
• C: Forcing a single vendor tool in 30 days addresses tooling, not the underlying absence of shared standards, and ignores each team's context.

pdlda.question: Application Lifecycle Management — A program with multiple concurrent releases wants every production change to pass through a single review body regardless of size, from a one-field label update to a major integration rollout. The Release Manager complains this is creating a backlog and slowing down low-risk changes. What is the best recommendation?

options.text: Remove the CAB from the process entirely and let developers deploy to production directly once tests pass.
Introduce tiered approval gates so low-risk changes pass through automated quality gates while only high-risk or high-impact changes require full CAB review.
Keep the single CAB body but have it meet twice as often to clear the backlog faster.
Require the CAB to pre-approve an entire quarter's worth of changes in one sitting to save time.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Risk-based tiering of approval gates matches governance overhead to actual risk, resolving the backlog for low-risk items while preserving rigorous review where it matters most. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Removing CAB entirely eliminates governance for genuinely high-risk changes, not just the low-risk ones causing the backlog.
• C: Doubling meeting frequency treats a process design flaw as a scheduling problem and doesn't reduce the review burden on low-risk items.
• D: Pre-approving a quarter of changes in one sitting defeats the purpose of change review, since specifics of each change aren't yet known.

pdlda.question: Application Lifecycle Management — Choose 2. An architect is evaluating whether a customer's current ALM approach fits a waterfall, agile, or hybrid methodology. The customer has a fixed regulatory certification deadline, stable and fully documented requirements, but multiple workstreams with varying levels of team experience. Which two factors most directly justify recommending a hybrid methodology over pure agile or pure waterfall? (Choose 2)

options.text: The presence of a fixed regulatory deadline with stable requirements, which favors phase-gated control typical of waterfall.
The existence of multiple workstreams with mixed team experience levels, which benefits from agile iteration within phase boundaries.
The customer's preference for using Jira over Azure DevOps for backlog tracking.
The fact that the company logo uses blue as its primary brand color.
The desire to eventually reduce the total number of Salesforce licenses purchased.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A regulatory deadline with stable, documented requirements favors waterfall-style phase gates for control and traceability, while mixed-experience workstreams benefit from agile's iterative feedback — combining both is the definition of a hybrid approach. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Tooling preference (Jira vs. Azure DevOps) is an implementation detail, not a driver of development methodology choice.
• D: Brand color has no bearing whatsoever on ALM methodology selection.
• E: License consolidation is a commercial/licensing consideration, unrelated to whether agile, waterfall, or hybrid delivery is appropriate.

pdlda.question: Application Lifecycle Management — A startup with five developers wants "just enough" governance to avoid chaos without slowing down its weekly release cadence. Which governance strategy best matches this profile?

options.text: Full ITIL change management with a formal CMDB, risk assessments, and traceability matrices for every change.
Lightweight governance: mandatory PR review and a basic deployment runbook, without a formal CAB.
SAFe with Program Increments and Release Trains spanning multiple Agile Release Trains.
No governance at all, relying entirely on individual developer judgment.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Small teams with low regulatory complexity need governance proportional to their risk profile — PR review plus a basic runbook provides quality control and repeatability without the overhead of enterprise frameworks. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Full ITIL governance with CMDB and formal risk assessments is enterprise-scale overhead that a five-person team cannot sustain alongside weekly releases.
• C: SAFe Program Increments assume multiple teams and Agile Release Trains; a five-developer startup has neither the scale nor the need for this structure.
• D: No governance at all reintroduces the ad hoc chaos the startup explicitly wants to avoid.

pdlda.question: Application Lifecycle Management — After a production incident caused by an emergency change deployed without any review, leadership wants a mechanism that preserves fast turnaround for genuine emergencies while restoring accountability. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Ban all emergency changes going forward, requiring every production change to go through the standard multi-week release cycle.
Allow any developer to self-approve emergency changes as long as they document it afterward.

Establish a pre-authorized emergency change process with defined trigger criteria, a short list of pre-authorized approvers, and mandatory post-change retrieval and back-propagation into source control within a fixed window.
Require the full standing CAB to convene in person for every emergency change, regardless of time of day.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A defined emergency change process preserves speed for genuine emergencies through pre-authorized approvers while restoring accountability via mandatory documentation and back-propagation into the ALM pipeline. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Banning emergency changes entirely ignores that some production issues genuinely require faster-than-standard turnaround, and will likely be circumvented anyway.
• B: Self-approval without independent sign-off is exactly the lack of accountability that caused the original incident.
• D: Requiring the full CAB to convene in person for every emergency defeats the purpose of an emergency path, which needs to be fast.

# Planning

pdlda.question: Planning — A customer has never used version control and deploys via Change Sets, but leadership wants to jump straight to a fully automated CI/CD pipeline with unlocked packages within the next month. As the architect assessing ALM maturity, what should you recommend regarding sequencing?

options.text: Proceed directly with the unlocked package and CI/CD rollout as requested, since faster tooling adoption always improves maturity.

Recommend a phased roadmap: introduce Git source control and a sandbox hierarchy first, then branching strategy and CLI-based deployment, before layering in CI validation and package-based development.
Skip source control but implement the CI/CD pipeline directly against the production org using Metadata API calls triggered by admin approval emails.
Recommend the customer wait a full year before making any tooling changes.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: ALM maturity improvements must be sequenced — source control and environment strategy are prerequisites for reliable CI/CD and packaging; skipping steps causes the automation to fail or be built on an unstable foundation. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Jumping to CI/CD and packaging without source control and sandbox discipline in place means there is nothing reliable for the pipeline to build from.
• C: Automating deployments straight to production without source control or testing gates removes the very safety net CI/CD is meant to add.
• D: A full year of inaction ignores that meaningful, sequenced progress can start immediately with source control adoption.

pdlda.question: Planning — An architect reviews a customer's environment and finds admins routinely making config changes directly in the sandbox used for UAT, without retrieving those changes into source control, causing UAT to diverge from what's deployed to production. What is the most direct mitigation?

options.text: Disable the UAT sandbox entirely until the project ends.
Establish a 'retrieve and commit' workflow requiring any declarative change made in a sandbox to be retrieved into source control before the sandbox is refreshed or the change is considered complete.
Increase the UAT sandbox refresh frequency to daily so drift is reset constantly.
Require all UAT testers to memorize the differences and manually document them in a spreadsheet after each session.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: The direct root cause is that declarative changes aren't being captured in source control; a retrieve-and-commit workflow closes that gap and prevents configuration drift from ever accumulating. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Disabling the sandbox halts UAT testing entirely rather than fixing the underlying process gap.
• C: Refreshing more frequently would destroy in-progress UAT work and does not address why changes aren't being captured in source control.
• D: Manual spreadsheet tracking doesn't fix drift — it just documents it after the fact, and is error-prone at scale.

pdlda.question: Planning — A customer's Full Copy staging sandbox contains unmasked production PII, and any developer with sandbox access can view real customer data including SSNs. Compliance flags this as a critical risk. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Downgrade the Full Copy sandbox to a Developer sandbox to eliminate the risk entirely.
Apply data masking or anonymization to the sandbox before granting broad developer access, and restrict truly unmasked Full Copy access to a small group of authorized personnel only.
Grant everyone access since the sandbox is not production and therefore not subject to compliance rules.
Encrypt the entire sandbox database at rest, which is sufficient to satisfy data privacy requirements for developer access.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Masking sensitive fields before granting broad access directly closes the data leakage risk while preserving the realistic, production-representative data volume Full Copy sandboxes are used for. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Downgrading loses the production-scale data needed for performance/staging testing and doesn't address the actual masking requirement for any environment holding real data.
• C: Non-production environments containing real PII are still subject to the same data privacy compliance obligations as production.
• D: Encryption at rest protects against external theft of the database file, not against authorized developers viewing live PII on screen — it doesn't substitute for masking.

pdlda.question: Planning — A customer with three independent project streams shares a single integration sandbox. Each week, one team's changes overwrite another's during deployment, and root cause is unclear because there's no test isolation. What is the best mitigation strategy?

options.text: Allocate dedicated developer sandboxes per team, use feature branches merged only when ready, and validate each branch in CI before merging into a scheduled integration sandbox refresh.
Merge all three teams into a single unified backlog so there is only one stream of work.
Have the three teams take turns deploying on alternating days of the week without any other process change.
Disable sandbox refreshes entirely so no team's work is ever lost.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Isolating each team's development in dedicated sandboxes and validating merges via CI before they reach the shared integration environment directly eliminates the collision and attribution problems described. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Merging backlogs doesn't solve the technical collision problem of shared sandbox metadata overwrites; it's an organizational, not architectural, fix.
• C: Alternating days without isolation or validation doesn't prevent overwrites, it just changes their timing.
• D: Disabling refreshes entirely doesn't address root-cause metadata collisions and eventually causes the sandbox to diverge badly from production.

pdlda.question: Planning — A UAT sandbox hasn't been refreshed in 10 months while production has had six releases in that time. Testers report tests failing due to stale configuration, and nobody can tell if failures are real defects or environment drift. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Have testers manually reconfigure the sandbox to match production every time a test fails.

Define a sandbox refresh schedule aligned to release cadence (e.g., refresh UAT after each production release), automate post-refresh steps, and track sandbox age with alerts when it exceeds a threshold.
Stop using UAT sandboxes altogether and test only in production going forward.
Refresh the UAT sandbox only once a year regardless of release cadence, to keep costs down.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Aligning refresh cadence to release cycles, automating the post-refresh setup, and tracking sandbox age directly resolves the drift causing indistinguishable test failures. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Manual reconfiguration on every failure is unsustainable and doesn't establish a repeatable, scheduled process.
• C: Testing directly in production eliminates the safety of a pre-production gate and introduces unacceptable risk to real customers and data.
• D: An annual refresh cadence is far too infrequent relative to six production releases in ten months and guarantees continued drift.

pdlda.question: Planning — Choose 2. A customer engaged three vendors on a single Salesforce program without a clear release coordination model. Vendor A deployed a component that broke Vendor B's integration, and no one could determine who owned the shared release calendar or the code repository. Which two governance actions should the architect recommend? (Choose 2)

options.text: Designate a vendor-neutral release manager (typically customer staff) who owns a shared release calendar visible to all vendors.
Ensure the customer owns the source control repository and CI/CD pipeline, with vendor teams contributing via pull requests rather than deploying directly to production.
Let each vendor maintain its own separate, private repository with no cross-visibility to protect vendor IP.
Allow whichever vendor deploys first each week to have deployment priority, decided informally.
Require all three vendors to use the exact same page layout naming convention.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A vendor-neutral release manager with a shared calendar and centralized, customer-owned source control with PR-based contribution are the structural fixes that establish clear ownership and prevent conflicting, uncoordinated deployments. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Separate private repositories with no cross-visibility is precisely what caused the conflict — it prevents any coordination between vendors.
• D: Informal first-come deployment priority is not a governance mechanism and doesn't prevent future conflicts.
• E: A shared naming convention for layouts is a coding standard detail, not a structural fix for multi-vendor release coordination.

pdlda.question: Planning — A multi-vendor Salesforce program is ending its contract with one vendor. The customer discovers that vendor-developed Apex code and metadata live only in that vendor's private Git repository, and the customer has no rights to access it going forward. What planning step would have prevented this?

options.text: Requiring code reviews on every pull request during development.
Contractually defining that the customer owns the source control repository and retains full IP rights to custom metadata and Apex code regardless of which vendor authored it.
Requiring the vendor to use Salesforce DX project format for their codebase.
Mandating that the vendor use scratch orgs instead of sandboxes for development.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: IP ownership and repository custody must be contractually defined upfront; owning the repository ensures the customer retains access and rights to all code regardless of vendor relationship changes. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Code review process quality has no bearing on who legally owns the resulting code or where it's stored.
• C: Using SFDX project format is a technical convention and doesn't establish IP ownership or repository access rights.
• D: Scratch org usage is a development environment choice unrelated to contractual IP and repository ownership.

pdlda.question: Planning — A customer is six weeks away from a Salesforce seasonal release upgrade to production. The architect wants to proactively identify risk areas. Which approach is most effective?

options.text: Wait until the day of the production upgrade to test, since Salesforce guarantees backward compatibility.

Analyze release notes for 'Enforce by default' and 'Critical Update' items, deploy to a preview sandbox during the release preview window, and run the full regression suite plus targeted testing on flagged features.
Only test features the customer plans to build in the next quarter, ignoring existing functionality.
Rely exclusively on Salesforce's own internal testing and skip customer-side regression testing altogether.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Combining release notes analysis with hands-on preview sandbox testing and full regression is the standard proactive risk-mitigation approach for seasonal releases, surfacing issues weeks before the mandatory production upgrade. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Salesforce does not guarantee zero-impact upgrades — behavior changes, enforced defaults, and API changes can break existing customizations.
• C: Ignoring existing functionality misses the primary risk, since seasonal releases most often affect current customizations, not unbuilt future features.
• D: Salesforce's internal testing covers platform-level quality, not customer-specific customizations, integrations, or Apex — customer-side regression testing is essential.

pdlda.question: Planning — A customer wants to opt out of the sandbox release preview upgrade for their UAT sandbox because they have a critical UAT cycle in progress and don't want the seasonal release changing behavior mid-cycle. What is the key planning constraint they must account for?

options.text: Opt-out requests can be submitted at any time, even after the sandbox has already been upgraded.

The opt-out window is limited and must be requested from Salesforce support before a defined cutoff date, typically a few weeks before the sandbox upgrade — missing it means the sandbox will upgrade on schedule.
Only Full Copy sandboxes are eligible for release preview, so this sandbox would not be affected regardless.
Opting out of preview also delays the production org's upgrade by the same amount of time.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: The opt-out window for sandbox release preview is time-limited and must be requested proactively through Salesforce support before the cutoff — this is the key planning constraint the customer needs to know to protect their UAT cycle. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Opt-out requests cannot be made retroactively after the sandbox has already upgraded; the window closes before the scheduled upgrade.
• C: Developer, Developer Pro, and Partial Copy sandboxes typically receive preview; Full Copy sandboxes are the ones that typically do NOT receive the preview upgrade — the reverse of this option's claim.
• D: Opting a sandbox out of preview has no effect on the production org's own mandatory upgrade schedule.

pdlda.question: Planning — Following a seasonal release preview test cycle, the architect discovers that several existing Apex unit tests now fail due to a platform behavior change flagged as a Critical Update (Release Update) with a mandatory auto-activation date six weeks away. What is the correct planning response?

options.text: Ignore the failures since Critical Updates can always be deferred indefinitely with no consequence.
Opt in to the update now in a sandbox, fix the failing Apex logic and tests proactively, and deploy the fix to production before the mandatory auto-activation date.
Wait until the auto-activation date passes and address any resulting production incidents reactively.
File a support case asking Salesforce to permanently exempt the org from ever activating the update.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Because auto-activation is time-bound and unavoidable, proactively fixing and deploying the corrected logic before the deadline avoids a production incident and keeps the fix within the normal ALM pipeline. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Release Updates (formerly Critical Updates) auto-activate on a fixed timeline; they cannot be deferred indefinitely.
• C: Waiting for auto-activation to cause a production incident is the exact failure mode proactive planning is meant to avoid.
• D: Salesforce does not offer permanent exemptions from mandatory Release Update auto-activation; deferral is time-limited, not indefinite.

pdlda.question: Planning — A CI pipeline deploys using a hardcoded, older Salesforce API version in its scripts. The upcoming seasonal release is expected to deprecate that API version. What risk should the architect flag to the delivery team, and what is the fix?

options.text: No risk exists, since Salesforce CLI automatically upgrades API versions referenced in pipeline scripts without any changes needed.

The pipeline deployments may begin failing once the API version is deprecated; the fix is to update the API version referenced in pipeline scripts and metadata before the release, and validate this in the preview sandbox.
The only risk is a minor UI warning banner in Setup; no functional impact will occur.
This risk only affects package-based development, not org-based CI pipelines using Metadata API deployments.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Deprecated API versions can cause deployment failures once fully retired, so proactively updating the API version in pipeline scripts and metadata, then validating against the preview sandbox, prevents a broken pipeline at release time. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Salesforce CLI does not automatically rewrite API version references embedded in a customer's own deployment metadata and scripts.
• C: A deprecated API version can cause actual deployment failures, not merely a cosmetic warning.
• D: This risk applies to any deployment mechanism referencing a specific API version, including org-based Metadata API deployments, not just packages.

pdlda.question: Planning — Business stakeholders are frustrated because they were surprised by UI behavior changes after a Salesforce seasonal release went to production, despite the technical team having tested it thoroughly in the preview sandbox. What planning gap does this reveal?

options.text: The technical testing was insufficient and should be repeated with more test cases.

There was no non-technical release impact communication to business stakeholders describing what would change, when, and what actions they needed to take, and no stakeholder-facing UAT cycle scheduled before the production upgrade window.
The seasonal release should have been declined entirely, since seasonal releases are optional for customers.
The preview sandbox window was too short to catch the change, so Salesforce should be asked to extend it indefinitely.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Even thorough technical testing doesn't address stakeholder communication — a non-technical release impact summary and a pre-upgrade stakeholder UAT cycle are the specific planning steps that prevent business-side surprises. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: The scenario states technical testing was thorough; the gap is communication and stakeholder involvement, not test coverage.
• C: Salesforce seasonal releases are mandatory platform-wide upgrades for all customers; declining them entirely is not an available option.
• D: The preview window length isn't the root cause here — the technical team already caught the change; the failure was in cascading that information to the business.

pdlda.question: Planning — A company is preparing a formal, evidence-based governance framework proposal for a new enterprise-wide Salesforce program spanning five business units, each with different SLAs and compliance obligations. Leadership wants a data-driven audit trail for every change. Which framework should the architect most likely recommend as the primary foundation?

options.text: A lightweight PR-review-only process with no formal change records.

ITIL-based governance, given its strength in formal change management, incident management, and audit-trail-oriented CMDB practices suited to SLA- and compliance-driven, IT-operations-heavy environments.
Pure Kanban with no defined release cadence or approval gates.
A single informal Slack channel where any team member can approve any other team's change.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: ITIL's formal change management, incident management, and audit-trail-oriented practices directly match the requirement for SLA compliance and a data-driven, auditable governance foundation across multiple business units. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: A PR-review-only process lacks the formal, cross-business-unit change and incident tracking the compliance requirement demands.
• C: Pure Kanban with no approval gates provides workflow visualization but no formal audit trail or compliance-oriented change control.
• D: An informal approval channel provides no structured audit trail and no segregation of duties required for compliance obligations.

# System Design

pdlda.question: System Design — A Salesforce delivery team currently tracks work in spreadsheets emailed weekly. Leadership wants better cross-team visibility into sprint progress and impediments without adding heavy process. What is the most direct benefit of introducing an agile project management tool like Jira or Azure Boards in this context?

options.text: It eliminates the need for sprint planning meetings entirely.
It automatically writes Apex unit tests based on backlog descriptions.
It provides shared visibility into work in progress, velocity, and impediments without requiring additional status meetings, and enables backlog prioritization across teams.
It replaces the need for a sandbox environment strategy.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Agile tools centralize backlog, sprint, and impediment visibility so stakeholders and teams get real-time status without manual spreadsheet updates or extra meetings — directly solving the stated visibility problem. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Agile tools support sprint planning; they don't eliminate the need for the planning conversation itself.
• B: No agile tracking tool generates Apex test code from backlog text; this conflates project tracking with code generation.
• D: Sprint tracking tools and sandbox environment strategy address entirely different concerns; one doesn't substitute for the other.

pdlda.question: System Design — A customer wants full traceability from a user story to the exact metadata deployed to production, including which developer wrote it, which tests passed, and who approved the deployment. Which combination of practices best achieves this?

options.text: Rely on the Release Manager's memory and informal Slack threads to reconstruct history when needed.
Link Git commits to backlog tickets using smart commit syntax, have CI post build/test results back to the ticket, and use a deployment tool that ties user stories to specific deployed components.
Store all user stories only as PDF attachments in email, separate from any tooling.
Require developers to manually re-type ticket numbers into a spreadsheet after each deployment.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Linking commits to tickets, automating CI status back to the ticket, and using deployment tooling that maps stories to components creates an automated, auditable chain from requirement to deployed artifact. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Relying on memory and informal chat threads provides no reliable, auditable trace and fails under any real compliance scrutiny.
• C: PDF attachments disconnected from any tooling cannot be automatically linked to commits, builds, or deployments.
• D: Manual re-typing introduces human error and isn't a scalable or reliable traceability mechanism.

pdlda.question: System Design — A company recently acquired a competitor that runs its own separate Salesforce org with overlapping Account and Contact data and a different sales process. Leadership wants a recommendation on org strategy within 90 days. What should the architect propose first?

options.text: Immediately merge the two orgs into one within the 90-day window regardless of data overlap.
Conduct a formal feasibility study evaluating data overlap, process compatibility, technical complexity, and licensing before deciding between merging or having the orgs coexist.
Permanently maintain both orgs as separate silos with no future evaluation, since merging orgs is always too risky.
Immediately delete all data in the acquired company's org to avoid deduplication work.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Merging orgs is a significant undertaking with real risk of data loss and political friction from process standardization; a structured feasibility study is the appropriate first step before committing to either merge or coexist. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Merging within 90 days without assessing data overlap and process compatibility risks major data corruption and business disruption.
• C: Permanently avoiding evaluation ignores that coexistence has real long-term costs (duplicate licensing, fragmented reporting) that may outweigh merge risk.
• D: Deleting data without deduplication analysis destroys potentially critical business records and is not a legitimate strategy.

pdlda.question: System Design — A single Salesforce org supporting a high-volume contact center is regularly hitting synchronous SOQL query limits and CPU time limits during peak hours due to integration volume. What architectural approach should the architect evaluate first, before considering a multi-org split?

options.text: Immediately split the org into two separate orgs to spread the transaction volume.

Move high-volume, non-time-sensitive processing to asynchronous patterns (Queueable/Batch Apex, Platform Events) to flatten peak load within the existing single org before considering a more disruptive multi-org split.
Increase the number of System Administrator licenses to handle the load.
Disable all validation rules to reduce CPU time consumption during peak hours.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Async processing patterns directly address governor limit pressure caused by synchronous peak load without the massive organizational and technical cost of a multi-org split, which should be reserved for cases where single-org architecture genuinely cannot scale further. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Splitting into multiple orgs is a drastic, costly step that introduces significant integration and governance complexity, and should only be considered after less disruptive options are exhausted.
• C: Adding admin licenses has no effect on governor limits or transaction volume; it addresses a staffing concern, not a technical one.
• D: Disabling validation rules removes data integrity protections and does not meaningfully address CPU time consumption from the actual high-volume integration processing.

pdlda.question: System Design — Choose 2. An architect is deciding between a single-org and multi-org strategy for a company with two business units that share almost no customers, processes, or reporting needs, and one unit operates under separate regulatory data residency requirements. Which two factors most strongly justify a multi-org approach here? (Choose 2)

options.text: Regulatory data residency requirements mandating data separation between the business units.
Near-total lack of shared customers, processes, or reporting needs between the business units.
Both business units use the same corporate email domain.
Both business units want to use Lightning Experience instead of Salesforce Classic.
Both business units have fewer than 50 total users combined.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Regulatory data residency requirements are a hard driver for data isolation, and a near-total lack of shared data or process needs removes most of the benefit single-org architecture would otherwise provide (shared reporting, unified data model) — together these justify separate orgs. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Sharing an email domain is a corporate branding detail with no bearing on data architecture decisions.
• D: Lightning Experience is an interface choice available in either single-org or multi-org configurations; it doesn't drive the org-split decision.
• E: A small combined user count actually argues against the added operational overhead of multi-org, since governor limits and licensing costs are unlikely to be a constraint at that scale.

pdlda.question: System Design — A customer with five parallel development streams (three feature teams, a hotfix team, and a training initiative) asks you to design a sandbox environment hierarchy for an upcoming major release. Which structure best supports this without excessive risk of collision or drift?

options.text: A single shared Developer sandbox for all five streams to save on sandbox costs.

Individual Developer sandboxes per feature team, a shared Integration sandbox for merged work, a Partial Copy QA sandbox, a Partial Copy UAT sandbox, a Full Copy Staging sandbox, a dedicated hotfix sandbox kept near production parity, and a separate training sandbox refreshed only from UAT-approved builds.
One Full Copy sandbox shared by all teams including training, refreshed nightly.
No sandboxes at all; all five streams develop directly against production behind feature flags.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: This hierarchy isolates each feature team to prevent collisions, provides progressive convergence toward production-like environments for testing, keeps the hotfix path separate for emergency changes, and protects training from in-flight development churn. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: A single shared Developer sandbox across five parallel streams guarantees the exact metadata collision and attribution problems dedicated sandboxes are meant to prevent.
• C: Sharing one Full Copy sandbox across all streams including training mixes unreleased development work into the training environment and creates constant refresh conflicts (Full Copy refresh cycles are also much longer, at 29 days).
• D: Developing directly against production abandons any pre-production testing gate and is far riskier than even a minimal sandbox strategy.

pdlda.question: System Design — A team currently develops entirely in a single shared Full Copy sandbox and refreshes it only every 29 days, which is causing long waits whenever a developer needs a clean environment for a new feature. What environment change would most directly relieve this bottleneck for individual feature development, without abandoning production-like testing entirely?

options.text: Ask Salesforce support to reduce the Full Copy refresh interval to daily for this org.
Introduce Developer or Developer Pro sandboxes (refreshable every day) for individual feature development, reserving the Full Copy sandbox for staging/pre-production validation only.
Have every developer share login credentials to the same Developer sandbox to reduce the number of environments needed.
Eliminate the Full Copy sandbox entirely and do all testing, including staging validation, in scratch orgs.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Developer/Developer Pro sandboxes refresh every day and are purpose-built for individual feature work, relieving the wait time, while preserving the Full Copy sandbox's role for production-equivalent staging validation. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Salesforce does not allow arbitrary reduction of the Full Copy sandbox's fixed 29-day refresh interval.
• C: Shared credentials on one sandbox reintroduces the same collision problem the team is trying to avoid and provides no real isolation.
• D: Removing the Full Copy sandbox eliminates the production-equivalent data volume and configuration needed for meaningful staging and performance validation.

pdlda.question: System Design — A customer's QA sandbox refresh always resets custom setting values and unassigns permission sets that testers depend on, delaying every QA cycle by a day while admins manually reconfigure. How should the architect address this recurring pain point?

options.text: Stop refreshing the QA sandbox altogether to avoid the reconfiguration work.
Automate post-refresh setup steps (custom setting values, permission set assignments, test data seeding) as a scripted step that runs immediately after every scheduled refresh.
Assign System Administrator profile to all QA testers so permission sets are no longer needed.
Move QA testing into the Staging Full Copy sandbox instead, since it never needs to be refreshed.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Automating the post-refresh configuration steps removes the recurring manual delay while preserving the benefit of a regularly refreshed, production-aligned QA environment. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Never refreshing the QA sandbox reintroduces configuration drift and stale data, trading one problem for a worse one.
• C: Granting System Administrator to all testers bypasses the permission-based testing QA is meant to validate, undermining the purpose of the test cycle.
• D: Full Copy sandboxes also require refreshing (every 29 days) and post-refresh reconfiguration; moving testing there doesn't eliminate the underlying automation gap.

pdlda.question: System Design — A team currently uses Change Sets exclusively. They now need to delete three deprecated custom fields as part of an upcoming release, and also want an audit trail of exactly what was deployed and when. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Continue using Change Sets, and manually delete the deprecated fields directly in production after the Change Set deployment completes.
Migrate this deployment to Salesforce CLI using a package with a destructiveChanges.xml for the field deletions, tracked in source control to provide the audit trail Change Sets cannot offer.
Use the ANT Migration Tool exclusively going forward, since it is the modern standard for all Salesforce deployments.
Request that Salesforce support manually delete the fields in production on the team's behalf.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Change Sets cannot perform destructive changes in the same deployment and provide no deployment history; CLI deployments with a destructiveChanges.xml, tracked in source control, solve both the deletion requirement and the audit trail need. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Manually deleting fields directly in production after a Change Set deploy bypasses any tracked, auditable process and risks human error with no rollback record.
• C: The ANT Migration Tool is a legacy tool that has been superseded by Salesforce CLI; it is not the modern recommended standard.
• D: Salesforce support does not perform ad hoc metadata deletions on a customer's behalf as a substitute for the customer's own deployment tooling.

pdlda.question: System Design — Choose 2. A team is choosing a CI/CD platform for a new Salesforce program. They are already on GitHub for source control, want strong Salesforce CLI community support, and have no existing Jenkins infrastructure or dedicated DevOps engineers to maintain one. Which two factors should most strongly influence the recommendation toward GitHub Actions over Jenkins? (Choose 2)

options.text: GitHub Actions is native to GitHub repositories and has strong Salesforce community-maintained actions, reducing integration friction.
The team lacks the infrastructure and dedicated staff typically needed to self-host and maintain Jenkins.
Jenkins cannot technically run Salesforce CLI commands under any configuration.
GitHub Actions guarantees zero cost regardless of usage volume for any team size.
The team's preferred programming language is Apex.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Native GitHub integration with community-supported Salesforce actions minimizes setup friction, and the absence of Jenkins infrastructure or dedicated staff makes a self-hosted Jenkins deployment a poor operational fit — both point toward GitHub Actions. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Jenkins can absolutely run Salesforce CLI commands via shell steps in a Jenkinsfile; this claim is factually incorrect.
• D: GitHub Actions has usage-based billing beyond a free tier; it is not unconditionally free at every usage volume.
• E: Apex being the team's Salesforce language has no bearing on which CI/CD orchestration platform (which runs shell/CLI commands, not Apex itself) is appropriate.

pdlda.question: System Design — A customer wants to move off Change Sets but has a small admin-heavy team, a limited budget for third-party DevOps tooling, and is already using GitHub as their source of truth. Which native Salesforce release management option best fits this profile?

options.text: Salesforce DevOps Center, which provides a guided GUI experience with GitHub-based source control integration, pipeline visualization, and work item tracking without third-party licensing costs.
Copado, given its enterprise-grade governance and AI-assisted features.
A fully custom Jenkins pipeline built from scratch by the admin team.
Continue using Change Sets but add a shared spreadsheet to track what was deployed.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: DevOps Center is Salesforce-native, integrates with GitHub (already their SCM), provides a guided GUI suited to admin-heavy teams without deep CLI/CI expertise, and has no additional per-seat third-party licensing cost. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Copado is a strong enterprise platform but adds licensing cost this budget-constrained team explicitly wants to avoid.
• C: Building a custom Jenkins pipeline from scratch requires DevOps expertise this admin-heavy team does not have, contradicting the stated constraint.
• D: A spreadsheet doesn't address any of the core Change Set limitations (no destructive changes, no automated testing, no versioning) and isn't a genuine tooling upgrade.

pdlda.question: System Design — During a production deployment, an Apex class references a custom field that has not yet been deployed, causing the deployment to fail with a dependency error. The team deploys components individually rather than as a single package. What is the best architectural fix?

options.text: Rename the custom field to something unrelated so the dependency error no longer appears.

Bundle all interdependent components (the custom field and the Apex class that references it) into a single deployment package so the Metadata API can resolve dependencies together, or sequence foundational components first.
Convert the custom field to a formula field, which does not require dependency resolution.
Disable the Apex class temporarily and redeploy it manually after the field is confirmed to exist.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Metadata API deployments must respect component dependency order; bundling dependent components into a single deployment (or explicitly sequencing foundational components first) is the standard fix for this class of dependency failure. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Renaming the field does not address the underlying dependency ordering issue and would break other references to the original field name.
• C: Formula fields are still subject to the same dependency resolution rules as any other custom field; converting field type does not bypass this.
• D: Manually disabling and redeploying the Apex class separately doesn't establish a repeatable process and reintroduces the same risk on every future deployment involving dependencies.

pdlda.question: System Design — Choose 2. An architect is designing a CI/CD pipeline for a Salesforce program that must run Apex tests, static analysis, and metadata deployment as separate stages. Which two capabilities are essential for the pipeline to reliably gate promotion to production? (Choose 2)

options.text: A validation-only deployment stage that runs tests against the target org without committing changes, used to confirm deployability before a real deploy.
A static analysis stage (e.g., PMD or Salesforce Code Analyzer) that can fail the build on critical violations introduced in the change.
A stage that automatically increases the org's API request limit for the day.
A stage that renames all Apex classes to remove vowels for faster compilation.
A stage that permanently disables all validation rules in the target org before every deployment.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A validation-only deploy stage confirms deployability and test pass rate without side effects, and a static analysis gate catches code-quality regressions before they reach production — both are standard, essential quality gates in a Salesforce CI/CD pipeline. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: There is no pipeline stage that increases an org's daily API limit; this is not a real capability.
• D: Renaming classes to remove vowels is nonsensical and would break every reference to those classes; it has no relationship to compilation speed.
• E: Permanently disabling validation rules removes real data integrity protections and is a governance anti-pattern, not a legitimate pipeline stage.

pdlda.question: System Design — A team's current package-based project has three unlocked packages: a Utilities package with shared Apex helper classes, a Billing package that calls those helpers, and a Reporting package that depends on Billing. During a deployment, Reporting fails to install because Billing hasn't been installed yet in the target org. What is the correct architectural fix?

options.text: Merge all three packages into a single package to eliminate dependency management entirely.
Declare the dependency relationships explicitly in sfdx-project.json (Reporting depends on Billing, Billing depends on Utilities) so the tooling installs packages in the correct order automatically.
Rename the Reporting package so it alphabetically sorts before Billing, forcing earlier installation.
Remove the dependency on Billing from Reporting's code without changing any functionality.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Explicitly declaring package dependencies in sfdx-project.json lets Salesforce CLI resolve and enforce the correct installation order automatically, which is exactly the mechanism designed to prevent this class of failure. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Merging all packages into one eliminates the modular, independently releasable architecture the team presumably chose unlocked packages to achieve in the first place.
• C: Alphabetical naming has no effect on Salesforce CLI's package installation order, which is driven by declared dependencies, not naming.
• D: Removing the dependency without changing functionality is not actually possible if Reporting's code genuinely calls Billing's components; this would break the application.

pdlda.question: System Design — A customer's current deployment approach uses raw Metadata API calls scripted by hand, and the developer who understands the dependency ordering is leaving the company. Leadership wants to reduce reliance on tribal knowledge for handling deployment dependencies going forward. What is the best long-term recommendation?

options.text: Document the departing developer's knowledge in a single onboarding email and hope future developers read it.
Adopt a DevOps tool (e.g., Copado, Gearset) or Salesforce DevOps Center that automatically resolves and manages component dependency order, reducing reliance on any one individual's manual knowledge.
Ask the departing developer to stay on call indefinitely after leaving to answer dependency questions.
Freeze all further deployments until a replacement developer with equivalent tribal knowledge is hired.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Tooling that automates dependency resolution converts tribal knowledge into a repeatable, tool-enforced process, directly reducing single-person-dependency risk going forward. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: A single onboarding email is not a durable knowledge transfer mechanism and doesn't scale as the team or metadata complexity grows.
• C: Relying on an indefinite on-call arrangement with a former employee is not a sustainable or professionally realistic risk mitigation.
• D: Freezing all deployments indefinitely halts business value delivery entirely rather than addressing the actual knowledge-transfer gap.

# Building

pdlda.question: Building — A high-maturity Salesforce team commits to a single main branch multiple times daily, using feature flags to hide incomplete work, and relies on strong automated test coverage. A new architect proposes switching to Gitflow with long-lived develop, release, and hotfix branches. What should you advise?

options.text: Adopt Gitflow immediately, since long-lived branches are always safer than trunk-based development regardless of team maturity.

Keep trunk-based development, since it already fits this team's high test automation maturity and frequent integration cadence; switching to Gitflow would introduce longer-lived branches and higher merge conflict risk without a corresponding benefit.
Adopt Gitflow only for hotfixes while keeping trunk-based development for everything else, without any team discussion.
Abandon branching entirely and have all developers commit directly to production metadata.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Trunk-based development is well-suited to teams with strong test automation and frequent integration; introducing Gitflow's long-lived branches would raise merge conflict risk in large metadata files without addressing any actual problem this team has. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Gitflow's long-lived branches are not universally safer — they increase merge conflict risk in Salesforce's large XML metadata files, which is a real cost for high-maturity teams.
• C: Mixing branching models ad hoc without evaluating trade-offs or aligning the team creates confusion rather than addressing an actual limitation of trunk-based development.
• D: Eliminating branching entirely removes any isolation for in-progress work and is not a serious source control strategy.

pdlda.question: Building — A critical production bug is found while a large feature branch is mid-development and not yet ready to release. The team needs to ship a hotfix without releasing the incomplete feature. What is the correct branching approach?

options.text: Merge the entire feature branch into production early just to access the hotfix code needed.

Create the hotfix branch from the production release tag (not from the in-progress feature or develop branch), fix and test it there, deploy it to production, then merge the hotfix back into develop and all active feature branches to prevent regression.
Apply the hotfix only to the feature branch, assuming it will naturally reach production once the feature ships.
Wait until the feature branch is complete and ship the hotfix bundled with the full feature release.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Branching the hotfix from the production tag isolates it from incomplete feature work, allowing an independent fast-tracked fix, and merging it back into all active branches afterward prevents the next regular release from silently reverting the fix. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Merging the entire incomplete feature branch into production to access hotfix code would release unfinished, untested functionality to end users.
• C: Applying the fix only to the feature branch means production remains broken until that unrelated feature ships, which could be weeks away.
• D: Bundling a critical fix with an unrelated feature release delays resolution of a production-impacting issue for no technical reason.

pdlda.question: Building — An admin makes several Flow and Page Layout changes directly in a sandbox as part of routine work, but forgets to retrieve them into source control before the sandbox is refreshed the following week, losing the changes. What process gap does this reveal, and what is the best fix?

options.text: Ban admins from making any declarative changes in sandboxes going forward.

Establish a mandatory 'retrieve and commit' step as part of every admin's daily workflow (or adopt source-tracked sandboxes/scratch orgs that automate change detection) so declarative changes are captured before any refresh.
Extend the sandbox refresh interval to once a year so this happens less often.
Require the admin to manually recreate the exact same Flow and Layout changes from memory after every refresh.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A disciplined retrieve-and-commit habit, or source-tracked environments that detect changes automatically, directly closes the gap between declarative work happening in a sandbox and it being captured in the permanent source-of-truth repository. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Banning declarative changes in sandboxes is impractical since admins routinely need to build and test Flows and layouts there.
• C: A longer refresh interval reduces frequency of loss but doesn't address the underlying process gap, and delays legitimate refresh needs for other reasons.
• D: Relying on memory to recreate lost configuration work is unreliable and not a real process fix.

pdlda.question: Building — Two developers each modify the same Profile XML file in separate feature branches, and merging causes a large, unreadable XML conflict that takes hours to resolve manually. What architectural change would most reduce this recurring problem going forward?

options.text: Have both developers always work on the same feature branch to avoid any possibility of conflicts.
Shift permission management from Profiles to Permission Sets where possible, reducing the size and conflict surface of Profile XML files, and keep feature branches short-lived to limit divergence.
Store all Profile changes as screenshots instead of XML so Git cannot flag conflicts.
Disable all permission changes for the remainder of the project.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Moving permission logic to Permission Sets directly shrinks Profile XML size and the resulting conflict surface, while short-lived branches limit how much divergence accumulates before a merge — both are established mitigations for this exact metadata conflict pattern. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Forcing both developers onto one branch defeats the purpose of feature isolation and doesn't scale as team size grows.
• C: Screenshots aren't deployable metadata and would break the actual deployment pipeline entirely; Git also cannot version or diff images meaningfully for this purpose.
• D: Disabling all permission changes halts legitimate development work rather than addressing the metadata conflict pattern.

pdlda.question: Building — After a production incident, the team wants a reliable way to identify the exact previous stable release to roll back to, and to correlate that release with its CAB approval record. What practice should the architect ensure is in place?

options.text: Rely on commit timestamps alone, since they are always sufficient to identify release boundaries.

Apply Git tags using semantic versioning at every production deployment, scripted into the CI/CD pipeline so tagging is never skipped, providing a clear rollback point and audit correlation to CAB approval records.
Keep no tags at all and instead ask developers to recall which commit was deployed from memory.
Tag only major releases, skipping minor and patch releases entirely.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Automated semantic version tagging at every production deployment gives a precise, unambiguous rollback point and a natural anchor to correlate with change records and CAB approvals — exactly what's needed for reliable incident recovery. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Commit timestamps alone don't indicate which commits constituted an actual deployed release boundary, especially with multiple merges close together.
• C: Relying on memory is unreliable and unauditable, especially under the pressure of an active incident.
• D: Skipping minor/patch tags leaves no precise rollback point for the majority of releases, which are typically minor or patch level.

pdlda.question: Building — A team's Apex trigger passes all its unit tests, but silently fails in production during a bulk data load of 500 records, hitting a governor limit. Code review revealed the tests only ever inserted a single record. What testing practice gap caused this to go undetected?

options.text: The team should have added more single-record tests with different field values.
The team failed to include a bulk unit test that inserts 200+ records in a single DML operation to verify the trigger's bulkified behavior under governor limits.
The team should have disabled the trigger in production to avoid the failure.
The team should have run the single-record test more frequently in CI.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Triggers must handle bulk operations correctly; a bulk test with 200+ records in a single DML statement is the standard way to catch governor-limit and non-bulkified logic issues before they reach production. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Additional single-record tests with varied field values would still never exercise the bulk code path where the actual defect lives.
• C: Disabling the trigger removes its business functionality entirely rather than fixing the underlying bulkification defect.
• D: Running the same single-record test more often doesn't change what scenario it covers; frequency isn't the issue, scope is.

pdlda.question: Building — A team's Apex tests all pass in the sandbox where they were written, but the exact same tests fail intermittently when run in a different sandbox. Investigation shows several test classes are annotated with SeeAllData=true and depend on existing Opportunity records with specific stage values. What is the root cause and fix?

options.text: The root cause is a Salesforce platform bug; file a support case and wait for a fix.

The root cause is environment-dependent test data caused by SeeAllData=true; the fix is to remove SeeAllData=true wherever possible and create all needed test data within the test itself (or in @testSetup), reserving SeeAllData=true only for cases that strictly require it, like standard price books.
The root cause is insufficient code coverage; add more assertions to the existing tests without changing their data dependency.
The root cause is a missing index on the Opportunity object; ask an admin to add one.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: SeeAllData=true makes tests dependent on whatever real records happen to exist in a given org, which is exactly why the same test behaves differently across sandboxes; removing it in favor of self-contained test data eliminates that environment dependency. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: This is a well-documented anti-pattern in test design, not a platform defect, so a support case would not resolve it.
• C: Adding assertions doesn't address the underlying data dependency causing environment-specific pass/fail behavior.
• D: Missing indexes affect query performance, not the presence or absence of specific Opportunity records with certain stage values that the test depends on.

pdlda.question: Building — A team wants to verify that users without a specific permission set cannot view or edit a sensitive custom field, as part of their Apex test suite. Which testing approach correctly validates this?

options.text: Query the field's metadata definition in a test and assert its type is Text.
Wrap the test logic in System.runAs(testUserWithoutPermission) to execute the DML/query operations in that user's security context, and assert that FLS/sharing restrictions are correctly enforced.
Run the test as the default test-running user (typically an admin) and assume permission enforcement is automatically validated.
Manually log in as that user in production after deployment to visually check the page layout.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: System.runAs() executes code in a specified user's security context, enforcing sharing rules, FLS, and CRUD permissions, which is precisely the mechanism needed to test permission-based access restrictions in Apex. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Checking a field's declared data type says nothing about field-level security enforcement for a specific user's permissions.
• C: The default test-running context typically runs with elevated System Administrator-like access, which would not surface a permission restriction that should apply to a lower-privilege user.
• D: Manually checking in production after deployment is not an automated, repeatable unit test and defeats the purpose of having this validation caught before release.

pdlda.question: Building — A team building Apex that calls an external REST service needs to unit test the callout logic without making real HTTP requests during test execution (which Salesforce does not allow anyway). What is the correct approach?

options.text: Skip testing the callout logic entirely and exclude that method from code coverage requirements.

Implement a class that implements HttpCalloutMock, override its respond() method to return a predefined HttpResponse, and register it with Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mockInstance) before invoking the code under test.
Deploy the code without tests first, then add tests after confirming it works by manually calling the real endpoint from Execute Anonymous in production.
Use SeeAllData=true so the test can make an actual outbound HTTP callout to the real service.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: HttpCalloutMock combined with Test.setMock() is the standard Apex testing pattern for deterministically simulating external HTTP responses, since real callouts are disallowed during test execution. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Excluding callout logic from coverage leaves a significant, often error-prone code path completely unverified.
• C: Manually testing in production via Execute Anonymous is not a repeatable automated test and bypasses the standard unit test requirement entirely.
• D: SeeAllData=true controls visibility to org data, not outbound HTTP behavior; Apex tests cannot make real callouts regardless of that annotation.

pdlda.question: Building — A customer currently deploys all customizations as one large monolithic set of metadata via Change Sets across a single sandbox path, and wants to move toward a more modular, scalable architecture as their team grows to 15 developers. Which development model transition should the architect recommend?

options.text: Stay with org-based development and Change Sets indefinitely, since team size has no bearing on development model choice.

Transition toward package-based development, likely starting with unlocked packages that decompose the org into bounded domains (e.g., Account, Billing), enabling independent, modular releases as the team scales.
Immediately adopt fully namespaced managed packages, even though there is no plan to distribute externally.
Switch every developer to work only in the production org directly, since that removes the need for packaging altogether.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: As team size and codebase complexity grow, package-based development with unlocked packages provides the modularity, independent release cadence, and source-driven structure needed to scale beyond what monolithic org-based Change Set deployments can support. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Team size and codebase complexity are exactly the factors that make monolithic Change Set deployment increasingly unmanageable, contradicting this option's claim.
• C: Managed packages require a namespace and are designed for external ISV distribution with IP protection; adopting one for purely internal modularity adds unnecessary constraints and irreversible namespace commitment.
• D: Working directly in production removes all pre-production safety and testing, and has nothing to do with modularity or packaging.

pdlda.question: Building — A developer's scratch org is set to expire in 3 days, but their feature branch work is not yet complete and would take another two weeks. What is the correct way to avoid losing their work?

options.text: Do nothing; scratch orgs automatically extend themselves indefinitely if work is still incomplete.

Ensure all changes are committed and pushed to source control regularly (the permanent record), and either extend the scratch org's duration (up to the 30-day maximum) or recreate a new scratch org from source control and re-seed it when needed.
Copy the entire scratch org database to a local spreadsheet as a backup before it expires.
Convert the scratch org into a Developer sandbox to avoid the expiration policy.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Since scratch orgs are inherently temporary (max 30 days) and all work is lost at expiration, the safe pattern is treating source control as the permanent record via frequent commits, and extending or recreating the scratch org as needed. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Scratch orgs do not auto-extend; they expire strictly according to their configured duration regardless of whether work is finished.
• C: Metadata and configuration in a scratch org cannot be meaningfully captured as a spreadsheet backup; this isn't how Salesforce metadata is structured or restorable.
• D: There is no supported conversion path from a scratch org to a Developer sandbox; they are fundamentally different environment types.

pdlda.question: Building — A code review checklist currently only checks for compiling code and passing tests. After several incidents involving SOQL queries inside loops causing governor limit failures in production, the architect wants to strengthen the review process. What should be added, and how should it be enforced?

options.text: Add a note to the team wiki asking developers to remember not to put SOQL in loops, with no automated enforcement.

Integrate a static analysis tool such as PMD or Salesforce Code Analyzer into the CI pipeline with a rule that flags SOQL-in-loop and DML-in-loop patterns, configured to fail the build on such violations introduced in a pull request.
Require every pull request to be reviewed by the entire engineering organization before merging.
Remove code review from the process entirely and rely solely on production monitoring to catch these issues after deployment.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Automated static analysis rules for SOQL/DML-in-loop patterns catch this exact defect class consistently and objectively in CI, before code reaches production, which is far more reliable than relying on memory during manual review. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: A wiki note with no automated enforcement relies purely on individual developers remembering a rule, which is exactly the failure mode that caused the incidents.
• C: Requiring the entire organization to review every PR doesn't specifically target this defect pattern and creates an unsustainable review bottleneck.
• D: Removing code review and relying only on production monitoring means the defect reaches production before being caught, which is strictly worse than a pre-merge gate.

pdlda.question: Building — A team introduces a hard static analysis gate that fails any build with a single PMD violation, on a 5-year-old codebase with over 800 existing violations. Within a week, all pull requests are blocked and developers are bypassing the pipeline entirely to ship code. What went wrong, and what is the better approach?

options.text: Nothing went wrong; the team should simply fix all 800 violations before doing any other work.

The hard gate should have used a 'ratchet' approach — failing builds only on new violations introduced in the pull request's diff, while reporting (not blocking on) the pre-existing violations, allowing the team to progressively pay down debt without halting delivery.
The static analysis tool should be permanently removed from the pipeline since it caused this disruption.
The severity threshold should be raised so no violations are ever flagged, regardless of type.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A ratchet approach — gating only on newly introduced violations — lets a legacy codebase adopt static analysis without an impossible all-or-nothing remediation blocking all delivery, which is the standard pattern for introducing hard gates into brownfield code. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Demanding all 800 violations be fixed before any other work proceeds is unrealistic and exactly the all-or-nothing trap that caused developers to bypass the pipeline.
• C: Removing static analysis entirely throws away real code quality value instead of fixing the rollout approach that caused the disruption.
• D: Setting the threshold so nothing is ever flagged defeats the entire purpose of static analysis and leaves no quality gate at all.

pdlda.question: Building — A pull request author and the person who deploys that same change to production are, per current process, frequently the same individual, with no independent review. After a compliance audit flags this, what change should the architect recommend?

options.text: Continue the current process but add a note in the ticket saying the author reviewed their own work.

Require a minimum of one independent peer reviewer approval on every pull request (with a tech lead review for major changes), and ensure the person deploying to production is not the sole author of the change, to satisfy segregation of duties.
Eliminate the pull request process entirely to speed up delivery.
Allow the author to approve their own pull request as long as they wait 24 hours before merging.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Segregation of duties requires that the person authoring a change is not the sole approver or deployer of that same change; mandatory independent peer review directly satisfies this compliance requirement. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: A self-review note does not constitute independent review and would not satisfy a segregation-of-duties compliance requirement.
• C: Eliminating PR review entirely removes any quality or compliance gate rather than fixing the self-approval problem.
• D: A time delay does not introduce an independent reviewer; the same individual is still both author and sole approver, which is the exact issue being audited.

# Deploying

pdlda.question: Deploying — A team needs to deploy 8,500 metadata components in a single release, including new custom objects, fields, Apex classes, and Lightning components, to a connected sandbox that is not the org they originally developed in. Change Sets aren't an option since it isn't a directly connected org. What deployment approach should they use?

options.text: Manually recreate every component by hand in the target org through Setup.

Use Metadata API (via Salesforce CLI) to deploy the package to the target org, since it supports deployment to any connected org (not just point-to-point) and can handle large component counts up to the API's per-deployment file limit.
Use the ANT Migration Tool exclusively, since Metadata API cannot handle more than 100 components per deployment.
Split the deployment into ten separate Change Sets and deploy them sequentially between the same two orgs over several days.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Metadata API (accessed via CLI) can deploy to any connected org regardless of a pre-established Change Set connection, and supports large deployments (up to 10,000 files per deploy), making it the right tool for this scenario. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Manually recreating 8,500 components is operationally infeasible and defeats the purpose of having deployment tooling at all.
• C: The claim that Metadata API is limited to 100 components is false; it supports far larger deployments, and ANT is a legacy tool with no advantage here.
• D: Change Sets require a point-to-point deployment connection between the specific orgs involved, which the scenario states doesn't exist here; splitting into multiple Change Sets doesn't solve that missing connection.

pdlda.question: Deploying — A release includes a change to a Connected App's OAuth configuration and a new Custom Setting with default values that integrations depend on. The team assumes their standard Metadata API deployment will fully handle both. What should the architect flag?

options.text: Both items deploy completely automatically with no manual steps required.

The Connected App metadata type is deployable but its OAuth consumer key/secret must be reconfigured manually in the target org; and while the Custom Setting object type is deployable, the actual data/default values held in Custom Settings records typically require a separate step (Data Loader, CLI data commands, or Hierarchy default values) beyond the base metadata deploy.
Custom Settings can never be deployed by any means and must always be entered manually field by field with no automation option.
Connected Apps cannot be included in any Metadata API deployment under any circumstances.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: These are documented Metadata API limitations — OAuth secrets require manual reconfiguration per org for security reasons, and Custom Settings data (versus the object type itself) typically needs a separate data deployment step, both of which should be called out explicitly in the deployment runbook. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Assuming full automation for these two specific items risks a broken integration post-deployment since manual/separate steps are genuinely required.
• C: Custom Settings data can be deployed via automated means like CLI data commands; claiming it can never be automated overstates the limitation.
• D: Connected App metadata itself is deployable via Metadata API; only the OAuth secret requires manual reconfiguration, not the entire component.

pdlda.question: Deploying — A team needs to permanently remove two deprecated custom fields and one Apex class from production as part of an upcoming release, using Salesforce CLI. What is the correct mechanism, and what key risk should be flagged?

options.text: Simply omit the components from the package.xml; Metadata API will automatically infer they should be deleted.
