Include a destructiveChanges.xml (or destructiveChangesPre.xml if deletion must precede additive changes) listing the components to delete, alongside the package.xml; flag that Salesforce has no native one-click rollback for destructive deployments, so a backup of the current metadata should be taken first.
Use a Change Set, which fully supports combining destructive and additive changes in a single deployment.
Ask end users to manually delete the fields and class themselves after the deployment completes.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Destructive changes require an explicit destructiveChanges.xml (or Pre variant) in the deployment package; because there's no native rollback for deletions, taking a metadata backup beforehand is the standard risk mitigation. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Omitting a component from package.xml simply means it isn't touched by that deployment; Metadata API does not infer deletion intent from absence.
• C: Change Sets explicitly do not support combining destructive and additive changes in the same deployment, unlike CLI-based Metadata API deployments.
• D: Asking end users, who typically lack the necessary permissions and expertise, to manually delete metadata components is not a controlled or auditable release process.

pdlda.question: Deploying — A production deployment fails midway due to an unrelated validation error in a component nobody intended to change, and the team has no documented way to know what production looked like immediately beforehand. What deployment practice gap does this expose?

options.text: The team should have deployed on a Friday afternoon to reduce user impact.

The team lacked a pre-deployment backup of current production metadata (a 'rollback package' retrieved and stored in source control) and a validated rollback procedure, both of which should be standard pre-deployment checklist items.
The team should stop using Metadata API entirely and switch exclusively to manual Setup changes.
The team should have skipped running any tests to save time before this deployment.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Retrieving and storing a pre-deployment metadata snapshot, and having a validated rollback procedure, is the standard mitigation for exactly this situation — an unexpected mid-deployment failure with no clear path back to the prior known-good state. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Deployment timing doesn't address the missing backup and rollback procedure, which is the actual structural gap.
• C: Abandoning Metadata API in favor of manual Setup changes removes automation and traceability entirely, making the situation worse, not better.
• D: Skipping tests would increase risk further and has no relationship to having a documented rollback path.

pdlda.question: Deploying — Choose 2. A team plans a production deployment during a defined maintenance window and needs to prevent user-triggered automation from firing on records created or modified as part of the deployment or related data scripts. Which two pre-deployment steps should be included in the runbook to mitigate this? (Choose 2)

options.text: Deactivate the specific Flows, Process Builders, or workflow rules that could trigger unintended automation during the deployment window, with a plan to reactivate them post-deployment.
Pause any scheduled batch jobs that could run and interact with data during the deployment window.
Permanently delete all automation in the org so it can never interfere with any future deployment.
Grant every user temporary System Administrator access during the deployment window.
Change all users' passwords immediately before the deployment begins.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Temporarily deactivating relevant automation and pausing scheduled jobs during the deployment window are standard, reversible pre-deployment steps that prevent unintended automation firing on in-flight changes without permanently altering the org's configuration. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Permanently deleting automation removes legitimate business logic the org depends on well beyond the deployment window, which is a drastically disproportionate and irreversible step.
• D: Granting every user admin access during a deployment window is a serious security risk and has no relationship to preventing automation from firing.
• E: Forcing a password change has no effect on whether Flows, Process Builders, or workflow rules fire during the deployment.

pdlda.question: Deploying — After a production deployment completes successfully, several new permission sets exist in the org but no users have access to the features they were built to expose, and a new record type isn't showing up on any page layout assignment. What deployment step was likely missed?

options.text: The Metadata API deployment itself failed silently and needs to be re-run from scratch.

The post-deployment steps — assigning the new permission sets to appropriate users/public groups and updating page layout assignments for the new record type — were not executed, since these actions are typically not automated by the metadata deployment itself.
The org has reached its permission set license limit, which is why nothing appears.
Custom Metadata Types need to be manually re-enabled after every deployment for any new features to appear.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Permission set assignment to users/groups and layout assignment for new record types are common post-deployment activities that Metadata API deployment does not automatically perform; they must be executed as explicit post-deploy steps in the runbook. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: The scenario states the deployment completed successfully; a silent full failure would typically surface as missing metadata entirely, not just missing assignments.
• C: A permission set license limit would produce an explicit licensing error, not simply an absence of any user assignment.
• D: Custom Metadata Types have no bearing on permission set assignment or record type layout visibility; this is an invented mechanism.

pdlda.question: Deploying — A release introduces a new required field on the Account object that must be populated for all 2 million existing Account records before the dependent Apex validation goes live, or the validation will block every subsequent Account update. What is the best approach to handle this?

options.text: Deploy the validation rule first and let users manually populate the field on each Account as they happen to edit it.

Run a backfill data migration (via Batch Apex or a bulk data tool) to populate the new field on all existing records as a scheduled pre- or post-deployment step, validated first in a staging sandbox, before or alongside activating the dependent validation.
Apply the required field and validation rule only to newly created Accounts going forward, ignoring the 2 million existing records entirely.
Ask each of the org's business users to manually export and re-import their own subset of Account records with the field populated.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A scheduled batch backfill, tested first in staging, ensures the new required field is populated across all existing records before the dependent validation is enforced, avoiding a mass lockout of Account updates. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Deploying the validation before the backfill means any user editing an Account without the new field populated would be immediately blocked, causing widespread disruption.
• C: Ignoring existing records leaves 2 million Accounts permanently unable to satisfy the new business rule, and validation logic often needs to apply org-wide, not just to new records.
• D: Relying on individual business users to manually export/import data at this scale is unrealistic, error-prone, and not a controlled data migration process.

pdlda.question: Deploying — Choose 2. A deployment package includes a new Flow that references a custom field, and an Apex class that calls that Flow. The team deploys everything as a single package.xml with no destructive changes involved. Which two statements about dependency handling are accurate for this deployment? (Choose 2)

options.text: Deploying all interdependent components (the custom field, Flow, and Apex class) together in a single package deployment lets Metadata API resolve their interdependencies without requiring manual ordering.
If the custom field the Flow references doesn't already exist in the target org and isn't included in this same deployment, the deployment will fail due to the missing dependency.
Metadata API deployments never fail due to missing dependencies as long as test coverage is above 75%.
Flows and Apex are deployed via entirely separate APIs that cannot be combined in the same deployment transaction.
Destructive changes must always be included in every deployment package regardless of whether anything is being deleted.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Bundling interdependent components together lets the platform resolve their dependencies as part of one atomic deployment, and a genuinely missing dependency (the field neither existing nor included) will cause deployment failure regardless of test coverage. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Code coverage percentage is unrelated to whether component dependencies (like a missing custom field) resolve correctly; coverage is a separate deployment gate.
• D: Flows and Apex classes are both deployable via Metadata API and can be included in the very same deployment package and transaction.
• E: Destructive changes files are only needed when components are actually being deleted; they are not a mandatory part of every deployment.

pdlda.question: Deploying — A team wants to reduce production deployment downtime for a release that was already validated successfully two days ago with all tests passing at 82% coverage. No metadata has changed in the target org since that validation. What deployment option should they use?

options.text: Re-run a full deployment with RunAllTests to be extra safe, even though this significantly increases deployment time.

Use Quick Deploy to deploy the already-validated changes without re-running tests, since the validation succeeded within the last 10 days, coverage requirements were already met, and no changes have been made to the validated metadata since.
Deploy with NoTestRun, since the Apex classes were already tested two days ago and don't need to be tested again in this specific deployment.
Wait an additional 8 days so the validation is closer to its expiration before deploying.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Quick Deploy is designed exactly for this scenario — a successful validation within the 10-day window, met coverage thresholds, and no subsequent metadata changes — allowing deployment without re-running tests and significantly reducing downtime. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Re-running RunAllTests when Quick Deploy is available defeats the entire purpose of validating in advance and unnecessarily extends the deployment window.
• C: NoTestRun is rejected by Salesforce for any production deployment that includes Apex; it is not a valid way to skip tests based on a prior test run.
• D: Waiting longer only risks exceeding the 10-day Quick Deploy eligibility window, increasing risk rather than reducing it.

pdlda.question: Deploying — A customer wants to store integration endpoint URLs and feature toggle values in a way that can be included directly in their deployment package and version-controlled like other metadata, since these values must be consistent and auditable across dev, QA, and staging. Which storage mechanism should the architect recommend, and why?

options.text: Custom Settings, since their records are metadata and are automatically included in every Metadata API deployment package alongside the object type.

Custom Metadata Types, since their records are themselves metadata (not object data), can be queried in SOQL, and can be included directly in a deployment package and version-controlled, unlike Custom Setting record data.
Standard picklist values on a custom field, since picklists are inherently deployable and versioned.
A spreadsheet maintained outside Salesforce and manually re-entered into each environment after every deployment.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Custom Metadata Type records are metadata, not object data, meaning they deploy with the package and are naturally version-controlled and consistent across environments, exactly matching the stated requirement. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Custom Settings records are object data, not metadata; only the Custom Setting's structure (the object type) deploys automatically, not the actual field values within its records.
• C: Picklist values represent a fixed list of options for a field, not structured configuration records with multiple attributes like endpoint URLs; this doesn't fit the described need.
• D: A manually maintained external spreadsheet reintroduces the exact consistency and auditability problem the customer is trying to solve by moving away from manual re-entry.

pdlda.question: Deploying — A support team needs a specific integration endpoint URL to differ between the Staging and Production orgs, while the underlying Apex logic that queries it stays identical across both. Using Custom Metadata Types, what is the correct approach?

options.text: Hardcode both URLs directly in the Apex class using an if/else statement checking the org's OrgId, then redeploy the class whenever a URL changes.

Create Custom Metadata Type records with an environment identifier field (or separate per-environment records), and have Apex query the correct record deterministically at runtime; deploy the appropriate record(s) to each environment as part of the release, or manage them independently per org outside the deployed package.
Store both URLs as hardcoded string literals inside a single Apex trigger with no metadata record involved.
Manually type the URL into the Setup UI in a random location in Production every time it changes, without touching any deployment artifact.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Using CMT records with an environment identifier (or per-environment records managed separately) lets identical Apex logic query the correct configuration value deterministically per org, cleanly separating environment-specific configuration from code logic. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Hardcoding URLs in an if/else statement means any URL change requires a full class redeployment, defeating the purpose of externalized configuration.
• C: Storing configuration values as string literals in a trigger mixes configuration with code and requires redeployment for any value change, the opposite of a clean CMT-based approach.
• D: Manually entering values with no deployment artifact or tracking mechanism reintroduces the same auditability and consistency problems CMT is meant to solve.

pdlda.question: Deploying — A customer's release includes updated Report Type metadata and several new Dashboards, along with a request to have those dashboards automatically emailed to a specific distribution list every Monday. The team assumes the entire configuration, including the schedule, will deploy via Metadata API. What should the architect flag?

options.text: Report Type metadata and Dashboard XML are generally deployable via Metadata API, but dashboard running-user settings and scheduled subscription/email delivery configuration are typically not part of the deployable metadata and must be configured manually in the target org after deployment.
Reports and Dashboards cannot be deployed via Metadata API under any circumstances and must always be manually recreated from scratch in each org.
Scheduled dashboard email delivery is fully included in the Metadata API package and requires no manual configuration whatsoever.
Reports and Dashboards deploy automatically only if the org has Report Builder enabled as a separate paid add-on.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: While the structural metadata (report types, dashboard XML) is deployable, operational settings like the dashboard's running user and scheduled email subscriptions are execution-time configuration that typically requires manual setup after deployment, and this should be explicitly documented in the runbook. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Report Type metadata and Dashboard definitions are, in fact, deployable via Metadata API; claiming they can never be deployed is incorrect.
• C: Scheduled email subscriptions are specifically one of the manual, non-deployable configuration items that must be set up after deployment, not something the package handles automatically.
• D: There is no such paid add-on requirement gating whether report/dashboard metadata deploys; this is a fabricated constraint.

pdlda.question: Deploying — A CI pipeline is configured to deploy to production using RunSpecifiedTests, listing only the five test classes the developer believes are relevant to their change. The deployment succeeds, but a production incident later reveals an untested code path in an unrelated class was broken by a shared utility change. What deployment testing gap does this reveal?

options.text: RunSpecifiedTests guarantees org-wide 75% coverage automatically regardless of which tests are listed, so this could not have been prevented.

RunSpecifiedTests only validates 75% coverage for the specific classes being deployed based on the specified tests, not org-wide impact; when a shared/utility component changes, the team should ensure tests covering all its dependents are included, or use RunLocalTests for changes to broadly shared components.
The incident was purely a platform bug unrelated to test selection strategy.
NoTestRun should have been used instead, since it provides broader test coverage than RunSpecifiedTests.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: RunSpecifiedTests coverage requirements apply narrowly to the deployed components covered by the listed tests, not the whole org; changes to widely shared/utility code require broader test selection (or RunLocalTests) to catch downstream impacts across dependent classes. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: RunSpecifiedTests does not guarantee org-wide coverage; it only confirms 75% coverage for the specific deployed components based on the tests actually run.
• C: This is a direct consequence of test selection scope, not an unrelated platform defect.
• D: NoTestRun skips test execution entirely for Apex-inclusive deployments to production and would be rejected by Salesforce; it does not provide broader coverage than RunSpecifiedTests.

pdlda.question: Deploying — Choose 2. An architect is reviewing a customer's approach to managing environment-specific reference data (e.g., differing tax rate tables between a UAT and Production org) that Apex code depends on at runtime. Which two approaches are valid, given the trade-offs between deployability and flexibility? (Choose 2)

options.text: Store the values as Custom Metadata Type records included directly in the deployed package, giving strong deployability and version control at the cost of needing a new package version for every value change.

Store the values in Custom Settings and use Salesforce CLI data commands or a scripted post-deploy step to set the correct environment-specific values after each deployment, trading some deployment automation for more flexible, code-free updates.
Hardcode both the UAT and Production tax rate values directly inside a shared Apex trigger with no conditional logic distinguishing environments.
Store the values only in a developer's personal notes app, to be manually re-entered from memory whenever asked.
Disable all tax calculation logic in UAT permanently so the values never need to be managed there at all.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Both CMT-in-package and Custom-Settings-with-scripted-post-deploy-values are legitimate, documented patterns for managing environment-specific reference data, each with a real trade-off between strict deployability/versioning and flexible, code-free updates. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Hardcoding both environments' values with no conditional logic to distinguish them means the wrong value could apply in either org, and any change requires a full class redeploy.
• D: Personal notes with no system of record provide no auditability, consistency, or deployability whatsoever.
• E: Disabling tax logic in UAT prevents any meaningful testing of tax-related functionality before it reaches production, undermining the purpose of the UAT environment.

# Testing

pdlda.question: Testing — A customer's current test approach is almost entirely manual UI testing performed by a QA team over a full week before every release, with very few Apex unit tests. Releases have slowed as functionality has grown. What testing methodology shift should the architect recommend?

options.text: Hire more manual QA testers to cover the growing functionality faster.

Rebalance toward the testing pyramid: invest heavily in fast, developer-owned Apex unit tests as the broad base, add focused integration tests for cross-component behavior, and reserve manual/UI testing for a smaller set of high-value end-to-end and exploratory scenarios.
Eliminate all manual testing immediately and rely solely on UI automation for every test case, including trivial unit-level logic.
Extend the QA week to two weeks to allow more thorough manual coverage without changing the test mix.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Rebalancing toward the testing pyramid — more cheap, fast unit tests at the base and fewer expensive manual/UI tests at the top — reduces cycle time while improving defect detection, which directly addresses the slowing release cadence. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Adding more manual testers scales cost linearly with functionality growth without addressing the inverted, slow-by-design pyramid shape causing the bottleneck.
• C: Replacing all manual testing with UI automation, including trivial unit-level logic, misapplies UI automation to cases better and more cheaply covered by fast unit tests.
• D: Extending the QA week without changing the test mix just accepts a slower cadence rather than fixing the structural inefficiency.

pdlda.question: Testing — A team currently only runs static analysis and Apex tests in a nightly batch job, separate from the CI pipeline, meaning defects are discovered up to 24 hours after being introduced. What is the recommended shift-left change, and why?

options.text: Reduce the nightly batch job frequency to weekly to reduce noise from frequent failures.

Move static analysis and Apex test execution into the CI pipeline so they run on every pull request, catching defects at commit time rather than up to a day later, since earlier detection is significantly cheaper to fix.
Keep the nightly batch job as-is, since defect discovery timing has no cost impact regardless of when it happens.
Move static analysis and test execution entirely into UAT, so business users can discover code-level defects during acceptance testing.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Shift-left testing means moving quality checks as early as possible in the pipeline; running static analysis and tests on every PR catches issues at commit time, which is dramatically cheaper to fix than after a day-long delay or in later stages. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Reducing frequency to weekly increases, not decreases, the average time between defect introduction and discovery, the opposite of shift-left.
• C: Defect discovery timing has a well-documented cost multiplier (the later a bug is found, the more expensive it is to fix), so timing absolutely matters.
• D: Pushing static analysis and unit-level test execution into UAT moves code-level quality checks to the wrong audience and the wrong (very late) stage of the pipeline.

pdlda.question: Testing — A complex org with heavy Flow-based automation and multiple external integrations wants a testing methodology that covers this landscape appropriately. Apex unit tests alone aren't verifying the Flow logic or integration behavior. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Rely exclusively on Apex unit tests and skip any dedicated verification of Flow logic or integration endpoints, since Apex coverage requirements are the only mandatory testing gate.

Combine Apex unit and integration tests for code-level logic, add end-to-end automated tests (e.g., Provar or Copado Robotic Testing) for critical cross-object business processes touching Flows, and use callout mocking to isolate integration endpoint testing, supplemented by targeted manual exploratory testing for edge cases.
Manually test every possible combination of Flow branches and integration responses by hand before every release, with no automation at all.
Disable all Flows during testing since they cannot be tested reliably, and re-enable them only after deployment to production.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A layered approach — Apex tests for code logic, end-to-end automation for cross-object/Flow-driven processes, mocked callouts for integration isolation, and targeted manual testing for edge cases — covers the full breadth of a complex, Flow- and integration-heavy org that Apex tests alone cannot verify. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Apex coverage requirements only measure Apex code; they say nothing about whether Flow logic or integration behavior actually works correctly.
• C: Manually testing every Flow branch and integration response combination by hand doesn't scale and isn't sustainable release over release.
• D: Disabling Flows during testing means the automation that drives major business processes is never actually verified before reaching production.

pdlda.question: Testing — A team releases weekly and has accumulated a 6-hour automated regression suite that is now delaying every release window. Some tests cover low-risk configuration items like email template formatting that rarely change or break. What should the architect recommend to right-size the suite?

options.text: Keep every existing test forever regardless of value, since removing any test always increases risk.

Review and prune the regression suite periodically: keep automated coverage focused on high-value, stable, frequently-exercised core business processes and critical Apex logic, and deprioritize or remove low-risk, rarely-changing configuration checks like email template formatting, aiming to keep the suite fast enough to fit the release cadence.
Double the size of the QA team so they can run the full 6-hour suite manually alongside automation every week.
Run the regression suite only once per quarter regardless of weekly release cadence.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Periodic suite review that focuses automation on high-value, high-risk areas and prunes low-value, rarely-changing checks keeps the suite fast and relevant to actual risk, which is the standard fix for a bloated regression suite outpacing release cadence. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Keeping every test forever regardless of value is exactly what caused the suite to bloat to 6 hours in the first place; not all tests carry equal risk-reduction value.
• C: Adding manual testers to run the same tests in parallel adds cost without addressing the suite's underlying inefficiency or its mismatch with release cadence.
• D: Running regression only quarterly against a weekly release cadence leaves most weekly releases essentially unregression-tested, which increases risk.

pdlda.question: Testing — A team wants to introduce UI automation for Salesforce Lightning but has no prior experience and a limited budget. Their manual regression of the 5 most business-critical end-to-end flows currently takes about 3 hours per weekly release. What is the most appropriate starting approach?

options.text: Attempt to automate 100% of all UI test cases, including every minor edge case, in the first sprint using Selenium built entirely from scratch.

Start with automating the 5-10 highest-value, most business-critical end-to-end scenarios first (using a Salesforce-purpose-built tool suited to their budget and skill level), rather than trying to automate everything immediately.
Skip UI automation entirely forever, since 3 hours of manual regression per week is considered acceptable at any team size or release frequency.
Only automate low-value, rarely-used test cases first, saving the business-critical scenarios for manual testing indefinitely.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Starting with a small set of high-value, high-risk end-to-end scenarios lets a team new to UI automation build confidence and see quick ROI, rather than attempting comprehensive automation immediately, which commonly fails for inexperienced teams. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Attempting to automate every scenario immediately, especially with no prior experience, sets an unrealistic scope that typically stalls or fails outright.
• C: Whether 3 hours is 'acceptable' depends on team capacity and growth trajectory; dismissing automation entirely ignores the value of reducing recurring manual effort over time.
• D: Automating low-value cases first while leaving critical scenarios manual inverts the priority; the highest-risk flows should be automated first for the best return.

pdlda.question: Testing — An org-wide Apex coverage report shows 78% coverage, comfortably above the 75% deployment threshold. A developer is about to deploy a brand-new class with 0% coverage as part of an unrelated feature. What should the architect flag as the risk here, and is the deployment technically possible?

options.text: The deployment is impossible; Salesforce blocks any deployment containing a class with 0% coverage regardless of org-wide totals.

The deployment is technically possible as long as the resulting org-wide coverage (including the new 0%-covered class) remains at or above 75%; however, the architect should flag that a large 0%-covered class can be enough to drag the overall percentage below the threshold, and recommend adding real tests before deployment regardless of whether it's technically permitted.
Org-wide coverage is recalculated to exclude any newly deployed classes for the first 30 days, so this has no impact on the coverage threshold.
A class with 0% coverage automatically triggers a mandatory CAB review with no exceptions, regardless of org-wide totals.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Salesforce evaluates coverage org-wide, not per-class, so a new 0%-covered class can still deploy if the org-wide total stays at or above 75% — but this is a real risk since a large enough untested class can single-handedly drag the average below threshold on a future deployment. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Salesforce does not block deployment purely because a specific class has 0% coverage; it evaluates the org-wide aggregate against the 75% threshold.
• C: There is no such 30-day grace period exclusion for newly deployed classes in Salesforce's coverage calculation.
• D: There is no platform mechanism that automatically triggers a mandatory CAB review based on a class's coverage percentage; that would be a customer-defined governance policy, not a platform behavior.

pdlda.question: Testing — A CI pipeline currently uses RunAllTests for every feature branch validation, including managed package tests, and pipeline runs now take over an hour, frustrating developers waiting for feedback on small changes. What change should the architect recommend for the feature-branch validation stage specifically?

options.text: Switch feature-branch CI validation to RunSpecifiedTests, scoped to the tests relevant to the changed components, to get fast targeted feedback, while reserving RunAllTests (or RunLocalTests) for less frequent, comprehensive regression runs or production deployment.
Switch to NoTestRun for feature-branch validation to eliminate test execution time entirely, since tests will run eventually in production anyway.
Keep RunAllTests for every single feature branch validation forever, since faster feedback isn't actually valuable to developers.
Disable the CI pipeline for feature branches entirely and only run tests once a quarter.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: RunSpecifiedTests scoped to relevant tests gives fast, targeted feedback appropriate for frequent feature-branch validation, while comprehensive RunAllTests/RunLocalTests runs are better reserved for less frequent full-regression or production-bound validation, balancing speed and thoroughness. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: NoTestRun is rejected for any production deployment containing Apex, and skipping tests entirely in CI removes the fast feedback loop the pipeline exists to provide.
• C: Fast feedback is a well-established value driver for developer productivity; dismissing it ignores the actual problem the team is experiencing.
• D: Disabling CI validation for feature branches removes the ability to catch defects before merge entirely, which is a much bigger risk than a slow pipeline.

pdlda.question: Testing — Choose 2. A package-based development team has several unlocked packages, each maintaining its own Apex test classes. During a production deployment via RunLocalTests, the team is surprised the org-wide coverage doesn't reflect certain managed package Apex they rely on for a shared integration utility. Which two statements accurately explain this behavior and the correct response? (Choose 2)

options.text: RunLocalTests explicitly excludes managed package tests from the coverage calculation, which is why that Apex isn't reflected; if managed package Apex meaningfully contributes to relied-upon logic, the team should use RunAllTests when that dependency's coverage needs to be included.

Each unlocked package independently needs to maintain its own 75% coverage for its own Apex components; package-scoped CI runs (e.g., 'sf apex run test' scoped to a package directory) help validate this at the package level during development.
Managed package Apex is always automatically counted in org-wide coverage under every test run option with no exceptions.
Unlocked packages are exempt from the org-wide 75% coverage requirement entirely, regardless of what RunLocalTests or RunAllTests is used.
Coverage calculations are always identical between RunLocalTests and RunAllTests, since both execute the exact same set of test classes.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: RunLocalTests specifically omits managed package tests from the coverage calculation (explaining the surprise), and each unlocked package must independently satisfy 75% coverage for its own Apex, which package-scoped CI test runs help verify during development. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Managed package Apex coverage is explicitly excluded under RunLocalTests, contradicting the claim that it's always counted under every test run option.
• D: Unlocked packages are not exempt from the 75% coverage requirement; their own Apex components must independently meet it.
• E: RunLocalTests and RunAllTests differ specifically in whether they include managed package tests, so their resulting test sets and coverage calculations are not identical.

pdlda.question: Testing — A QA sandbox is refreshed as a Partial Copy sandbox containing a 10,000-record sample of production Accounts, but testers report the sample doesn't include enough of the specific record types and edge-case data combinations they need to validate a new feature. What is the best way to address this without resorting to a Full Copy sandbox?

options.text: Give up on using the Partial Copy sandbox and always test exclusively in production going forward.

Adjust the Partial Copy sandbox template's object criteria/filters to better target the specific record types and data combinations needed, and supplement with a test data factory or scripted seeding of additional edge-case records specifically for the new feature.
Manually create every single edge-case record by hand in the UI each time a new sandbox refresh occurs, with no scripting or reusable process.
Convert the QA sandbox into a Developer sandbox, which will automatically contain more representative production data.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Refining the Partial Copy template's sampling criteria targets more relevant production-like data, and supplementing with scripted seeding of specific edge cases directly closes the gap without the cost and long refresh cycle of a Full Copy sandbox. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Testing exclusively in production abandons any pre-production safety net and risks impacting real customers and data.
• C: Manual, unscripted recreation of edge cases after every refresh is not sustainable and is exactly the kind of repetitive manual work automation is meant to eliminate.
• D: Developer sandboxes contain no production data at all by default; converting to one would move in the opposite direction of having representative data.

pdlda.question: Testing — A customer wants to give developers realistic-looking test data in lower sandboxes without ever exposing real customer PII, and currently exports raw Full Copy sandbox data directly into Developer sandboxes with no changes. What should the architect recommend, and at what point in the process?

options.text: Apply data masking/anonymization (e.g., via Salesforce Data Mask or a custom batch process) to transform PII into realistic but fake data before it is placed into any non-production environment accessible to a broader developer population, not after.
Continue exporting raw production data unchanged, since Developer sandboxes are considered fully secure environments with no compliance exposure.
Mask the data only after developers have already had access to it for a few weeks, since masking timing doesn't materially affect risk.
Encrypt the exported CSV file with a password but keep the actual field values as real, unmasked production data.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Masking or anonymizing PII before it lands in any environment accessible to a broader (often less-trusted) developer population is the standard control point; doing it before, not after, exposure is what actually prevents the leakage risk. Why each wrong answer fails:

• B: Developer sandboxes are not exempt from data privacy obligations just because they're non-production; real PII there still carries compliance risk.
• C: Masking after weeks of exposure means the PII was already accessible to developers during that window, which is exactly the risk masking is meant to prevent.
• D: Password-encrypting a file containing unmasked values still exposes real PII to anyone who has (or obtains) the password; it doesn't substitute for actually anonymizing the field values.

pdlda.question: Testing — Six months after a major data model change, a team's regression test suite still creates test records using the old field structure via a test data factory that was never updated. Some tests silently pass despite bypassing new required validation logic that would apply to real user data. What process gap does this reveal?

options.text: Test data factories, once written, never need to be revisited regardless of schema changes.

Test data factory code should be stored in source control alongside application code and updated whenever the schema changes, and test data should be periodically reviewed against current business processes to catch drift like this before it produces false-passing tests.
The correct fix is to disable the new required field validation instead of updating the aging test data factory.
Regression tests should be deleted entirely rather than maintained going forward.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Keeping test data factories in source control alongside the schema they model, and periodically reviewing test data against current business processes, is exactly the maintenance discipline that prevents stale test data from silently masking real validation gaps. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Test data factories absolutely need to evolve alongside schema changes; treating them as permanently static is what caused this exact drift.
• C: Disabling new required validation logic to accommodate outdated test data addresses the symptom in the wrong direction and removes a legitimate business rule.
• D: Deleting the regression suite entirely removes all automated protection rather than fixing the specific maintenance gap that caused stale data.

pdlda.question: Testing — Choose 2. An architect is designing a unified test data strategy across a customer's Developer sandboxes, QA Partial Copy sandbox, and Staging Full Copy sandbox, with a requirement that no real PII ever appears in any environment below Staging. Which two elements should be included in the strategy? (Choose 2)

options.text: Use masked/anonymized data derived from the Partial Copy sandbox (or a data classification-driven masking process) to seed Developer sandboxes, ensuring consistent, representative, but non-identifying data below Staging.
Automate data seeding as part of the sandbox refresh pipeline so environments are reliably repopulated with the correct dataset after every refresh, rather than relying on manual re-entry.
Populate Developer sandboxes directly from an unmasked Full Copy export, since Developer sandboxes are considered low-risk by default.
Require every developer to manually request individual production records be emailed to them whenever test data is needed.
Store all test data exclusively as hardcoded values inside page layouts.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Deriving masked, representative data for lower environments and automating its seeding as part of the refresh pipeline directly satisfies both the 'no PII below Staging' requirement and the need for consistent, repeatable environment setup. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Populating Developer sandboxes from an unmasked Full Copy export directly violates the stated requirement that no real PII appear below Staging.
• D: Emailing individual production records to developers on request is an ungoverned, ad hoc data distribution channel that both violates the PII requirement and doesn't scale.
• E: Page layouts are UI configuration, not a data storage mechanism, and cannot hold test records at all.

pdlda.question: Testing — A QA team reports that automated regression tests pass reliably in isolation but frequently fail when run in parallel with other test classes in the same CI job, due to shared static Apex variables and inconsistent record states across tests. What is the correct fix, and why does it matter for CI performance?

options.text: Disable parallel test execution across the entire org permanently, accepting a much slower CI pipeline as an unavoidable trade-off.

Refactor tests to avoid shared static state and ensure each test method creates and depends only on its own isolated data (via proper @testSetup or factory-created records scoped to that test), preserving the ability to run tests in parallel, which Salesforce does by default, for faster CI feedback.
Run all tests sequentially one at a time forever, since Salesforce does not support any form of parallel Apex test execution.
Increase the org's Apex CPU time limit to eliminate the interference between test classes.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Eliminating shared static state and cross-test data dependencies is the standard fix for parallel test interference, and preserving parallel execution (which Salesforce supports by default) keeps CI feedback fast rather than accepting a slow, fully sequential run. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Permanently disabling parallel execution accepts a major CI performance regression instead of fixing the actual root cause (test isolation).
• C: Salesforce does support parallel Apex test execution by default; the claim that it isn't supported at all is factually incorrect.
• D: CPU time limits govern execution time per transaction and have nothing to do with shared static variables or inconsistent record state causing test interference.

# Releasing

pdlda.question: Releasing — An ISV wants to distribute a Salesforce application on AppExchange to hundreds of external subscriber orgs, protect their Apex source code from being viewed or modified by subscribers, and support a formal version upgrade lifecycle. Which packaging approach fits, and what constraint should they plan for post-release?

options.text: Unlocked packages, since they support external distribution and don't require a namespace or IP protection commitment.

Managed packages, since they support namespace-based IP protection and a formal subscriber upgrade lifecycle appropriate for AppExchange distribution; the key constraint is that once a version is released, fields, objects, or classes cannot be removed from it — only deprecated — and API names cannot change.
Unmanaged packages, since they allow subscribers to freely modify the installed code with no upgrade path needed.
A single Change Set repeatedly deployed to each subscriber org whenever an update is needed.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Managed packages provide namespace-based IP protection and a structured version upgrade model designed exactly for AppExchange-style external distribution, with the well-documented constraint that released components can only be deprecated, never outright removed, from a released version. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Unlocked packages don't provide the IP protection an ISV distributing proprietary code externally typically needs, since components aren't obfuscated or locked.
• C: Unmanaged packages have no formal upgrade path at all, which contradicts the requirement for a subscriber upgrade lifecycle.
• D: Change Sets require a point-to-point connection between specific orgs and cannot scale to hundreds of independent subscriber orgs; they are not an AppExchange distribution mechanism.

pdlda.question: Releasing — An internal enterprise program wants to decompose a large, monolithic org into independently releasable domains (Billing, Account Management, Reporting) shared across several internal Salesforce orgs, without needing external IP protection or a namespace. Which packaging model fits best?

options.text: Managed packages with a namespace, since namespaces are always required for any form of modular packaging.

Unlocked packages, since they support source-driven, modular internal delivery without requiring a namespace, and allow the team to evolve components more freely than a namespace-locked managed package would.
Unmanaged packages, since they provide the strongest IP protection for internal domains.
A single combined package containing all three domains merged together, to avoid any dependency management.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Unlocked packages are purpose-built for internal, source-driven modular delivery without requiring a namespace, letting the team decompose the monolith into independently releasable domains while retaining more flexibility to evolve than a namespaced managed package. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: A namespace is required specifically for managed packages, not for packaging in general; unlocked packages can be created without one.
• C: Unmanaged packages provide no IP protection at all (subscribers can freely view and modify the code), the opposite of what this option claims.
• D: Merging all three domains into one package eliminates the independent release cadence and modularity the program is explicitly trying to achieve.

pdlda.question: Releasing — A subscriber org has been using version 3.2.0 of an unlocked package for a year. The publishing team releases version 4.0.0 with a breaking dependency change, alongside 3.3.0 with a minor backward-compatible feature addition. What should the subscriber understand about how these versions apply to their org?

options.text: Both 3.3.0 and 4.0.0 will automatically install in the subscriber org overnight with no action required, since all package updates are automatically pushed.
Neither version can ever be installed without completely uninstalling the existing package first and losing all configuration.

The subscriber controls their own upgrade timing for unlocked packages; they can adopt 3.3.0 with lower risk since it's backward-compatible, while 4.0.0 (a major version with breaking changes) warrants more careful review and explicit opt-in due to its higher risk of disruption.
Major version numbers in Salesforce packaging are purely cosmetic and carry no semantic meaning about compatibility risk.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Unlocked package subscribers control their own upgrade timing (unlike some automatic managed package update models), and semantic versioning signals real risk differences — a MINOR version is lower-risk to adopt than a MAJOR version with breaking changes, which warrants deliberate review before upgrading. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Unlocked package version upgrades are not automatically pushed to subscriber orgs; the subscribing org's team controls and initiates the upgrade.
• B: Upgrading to a new package version does not require full uninstallation and loss of configuration in the general case; that would defeat the purpose of package versioning entirely.
• D: Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) is a meaningful, structured signal about the type and risk level of changes, not just a cosmetic label.

pdlda.question: Releasing — An architect designs a release plan with three parallel development streams (two feature teams and one hotfix team) that must eventually converge into a single production deployment. Which environment sequencing correctly reflects a sound release plan?

options.text: Each stream deploys directly to production independently and simultaneously with no shared integration point.

Each stream develops in its own isolated sandbox, merges into a shared Integration sandbox for combined testing, promotes to a Partial Copy QA sandbox for sign-off, then a Partial Copy UAT sandbox for business validation, then a Full Copy Staging sandbox for final pre-production validation, before production; the hotfix stream branches from the production tag and fast-tracks through this pipeline when urgent.
All three streams work directly in the Staging Full Copy sandbox from day one, skipping any lower environments.
Streams should never converge; each should permanently maintain its own separate production org.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: This sequencing isolates streams during active development, then progressively converges them through shared testing gates of increasing production-fidelity, with a defined fast-track path for genuinely urgent hotfixes — the standard, sound pattern for coordinating parallel streams toward one production release. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Simultaneous independent production deployment with no shared integration testing risks conflicting, uncoordinated changes colliding directly in production.
• C: Working directly in a Full Copy Staging sandbox from day one skips all the earlier, cheaper testing gates and risks colliding all three streams' unfinished work in the highest-fidelity, least frequently refreshed environment.
• D: Maintaining permanently separate production orgs for what is described as a single converging release plan contradicts the premise of one eventual production deployment.

pdlda.question: Releasing — A Staging (Full Copy) sandbox has not been refreshed from production in over a year, despite six intervening production releases, and the team just discovered a performance issue in Staging that doesn't reproduce in production. What is the likely cause, and what should the release plan enforce going forward?

options.text: The Staging sandbox is inherently unreliable for performance testing and should be abandoned in favor of testing directly in production.

Staging has drifted significantly from production's current metadata and data volume after a year without refresh; the release plan should mandate refreshing Staging from production after every production release to maintain parity for meaningful pre-production validation.
Full Copy sandboxes cannot be refreshed more often than once every five years, so this is an unavoidable limitation.
The performance issue should simply be ignored, since Staging is not a real environment that matters.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A year without refresh across six production releases means Staging's metadata and data almost certainly diverged significantly from current production, undermining the performance test's validity; mandating a post-release refresh cadence restores the parity Staging exists to provide. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Staging is specifically valuable for performance testing precisely because of its production-equivalent data volume; the problem is refresh cadence, not the sandbox type's suitability.
• C: Full Copy sandboxes can be refreshed as often as every 29 days; there's no five-year restriction, and the actual limitation here is process discipline, not platform capability.
• D: Ignoring a real performance issue discovered pre-production defeats the entire purpose of having a staging gate before customer-facing production impact.

pdlda.question: Releasing — A critical production defect surfaces mid-sprint, while two feature branches are mid-development and not yet merged. The team needs to ship the hotfix quickly without dragging in unfinished feature work, and without losing the fix once the regular release train resumes. What is the correct sequencing?

options.text: Merge one of the in-progress feature branches into the hotfix branch to speed up testing, since more code changes together is more efficient.

Branch the hotfix from the last production release tag, fix and validate it there, deploy it to production, then immediately merge the hotfix back into the main/develop branch and both active feature branches, and redeploy it into Integration/QA/UAT so it isn't reverted by the next regular release.
Wait for both feature branches to finish before addressing the critical defect, bundling the hotfix with the next full release.
Apply the hotfix by editing the compiled code directly in the production org's file system.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Branching from the production tag isolates the hotfix from unfinished work, and immediately merging it back into all active branches and redeploying it to lower environments ensures the next regular release doesn't silently overwrite or revert the fix. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Merging unfinished feature work into the hotfix branch would risk deploying incomplete functionality to production alongside the urgent fix.
• C: Delaying a critical production defect fix until unrelated feature branches finish leaves customers exposed to the defect far longer than necessary.
• D: Salesforce has no accessible 'file system' for editing compiled code directly; changes must go through supported deployment mechanisms (Metadata API, CLI, or Setup UI).

pdlda.question: Releasing — A customer wants to introduce a training sandbox for end users ahead of a major release, but keeps finding that in-progress, unapproved development changes leak into the training environment, confusing trainees. What refresh timing and isolation rule should the architect recommend?

options.text: Refresh the training sandbox continuously from the Integration sandbox in real time so trainees always see the very latest in-progress code.

Refresh the training sandbox only from officially UAT-approved feature sets, timed after UAT sign-off (but with enough lead time before the production go-live for training to occur), and ensure it never receives in-progress development changes directly.
Never refresh the training sandbox at all, so it always reflects the very first release the org ever had.
Let each individual developer refresh the training sandbox directly from their own personal Developer sandbox whenever convenient.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Restricting the training sandbox to only receive UAT-approved feature sets, refreshed after sign-off but ahead of go-live, isolates trainees from unfinished work while still letting them practice on the near-final feature set before it goes live. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Continuously syncing from Integration means trainees would be exposed to unapproved, in-progress, potentially broken work exactly as described in the problem.
• C: Never refreshing at all means training becomes permanently disconnected from the current release, defeating its purpose entirely.
• D: Letting individual developers push their own personal sandbox content into training reintroduces the exact uncontrolled leakage of in-progress work the customer is trying to eliminate.

pdlda.question: Releasing — Choose 2. A regulated financial services customer is deciding on a release cadence for their Salesforce program. They have moderate risk tolerance, a support team that can absorb monthly change volume, but not yet the test automation maturity for continuous deployment. Which two release cadence characteristics best fit this profile? (Choose 2)

options.text: A sprint-based cadence (e.g., every two weeks) with predictable, manageable release sizes appropriate for a support team that can absorb regular but not high-frequency change volume.
A defined change freeze period before each release, with go/no-go criteria checked before authorizing production deployment, appropriate given moderate risk tolerance in a regulated industry.
Full continuous deployment triggered automatically on every merged pull request with no human checkpoint, appropriate for teams without mature test automation.
A single release once every two years, regardless of business need, to minimize any change risk whatsoever.
No release cadence at all; deployments happen whenever any individual developer personally feels ready.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: A sprint-based cadence matches a support team's absorption capacity without requiring the high automation maturity continuous deployment demands, and a change freeze with go/no-go criteria provides the risk control a regulated financial services customer needs. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Continuous deployment with no human checkpoint requires high test automation maturity, which this customer explicitly does not yet have, making it a poor fit.
• D: A two-year cadence is disproportionately infrequent for a program with moderate risk tolerance and a support team able to absorb monthly volume, and would badly delay business value delivery.
• E: No defined cadence at all removes any predictability or governance, which is inappropriate for a regulated industry.

pdlda.question: Releasing — A product team wants to deploy a large new feature to production ahead of its planned announcement date, so the code is ready in advance, but without exposing it to any users until the actual launch date arrives. What release technique should the architect recommend?

options.text: Wait to deploy the code until the exact minute of the announcement, performing the deployment live during the announcement event.

Use feature flagging: deploy the code to production behind a Custom Metadata Type flag (or permission-set-gated visibility) that keeps the feature inactive/hidden until the flag is switched on at the announcement time, decoupling deployment from release.
Deploy the feature to a separate, permanent second production org reserved solely for unreleased features.
Store the entire feature's Apex code as inactive, uncompiled text files inside a Custom Setting record until launch day.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Feature flagging via Custom Metadata Type (or permission-set-gated component visibility) is the standard Salesforce pattern for decoupling deployment from release, letting code ship to production early while remaining inactive until intentionally activated. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Deploying live during the announcement event introduces unnecessary deployment risk at the highest-visibility, least forgiving moment possible.
• C: There is no concept of a 'second production org reserved for unreleased features' as a standard Salesforce release pattern; this invents an environment type that doesn't fit standard architecture.
• D: Apex code must be compiled to exist as a deployable, executable class; it cannot be stored as inactive raw text inside a Custom Setting record and activated later.

pdlda.question: Releasing — A team wants to gradually roll out a new Lightning feature to 5% of users first, monitor for issues, then expand to the full user base if stable, without doing a separate deployment for each rollout phase. What approach best achieves this canary-style rollout in Salesforce?

options.text: Deploy the feature separately to five different sandboxes, one for each 20% of users, and only merge to production once all five have signed off.

Deploy the feature once, gated behind a permission set (or custom metadata flag with user/profile conditions) that is initially assigned only to a small pilot group of users; expand the assignment to more users progressively as confidence grows, with no additional deployment needed for each expansion phase.
Deploy the feature to 100% of users immediately, then roll it back entirely if any user reports an issue.
Ask the 5% pilot group to manually disable the feature themselves using browser settings if they experience problems.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Gating the feature behind a permission set or CMT-driven condition lets the team control exposure by simply expanding user/group assignment, achieving a canary-style progressive rollout from a single deployment with no redeployment needed per phase. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Deploying separately to five sandboxes doesn't control production user exposure at all; sandboxes aren't where end users experience the live rollout.
• C: Deploying to 100% immediately and rolling back on any complaint is the opposite of a canary rollout, which is specifically designed to limit blast radius before wide exposure.
• D: There is no browser-level mechanism for end users to disable a Salesforce-side feature; this isn't a real or supported rollback lever.

pdlda.question: Releasing — A multi-org program has Org A providing a shared product catalog API that Org B's Apex integration consumes. The team is planning a coordinated release where both orgs have changes. What sequencing risk must the architect flag, and what is the correct order?

options.text: Deploy to whichever org's release is ready first, since sequencing between orgs never matters for shared APIs.

Deploy Org A (the API provider) first, since Org B's integration depends on it; deploying Org B first risks it calling an API contract that doesn't yet exist or has changed incompatibly in the target org.
Deploy both orgs at the exact same millisecond using a synchronized script, which eliminates any sequencing consideration entirely.
Always deploy the consuming org (Org
first, regardless of dependency direction, since consumers should always go first.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Since Org B's integration functionally depends on Org A's API, deploying the provider first ensures the contract Org B relies on is in place and stable before the dependent org's changes go live, preventing a broken integration window. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Sequencing absolutely matters when one org's changes depend on another's API contract; ignoring this creates a real risk of calling a non-existent or changed endpoint.
• C: True millisecond-synchronized deployment across independent orgs isn't a realistic or reliable mechanism, and doesn't remove the underlying dependency risk if something goes wrong in either deployment.
• D: Deploying the consumer before the provider it depends on directly causes the exact broken-integration risk this scenario is testing for.

pdlda.question: Releasing — A company distributes a shared "Foundation" unlocked package containing common utility Apex classes to five internal consuming orgs. A breaking change is needed in Foundation to fix a security issue. What release governance step is most critical before releasing the new Foundation version?

options.text: Release the new Foundation version and let each consuming org discover any breaking changes on their own after installing it.

Test the new Foundation version against all five consuming orgs (or representative test environments for each) before general release, given that a breaking change in a shared foundational package can silently break multiple downstream orgs simultaneously, and communicate a clear migration/changelog to all consuming teams.
Skip testing entirely for security fixes, since security patches are always assumed to be side-effect-free.
Only test the change in the org where the security issue was originally discovered, since the other four orgs use the package identically.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Because a foundational shared package's breaking change can silently propagate failures to every downstream consuming org, validating against all consumers (or representative environments) plus clear changelog communication is the critical governance step before release. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Letting each org discover breaking changes independently after installation risks simultaneous, uncoordinated production incidents across multiple orgs.
• C: Security fixes can still introduce breaking changes to dependent code; assuming they're always side-effect-free is not a safe assumption.
• D: Assuming all five orgs use the package identically ignores that each org may have different customizations or usage patterns interacting differently with the change.

pdlda.question: Releasing — A subscriber org has been running an unlocked package for two years without ever upgrading, while the publishing team has released four major versions since. The subscriber now needs a critical new feature only available in the latest major version. What should the architect flag as the key risk before upgrading?

options.text: There is no risk at all; unlocked package upgrades are always fully backward-compatible regardless of how many major versions are skipped.

Jumping across four major versions at once likely includes multiple accumulated breaking changes; the team should review the changelog/migration notes for each intervening major version, test thoroughly in a sandbox, and potentially upgrade incrementally rather than assuming a single direct jump is safe.
The subscriber should uninstall the package entirely and manually rebuild all its functionality from scratch instead of upgrading.
Major version numbers are unrelated to compatibility risk, so skipping versions carries the same risk as upgrading one minor version at a time.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Since MAJOR version increments signal breaking changes, skipping four of them likely means multiple accumulated incompatibilities; reviewing changelogs, testing thoroughly, and considering incremental upgrades is the appropriate risk mitigation before jumping straight to the latest version. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Assuming full backward compatibility across four skipped major versions ignores the very purpose of major version numbering, which explicitly signals breaking changes.
• C: Uninstalling and manually rebuilding discards the entire benefit of package-based delivery and is a drastically disproportionate response to a version upgrade challenge.
• D: Major and minor version increments carry fundamentally different risk profiles by design; treating them as equivalent misunderstands semantic versioning.

# Operating

pdlda.question: Operating — A VP insists a one-field label change be made directly in production right now, bypassing the pipeline, because "it's trivial and can't possibly cause harm." What should the architect explain about the implications of this specific request?

options.text: Agree immediately with no discussion, since label changes never have any downstream impact.

Explain that even a seemingly trivial direct production change breaks the source-of-truth alignment between production and source control, bypasses any peer review or CI validation, and creates a configuration drift that must be manually retrieved and back-propagated afterward — the risk isn't the field's complexity, it's the precedent and process bypass.
Refuse outright with no explanation, since all direct production changes are against company policy without exception.
Make the change directly but tell no one, since documenting it would take longer than the change itself.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: The core implication of any direct production change, regardless of its technical complexity, is that it silently diverges production from the tracked source of truth and skips governance gates; explaining this distinction (process risk vs. technical risk) is the architect's job here. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Even simple label changes can have downstream impacts on translations, integrations parsing label text, or reports, and more importantly break process discipline regardless of technical risk.
• C: A blanket refusal with no explanation misses the opportunity to educate the stakeholder on the actual risk and doesn't address the legitimate need for occasional emergency processes.
• D: Making an undocumented change is worse than either approving or declining transparently, since it guarantees future configuration drift with no trace of what happened.

pdlda.question: Operating — A stakeholder demands an emergency production fix for a customer-facing outage impacting revenue, and there is no time for the standard multi-day change window. What is the correct way to weigh and act on this request?

options.text: Always follow the standard multi-day process regardless of business impact, since deviating from process is never acceptable under any circumstances.

Quantify the actual business impact of not fixing it now versus the risk of an unreviewed direct change, and if it meets the org's defined emergency criteria, use the sanctioned emergency change process: a pre-authorized approver signs off, the minimal necessary fix is made, and it is retrieved into source control and back-propagated within a fixed window afterward.
Let any available developer make the fix immediately with no approval and no plan to document or back-propagate it later.
Escalate to the full standing CAB and wait for their next regularly scheduled monthly meeting before taking any action.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Weighing quantified business impact against process risk, then using a pre-defined emergency change path with pre-authorized approval and mandatory follow-up documentation, is exactly the balance a mature ALM program strikes between urgency and governance. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Rigidly following a multi-day process during a genuine revenue-impacting outage ignores that emergency paths exist precisely for scenarios like this.
• C: Letting anyone make an unapproved, undocumented change reintroduces the exact accountability gap that a sanctioned emergency process is designed to prevent.
• D: Waiting for the next monthly CAB meeting during an active revenue-impacting outage is a wholly inappropriate response time for the stated urgency.

pdlda.question: Operating — Following a legitimate emergency change made directly in production last week under an approved fast-track process, the change still has not been retrieved into source control or propagated to lower sandboxes. What operational risk does this create, and what should happen next?

options.text: No risk exists, since the change was already approved through the emergency process, so no further action is needed.

The uncommitted change creates ongoing configuration drift risk — the next regular deployment from source control could silently overwrite or conflict with it; the team should immediately retrieve the change, commit it to a branch with context on why it was made, get it peer reviewed, and deploy it to all lower environments to resync them with production.
The change should be reverted entirely now that a week has passed, regardless of whether the original issue is still resolved.
Lower sandboxes should be permanently excluded from ever receiving this specific change.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: An emergency change that hasn't been retrieved and back-propagated is exactly the seed of configuration drift; the next regular deployment could silently undo it, so completing the retrieve-commit-review-propagate cycle promptly is the necessary follow-up step regardless of the change having been pre-approved. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Approval for making the emergency change doesn't eliminate the separate, ongoing risk of it never being captured in source control.
• C: Reverting a fix that resolved a real production issue, simply because a week passed, would reintroduce the original problem for no good reason.
• D: Permanently excluding the change from lower sandboxes guarantees those environments never match production and any future testing there will be invalid.

pdlda.question: Operating — An org compare tool reveals that production contains several custom fields and one Apex trigger that do not exist anywhere in the team's Git repository, with no record of who added them or why. What is the correct reconciliation approach?

options.text: Immediately delete all unrecognized components from production without further investigation, since anything not in source control must be unauthorized.

Investigate each drifted item to determine whether it's an intentional, legitimate change that was never captured, or truly unauthorized; for legitimate items, retrieve and commit them to source control with documentation; for unauthorized items, follow the org's change management process to evaluate and remediate.
Add a note to the README file listing the drifted components as "known issues" and take no further action.
Disable all Apex triggers org-wide until the investigation concludes, regardless of business impact.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Configuration drift reconciliation requires distinguishing legitimate-but-uncaptured changes (which should be retrieved and documented) from truly unauthorized ones (which need remediation via change management) — deleting or ignoring drift without this investigation risks removing needed functionality or leaving a real gap unaddressed. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Deleting components without investigation risks breaking legitimate functionality that simply was never captured in source control, rather than being genuinely unauthorized.
• C: Documenting drift as a permanent "known issue" without remediation leaves the underlying governance gap and audit risk unresolved indefinitely.
• D: Disabling all triggers org-wide is a drastic, business-disrupting overreaction disproportionate to investigating a handful of drifted components.

pdlda.question: Operating — Choose 2. After repeated incidents of admins making unauthorized direct changes in production, leadership wants structural controls to prevent recurrence, not just better documentation after the fact. Which two governance controls would most directly prevent future unauthorized direct production changes? (Choose 2)

options.text: Restrict 'Modify All Data' and 'Customize Application' permissions to a dedicated CI/CD service account, removing them from individual admin profiles so production changes can only flow through the pipeline.
Configure monitoring/alerting on direct production logins and configuration changes not attributable to the CI/CD service account, so unauthorized changes are detected quickly.
Send a company-wide email reminding admins not to make direct changes, with no technical enforcement.
Grant every admin permanent 'Modify All Data' access but ask them to self-report any changes voluntarily.
Increase the number of admins with full production access to spread out the workload.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Removing broad modification permissions from individual admin profiles (forcing changes through the pipeline) and adding monitoring for out-of-band changes are structural, technically enforced controls that directly prevent and detect unauthorized direct changes, rather than relying on voluntary compliance. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: A reminder email with no technical enforcement is exactly the kind of non-structural control leadership explicitly said they want to move beyond.
• D: Granting permanent broad access and relying on voluntary self-reporting preserves the exact capability and incentive structure that caused the original incidents.
• E: Increasing the number of admins with full access expands, rather than restricts, the surface area for unauthorized direct changes.

pdlda.question: Operating — A holding company operates six semi-autonomous Salesforce orgs, each maintaining its own copy of a shared "corporate standards" Apex utility library, manually copy-pasted between orgs whenever updated. Updates are inconsistent, and three orgs are now running different, diverged versions. What structural approach should the architect recommend?

options.text: Continue manual copy-paste updates, but ask each admin to be more careful this time.

Package the shared utility library as a versioned unlocked package that each of the six orgs installs as a dependency; when the library is updated, a new package version is released, and each org's team explicitly controls when to adopt it, with governance defining ownership and a communicated changelog for each update.
Merge all six orgs into a single org immediately to eliminate the need for a shared library entirely.
Have each org maintain its own permanently separate fork of the utility library with no attempt at consistency going forward.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Packaging the shared library as a versioned unlocked package installed by each org gives consistent, trackable updates with clear versioning and changelogs, while letting each org control its own upgrade timing — directly solving the inconsistent manual copy-paste problem. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Asking for more care without changing the underlying manual, unversioned distribution mechanism doesn't address the structural cause of the inconsistency.
• C: Merging six semi-autonomous orgs is an enormous, high-risk undertaking disproportionate to fixing a shared utility library distribution problem, and isn't what was asked.
• D: Permanently forking with no consistency effort abandons any hope of the six orgs sharing a common, maintainable standard, which was the original intent of the shared library.

pdlda.question: Operating — Choose 2. A multi-org release requires updating a shared package installed in three consuming orgs, plus corresponding changes in each org's local Apex that calls the package's new methods. Which two coordination practices best reduce the risk of a broken cross-org rollout? (Choose 2)

options.text: Sequence deployments so the shared package version is installed in each consuming org before that org's local Apex changes referencing new package methods are deployed.

Run integration tests that exercise the actual cross-org interface (the specific new package methods and their expected behavior) after each org's deployment, not just isolated unit tests within a single org.
Deploy all three consuming orgs' local Apex changes first, and install the updated shared package afterward in each org, since order doesn't matter for package dependencies.
