Have each of the three orgs independently decide, with no communication between teams, exactly when to deploy their respective changes.
Skip integration testing entirely, relying solely on each org's existing unit test suite that predates the package update.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Installing the updated package before the local Apex that depends on its new methods avoids calling functionality that doesn't yet exist in that org, and integration tests targeting the actual cross-org interface catch problems that isolated unit tests, written before the update, cannot. Why each wrong answer fails:

• C: Deploying local Apex that calls new package methods before the package itself is installed would cause compilation or runtime errors referencing non-existent methods.
• D: Uncoordinated, independent timing across the three orgs risks exactly the kind of sequencing and interface mismatch this coordination effort is meant to prevent.
• E: Existing unit tests written before the package update cannot validate behavior against the new methods being introduced, leaving the actual change unverified.

pdlda.question: Operating — Two weeks after a production release, a spike in Apex exception emails reveals a previously undetected edge case is now failing in production, though nothing looked wrong immediately after deployment. What operational monitoring gap does this reveal, and what should be improved?

options.text: Nothing needs to change, since a two-week delay before problems surface is considered completely normal and expected for every release.

Extend structured post-release monitoring (Apex exception email review, error log/event monitoring queries, and key business process completion tracking) beyond the first 24-48 hours for releases touching higher-risk logic, since some edge cases only surface under specific data conditions that take time to occur naturally.
Disable Apex exception email notifications entirely, since they are apparently unreliable if the issue wasn't caught immediately.
Roll back the entire release two weeks later regardless of whether the specific edge case has since been identified and fixable in isolation.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Standard 24-48 hour post-release monitoring can miss edge cases that only manifest under rare data conditions; extending structured monitoring for higher-risk changes, and treating exception email spikes as an active signal, closes this specific detection gap. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: A two-week-delayed edge case is a real monitoring gap worth addressing, not something to dismiss as universally normal and unworthy of any process change.
• C: Disabling the very notification mechanism that successfully surfaced the issue removes the team's visibility rather than improving it.
• D: A full rollback two weeks later is a disproportionate response if the specific edge case can be identified and fixed with a targeted patch instead.

pdlda.question: Operating — A company with three connected Salesforce orgs wants a single, unambiguous decision framework for who approves changes to a shared component used by all three, given each org has its own local governance team. What governance structure should the architect recommend?

options.text: Let whichever org's team requests a change to the shared component unilaterally approve and deploy it themselves without input from the other two orgs.

Define clear cross-org ownership of the shared component (which team owns its quality/backward compatibility), require higher-level, cross-org approval for changes to it given the multi-org blast radius, and mandate the change be tested across all consuming orgs before release, with a distributed changelog.
Dissolve all three orgs' local governance teams and centralize every single governance decision, including unrelated local-only changes, under one committee.
Avoid ever changing the shared component again, freezing it permanently regardless of business need.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Clear ownership, elevated cross-org approval proportional to the shared component's multi-org blast radius, and mandatory cross-org testing with communicated changelogs is the standard governance pattern for shared release artifacts spanning multiple orgs. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Unilateral approval by whichever org happens to request the change ignores the impact on the other two consuming orgs entirely, risking uncoordinated breakage.
• C: Centralizing every decision, including unrelated local-only changes, is disproportionate overreach beyond what's needed to govern just the shared component.
• D: Permanently freezing the shared component regardless of legitimate business need is an extreme, unsustainable response that blocks necessary evolution indefinitely.

pdlda.question: Operating — A customer wants to detect production issues proactively rather than waiting for user complaints after a release. They currently have no visibility beyond checking Setup manually once a day. What combination of tools should the architect recommend for ongoing post-release operational monitoring?

options.text: Rely exclusively on user-submitted support tickets as the sole detection mechanism for production issues going forward.

Combine Apex Exception Email notifications for immediate alerting on unhandled exceptions, Salesforce Event Monitoring (where licensed) for detailed queryable event logs, the Setup Deployment Status history for deployment-level review, and targeted debug logs for specific users when diagnosing a reported issue.
Check Setup manually twice a day instead of once, with no other tooling changes.
Disable all error logging to reduce noise, since fewer visible errors implies a healthier org.

pdlda.explanation:
Why correct: Combining automated exception alerting, detailed event-level monitoring, deployment history review, and targeted debug logging gives proactive, layered visibility into production health, directly replacing the reactive, complaint-driven detection the customer currently has. Why each wrong answer fails:

• A: Waiting for user complaints is precisely the reactive detection model the customer explicitly wants to move away from.
• C: Doubling the frequency of manual Setup checks without adding any structured tooling doesn't meaningfully improve detection speed or coverage.
• D: Disabling error logging removes the very signal needed to detect issues; fewer visible errors would reflect reduced visibility, not improved org health.

agentops.question: A team lead insists that once an agent passes UAT with a fixed set of test utterances, it can be treated as "done" the same way a validated Apex trigger is. Which statement best explains why this assumption is flawed for Agentforce?

options.text: Apex triggers also require ongoing evaluation after UAT, so there is no real difference
LLM-driven responses are probabilistic and can vary with context, memory, and model updates, so behavior must be continuously monitored and re-evaluated after go-live
UAT environments cannot run Agent Script, so the "pass" is meaningless
Agentforce agents do not support version control, so UAT results cannot be trusted

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Agentforce responses are generated by a probabilistic LLM runtime, so behavior can shift with context, memory state, or underlying model updates even without a metadata change — this requires ongoing behavioral monitoring, not a one-time pass/fail gate. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Apex is deterministic; a validated trigger's behavior does not drift without a code change, unlike LLM-driven agents. - C: UAT sandboxes fully support Agent Script and agent testing; this claim contradicts standard Agentforce environment strategy. - D: Agentforce agents are fully source-controlled via AiAuthoringBundle; version control is a core part of the workflow.

agentops.question: A production incident report states "the agent stopped doing X" with no recent deployments. What is the most architecturally sound first diagnostic step?

options.text: Assume the report is inaccurate since no metadata changed
Immediately roll back to the previous BotVersion without further investigation
Compare current evaluation suite output against the stored behavioral regression baseline to determine if model-level drift occurred
Delete and republish the AiAuthoringBundle to force a fresh compile

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Because agent behavior can drift due to LLM platform updates independent of metadata changes, comparing current evaluation results to the stored baseline artifact is the correct way to distinguish deployment-caused issues from model-level drift. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Behavioral drift without a deployment is an expected AgentOps scenario, not evidence the report is wrong. - B: Rolling back without diagnosis wastes the fast-rollback option on possibly the wrong root cause and skips required investigation. - D: Republishing does not diagnose drift and risks a no-op if the bundle is unchanged.

agentops.question: An architect wants to relax a `ruleExpression` guard on a subagent that authorizes refund actions, to speed up a support workflow. Per the governance model, what is the required approval path?

options.text: PR peer review plus the standard evaluation suite pass, same as any Agent Script iteration
Full CAB review and Security sign-off, since this modifies a security guard on a high-risk action
Business Owner sign-off alone, since this is a business process change
No formal approval needed if the change is reverted within 24 hours

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The governance table explicitly classifies modifying `ruleExpression` security guards as High risk requiring full CAB review and Security sign-off, given these guards gate high-risk actions like financial transactions. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: That approval path applies only to low-risk Agent Script prompt-instruction iterations, not security guard changes. - C: Business Owner sign-off is part of UAT approval but does not substitute for the required Security and CAB review on a guard relaxation. - D: There is no exception in the governance model for temporary or quickly-reverted changes; risk classification is based on the change type, not duration.

agentops.question: A Release Manager discovers that a `Bot` record was modified directly in production outside the CI/CD service account. Which combination of controls should have prevented and would now correctly respond to this? (Choose 2\)

options.text: Restrict `Customize Application` permission in production to the CI/CD service account only
Enable Event Monitoring alerts on configuration changes to Bot, GenAiPlannerBundle, and AiAuthoringBundle not made by the CI/CD account
Grant all System Administrators standing edit access to Agentforce Builder in production for faster fixes
Retrieve the change to source control and back-propagate it to lower environments within 24 hours, documenting justification
Permanently disable Agentforce Builder access in all environments including sandboxes
Wait until the next scheduled release to reconcile the drift

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Restricting `Customize Application` to the CI/CD account is the preventive control recommended by Salesforce, and retrieving/back-propagating within 24 hours with documented justification is the standard corrective response when a direct production change occurs. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: Alerting is a detection control, not a corrective response to an already-discovered change; it doesn't resolve the drift itself. - C: Granting standing admin access is the opposite of the recommended control and reintroduces the risk. - E: Disabling Builder everywhere breaks legitimate sandbox development workflows. - F: Waiting until the next release leaves source control out of sync with production longer than the mandated 24-hour window.

agentops.question: Which role is specifically accountable for signing off on the `AiEvaluationDefinition` test suite and its LLM-as-a-Judge scoring criteria before UAT?

options.text: Release Manager
Agent Developer / Architect
QA / Evaluation Engineer
Business Owner / UAT Approver

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Ownership of the AiEvaluationDefinition suite — writing utterances, defining expected routing, configuring scoring, and signing off before UAT — belongs specifically to the QA/Evaluation Engineer role. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: The Release Manager tracks readiness metrics like pass rates but does not own or sign off on the test suite itself. - B: The Agent Developer owns Agent Script and behavioral baselining before integration, not evaluation sign-off. - D: The Business Owner validates business behavior in UAT, which happens after QA sign-off, not instead of it.

agentops.question: A team wants to add a new subagent to an existing published agent. According to the risk classification table, what is the minimum required approval path?

options.text: PR review plus evaluation suite pass, with QA sign-off
Full CAB review with cross-agent impact analysis
Pre-authorized emergency approver plus post-incident review
Peer review only, since subagents are low risk

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Adding or removing a subagent is classified as Medium risk, requiring PR review, the evaluation suite, and QA sign-off — a heavier bar than simple prompt iteration but lighter than a full CAB review. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: Full CAB with cross-agent impact analysis is reserved for changes to shared Prompt Templates used by multiple agents, not adding a single subagent. - C: That path is for emergency hotfixes, not planned feature additions. - D: Peer review alone matches the Low-risk path for prompt instruction iteration, not the Medium-risk subagent change.

agentops.question: A QA engineer refreshed the UAT sandbox from production mid-sprint, then immediately resumed running scheduled multi-turn evaluation tests. Results show unexpected failures that don't correspond to any recent code change. What is the most likely cause and correct remediation?

options.text: The evaluation suite itself is broken and should be rewritten
The refresh reset the active BotVersion to whatever was active in the production snapshot at refresh time; the full evaluation suite must be re-run as a baseline before continuing testing
Sandbox refreshes do not affect Agentforce, so the failures are unrelated and can be ignored
The Einstein Trust Layer automatically disables itself after a sandbox refresh, causing failures

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Sandbox refresh resets the agent's active BotVersion to the production snapshot's version; running the full evaluation suite immediately after any refresh, before resuming testing, avoids exactly this scenario. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: There's no evidence the suite is broken; the more direct cause is the documented refresh behavior on BotVersion state. - C: This directly contradicts the well-documented fact that refresh disrupts agent state. - D: The Trust Layer is an org-level configuration and is not disabled by sandbox refresh; this is a fabricated mechanism.

agentops.question: An agent uses knowledge grounding via the Agentforce Data Library and the team wants to query STDM telemetry for observability in a newly refreshed QA sandbox. Deployment of all relevant metadata succeeds. What is still required before this will work?

options.text: Nothing further; metadata deployment covers all Data Cloud configuration
The CRM Connector must be active and Data Cloud permissions provisioned separately in that environment, since this is not automated by metadata deployment
A new BotVersion must be activated to enable Data Cloud
The GenAiPlannerBundle must be redeployed using API version 64

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Data Cloud and STDM require separate setup — the CRM Connector and Data Cloud permissions must be provisioned per environment and are not part of metadata deployment. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: This contradicts the fact that Data Cloud setup is not automated by metadata deployment. - C: BotVersion activation controls which agent version is live, not Data Cloud connectivity. - D: API version has no bearing on CRM Connector activation; this is an unrelated mechanism.

agentops.question: A critical production defect must be fixed today. The team's `main` branch currently contains several unreleased features not yet promoted past QA. What is the correct branching approach for the hotfix?

options.text: Branch the hotfix from `main`, since that reflects the latest known-good state
Branch the hotfix from the production release tag, since `main` may contain unreleased features
Apply the fix directly in the production org via Agentforce Builder, then retrieve it later
Wait for the unreleased features to complete QA before branching the hotfix

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Standard hotfix process requires branching from the production release tag, not `main`, precisely because `main` may contain unreleased features that shouldn't be dragged into an emergency production fix. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: `main` may contain unreleased features, making it an unsafe hotfix base. - C: Direct production edits bypass source control and CI validation, violating standard governance controls. - D: Waiting for unreleased features defeats the purpose of an emergency hotfix process meant to bypass the normal queue.

agentops.question: Which environment in the recommended hierarchy is described as production-equivalent and used to dry-run the full deployment runbook, including disaster recovery procedures, before the production window opens?

options.text: Integration Sandbox
QA Sandbox (Partial Copy)
UAT Sandbox (Partial Copy)
Staging / Pre-Production Sandbox (Full Copy)

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Staging is the production-equivalent Full Copy environment used for final regression, performance load testing, disaster recovery validation, and executing the deployment runbook as a dry run. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Integration Sandbox receives merged feature branches and runs automated evaluation, but is not production-equivalent. - B: QA Sandbox is purpose-built for structured evaluation with masked representative data, not a full production-parity dry run. - C: UAT Sandbox is for business-facing validation and live preview, not deployment runbook rehearsal.

agentops.question: A developer wants to publish a bundle iteratively while still developing in a sandbox. Which `bundle-meta.xml` configuration is correct for this stage, and where should it live?

options.text: A draft bundle with no `<target>` field, in a `feature/*` branch
A committed bundle with `<target>` set to `{Bot}.{BotVersion}`, in a `feature/*` branch
A draft bundle with no `<target>` field, in the `release/*` branch
A committed bundle with `<target>` set, deployed directly to production

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Draft bundles (no `<target>`) are used in feature branches and developer sandboxes specifically because they support iterative publishing during active development. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: Committed bundles are immutable snapshots pinned to a BotVersion; they cannot be iteratively republished, which contradicts active development needs. - C: Draft bundles are explicitly disallowed on `release/*` branches, which require committed, versioned bundles. - D: Deploying directly to production skips the required environment hierarchy and governance gates entirely.

agentops.question: A release engineer runs a retrieval using `Agent:My_Agent` as the member in package.xml, intending to capture everything needed to review Agent Script changes in a PR. What is the critical gap in this approach?

options.text: The `Agent` pseudo-type retrieves Bot, BotVersion, GenAiPlannerBundle, GenAiPlugin, and GenAiFunction, but silently excludes AiAuthoringBundle, so the actual Agent Script source is missing
The `Agent` pseudo-type only retrieves BotVersion and nothing else
The `Agent` pseudo-type requires an explicit API version flag or it fails entirely
The `Agent` pseudo-type cannot be used in package.xml and only works via CLI flags

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The `Agent` pseudo-type excludes `AiAuthoringBundle`, meaning the human-readable Agent Script source — the very thing needed for a meaningful code review — would be missing from the retrieval. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: The pseudo-type retrieves several metadata types, not just BotVersion; this understates its actual (still incomplete) scope. - C: There's no such hard failure condition for the pseudo-type; the actual issue is silent exclusion, not an error. - D: The `Agent` pseudo-type is usable in package.xml and is commonly referenced in retrieval commands.

agentops.question: Which package.xml pattern correctly retrieves all BotVersions associated with an agent that has versions v1 through v3?

options.text: `<members>*</members>` under `BotVersion`
`<members>My_Agent.*</members>` under `BotVersion`
Three separate `<members>` entries explicitly naming `My_Agent.v1`, `My_Agent.v2`, and `My_Agent.v3`
A single `<members>My_Agent</members>` entry without version suffixes

agentops.explanation: Why correct: BotVersion does not support wildcard retrieval and every version must be named explicitly in package.xml, so each version needs its own fully-qualified member entry. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Wildcard retrieval on BotVersion fails silently or returns nothing. - B: Partial wildcarding (`My_Agent.*`) is not a supported pattern; BotVersion requires exact names. - D: Omitting the version suffix does not identify a specific BotVersion record and will not resolve to any of the three versions.

agentops.question: After retrieving an AiAuthoringBundle, a developer notices `localActions/` subdirectories are missing their `schema.json` files, though the CLI reported success. What does this indicate, and what is the correct verification technique?

options.text: This is normal; schema.json is optional and only generated at publish time
This indicates partial retrieval; run a two-pass verification — a wildcard retrieval followed by a named retrieval for the same bundle — and compare for structural inconsistencies
This means the bundle was committed rather than draft, which is expected behavior
This means the target org is on an unsupported API version and must be upgraded

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Missing schema.json files are a sign of partial retrieval; a two-pass wildcard-then-named verification technique detects structural inconsistencies. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Missing schema.json is a retrieval completeness red flag, not a normal or optional condition. - C: Draft vs. committed status is governed by the `<target>` field, unrelated to missing schema files. - D: API version mismatches cause different symptoms (format/version compatibility failures), not missing schema files specifically.

agentops.question: A developer manually edits the `.agent` file to add a new reasoning step but does not touch `agentGraph/graph.json`. What is the risk of deploying this change as-is?

options.text: None; graph.json is purely cosmetic documentation with no runtime effect
The deployment will be rejected automatically by the Metadata API

Runtime drift, because graph.json is machine-generated from the Agent Script and must be regenerated (via publish-to-sandbox and re-retrieval) to match; deploying a stale graph.json against an updated .agent file is a serious deployment risk
The change will silently be ignored and the prior reasoning step will remain active

agentops.explanation: Why correct: graph.json is machine-generated and must never be hand-edited; an updated Agent Script without a correspondingly regenerated graph.json causes runtime drift and is a serious deployment risk. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: graph.json is the compiled runtime routing structure, not cosmetic — it directly affects agent execution. - B: The Metadata API does not perform semantic validation that Agent Script and graph.json are in sync; it will accept the mismatched deployment. - D: There is no documented silent-ignore fallback; the actual outcome is behavioral drift, not preservation of prior behavior.

agentops.question: A code reviewer is checking a pull request against an `.agent` file. Which change should trigger the reviewer to specifically require CAB-level approval before merge, per the peer review checklist?

options.text: Adding a new conversation variable used only within one subagent
Relaxing a `ruleExpression` security guard
Rewording a subagent's error dialog message
Adding a new target reference to an already-deployed Flow

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The peer review checklist explicitly flags any relaxation of ruleExpression security guards as requiring CAB-level approval, since these guards gate high-risk actions. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Adding a scoped conversation variable is a routine Agent Script change requiring standard peer review, not CAB escalation. - C: Error dialog wording changes are cosmetic and don't affect security posture or routing logic requiring CAB review. - D: Verifying target references across environments is a checklist item, but simply adding one to an already-deployed Flow doesn't itself trigger CAB escalation the way a security guard relaxation does.

agentops.question: An architect needs to change which subagents and actions an agent can access, including tightening a security guard around a refund action. Which metadata layer should be modified?

options.text: Bot
BotVersion
GenAiPlannerBundle
AiAuthoringBundle

agentops.explanation: Why correct: GenAiPlannerBundle is the intelligence layer containing subagent/action definitions and `ruleExpressions` that gate them, making it the correct layer for adjusting access and security guards. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Bot controls identity — name, type, channels, and privacy settings — not subagent/action access. - B: BotVersion controls runtime scaffold like dialogs, tone, and the planner reference, not the guard logic itself. - D: AiAuthoringBundle is the human-readable Agent Script source; the guard's compiled security effect lives in the resulting GenAiPlannerBundle.

agentops.question: A net-new agent deployment to a fresh org fails with `Required fields are missing: [PlannerId]`. What does this indicate about the deployment package?

options.text: The AiAuthoringBundle was deployed without an accompanying GenAiPlannerBundle, and BotVersion requires PlannerId as a mandatory linkage for a net-new agent
The Bot record's botType field was left blank
The target org is missing the Einstein Agent license entirely
The agent user's permission set assignment is incomplete

agentops.explanation: Why correct: This exact error message is caused by deploying AiAuthoringBundle without the required GenAiPlannerBundle, since BotVersion.PlannerId is mandatory for net-new agents. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: A blank botType would produce a different validation error tied to Bot identity fields, not a PlannerId error. - C: A missing Einstein Agent license produces a licensing/feature-enablement error, not a metadata field requirement error. - D: Permission set issues surface at runtime (agent user cannot execute actions), not as a deployment-time required field error.

agentops.question: A preview sandbox is on API v65 while production is still on v64 during a seasonal preview window. Per the compatibility table, which combination will succeed when deploying from the sandbox to production?

options.text: v65-format metadata deployed with the v65 API version flag to the v64 production org
v65-format metadata deployed with the v64 API version flag to the v64 production org
v65-format metadata deployed with the v64 API version flag to a v65 sandbox
v65-format metadata deployed without setting any explicit API version flag to the v64 production org

agentops.explanation: Why correct: During a preview window the sandbox runs the newer API version (v65) while production remains on v64. To deploy v65-format metadata to the v64 production org, you must explicitly set the API version flag to match the target org (v64). This ensures the Metadata API processes the request at the version the target org understands. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Using the v65 API version flag against a v64 production org fails because the target org does not yet support that API version. - C: This describes deploying to a sandbox, not the production promotion scenario being tested. - D: Not explicitly setting the API version flag during a preview window risks the CLI defaulting to the sandbox's v65, which the v64 production org cannot process.

agentops.question: A team needs to move a Prompt Template that grounds via a Flow-backed retriever, and it references org-specific IDs. Which metadata property is most relevant to plan for during environment promotion?

options.text: botType
Einstein Search Retriever ID referenced within GenAiPromptTemplate
versionTag on BotVersion
localTopics within GenAiPlannerBundle

agentops.explanation: Why correct: GenAiPromptTemplate can reference Einstein Search Retrievers whose IDs are org-specific, requiring substitution between environments — this is explicitly called out as a portability consideration. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: botType is an identity field on Bot, unrelated to Prompt Template grounding. - C: versionTag is a traceability tag for release tracking, not related to retriever ID portability. - D: localTopics define local subagents within the planner bundle, not Prompt Template grounding sources.

agentops.question: A pipeline attempts to deploy GenAiPlannerBundle before the Apex classes and Flows referenced by its actions exist in the target org. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: The deployment succeeds because GenAiPlannerBundle has no hard dependency on Apex or Flow
The deployment fails with unresolved reference errors, since agent actions reference these underlying structures directly
The deployment succeeds but the agent silently disables the affected actions
The deployment queues automatically and retries after the dependencies deploy

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Phase 1 base platform dependencies (Apex, Flow, custom objects/fields) must exist before agent metadata that references them; deploying out of order produces unresolved reference errors per the standard dependency chain. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Violating this order produces immediate deployment failures, meaning there is a hard dependency. - C: There's no documented silent-disable fallback; deployment failure is the expected behavior, not partial success. - D: The Metadata API does not auto-queue and retry based on dependency resolution; ordering must be handled by the pipeline itself.

agentops.question: A team deploys a `GenAiPromptTemplate` that is grounded by a Template-Triggered Prompt Flow calling Invocable Apex, bundling the template, Flow, and Apex class into a single deployment transaction. What happens, and what is the correct fix?

options.text: The deployment succeeds; bundling related components together is best practice and reduces deployment count

It fails due to a compilation conflict where the Apex schema cannot be resolved simultaneously with generative AI entity validation; split into two sequential transactions — Flow/Apex first, then the AI entities
It fails because Invocable Apex is not supported by Prompt Templates at all
It succeeds only if deployed with `--ignore-warnings`

agentops.explanation: Why correct: This exact failure mode calls for the bifurcated deployment strategy — deploying Flow and Apex first, then GenAiPromptTemplate and AiAuthoringBundle in a second transaction — as the specific fix. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: This is precisely the anti-pattern to avoid; bundling them together triggers the compilation failure. - C: Invocable Apex is supported and commonly used for Template-Triggered Prompt Flows; the issue is deployment sequencing, not unsupported functionality. - D: There's no `--ignore-warnings` mechanism for resolving this specific compilation conflict; the fix is procedural (sequencing), not a flag.

agentops.question: For a voice-channel agent, where does `AiPlannerVoiceDef` fit in the deployment sequence?

options.text: Before GenAiPlannerBundle, since voice configuration is a prerequisite for the planner
After GenAiPlannerBundle deploys, since voice configuration for the planner comes after the reasoning layer is established
Before Phase 1 base platform dependencies
It has no dependency ordering relative to other phases

agentops.explanation: Why correct: AiPlannerVoiceDef deploys after GenAiPlannerBundle within Phase 4, since voice configuration attaches to an already-defined planner. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Deploying voice config before the planner exists would reference a bundle that isn't there yet, violating dependency order. - C: Base platform dependencies (Apex, Flow, custom objects) must come first in Phase 1, well before any voice-specific configuration. - D: Voice configuration sits within a specific phase sequence — after GenAiPlannerBundle — so ordering does matter.

agentops.question: A team updates only the Agent Script of an existing, already-deployed agent (no new subagents or actions). Which metadata is the minimum correct deployment set?

options.text: Only AiAuthoringBundle
AiAuthoringBundle plus the updated GenAiPlannerBundle carrying the regenerated graph.json
Bot, BotVersion, and GenAiPlannerBundle, but not AiAuthoringBundle
All five phases, including Apex and Flow, regardless of whether they changed

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Agent Script iteration requires AiAuthoringBundle plus the updated GenAiPlannerBundle carrying the regenerated graph.json — never deploying the .agent file without its matching graph.json. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Deploying AiAuthoringBundle alone without the regenerated GenAiPlannerBundle/graph.json risks runtime drift. - C: Skipping AiAuthoringBundle would deploy the compiled runtime without updating the human-readable source, breaking source-of-truth alignment. - D: Redeploying unchanged Apex/Flow adds unnecessary risk and deployment time with no benefit; only changed types need deployment.

agentops.question: A pipeline deploys an already-committed AiAuthoringBundle (target field already pinned to the current BotVersion) with no content changes. The deployment reports success. What should the team conclude?

options.text: The agent's behavior has definitely changed since deployment succeeded

This is likely a no-op — Salesforce treats an already-versioned, unmodified bundle as already at that version — so behavioral change must be confirmed via `sf agent test run` output, not deploy status alone
The deployment must have failed silently and should be retried with `--forceoverwrite`
The BotVersion was automatically incremented as a side effect

agentops.explanation: Why correct: This scenario is a "no-op with false success" — behavioral changes must always be verified through evaluation test output, never deploy status alone. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: A successful deploy status does not confirm behavioral change; that's the exact trap this scenario tests. - C: The deployment did succeed technically; retrying with a force flag doesn't address the actual issue, which is that nothing changed. - D: BotVersion numbers are not auto-incremented by a no-op deployment of an unchanged committed bundle.

agentops.question: Before promoting a change into any target environment, which two items should be verified in pre-flight to avoid misleading errors unrelated to the actual metadata? (Choose 2\)

options.text: Einstein Setup and Agentforce Agents feature are enabled in the target org
The default\_agent\_user exists in the target org with an Einstein Agent license and correct permission sets
The Git repository has fewer than 500 commits
The developer's local machine has the Salesforce CLI installed at the latest version
The organization-wide default sharing setting for Accounts is Private
The number of active BotVersions exceeds three

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The pre-flight checklist explicitly calls out verifying feature enablement (Einstein Setup, Agentforce Agents) and agent user provisioning with correct licensing/permission sets as prerequisites, since missing them produces misleading, hard-to-debug errors. Why each wrong answer fails: - C: Commit count has no bearing on documented deployment prerequisites. - D: CLI version isn't a pre-flight org-readiness check; it's a tooling concern, not an org-configuration one. - E: Account sharing settings are unrelated to Agentforce feature enablement or agent user provisioning. - F: Active BotVersion count relates to rollback readiness, not pre-deployment pre-flight checks.

agentops.question: During a PR peer review of `.agent` file changes, a reviewer finds a nested `if` block. What should happen?

options.text: Approve as-is; nested if blocks are fully supported by the Agent Script compiler
Reject the change; nested if blocks are rejected by the compiler and must be flattened
Approve but flag it for a future refactor since it will only cause a warning
Escalate to CAB review, since compiler syntax issues require governance sign-off

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The peer review checklist explicitly lists nested `if` blocks as rejected by the compiler and states they must be flattened — this is a hard compilation blocker, not a style preference. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Nested if blocks are rejected by the compiler, directly contradicting this option. - C: This isn't a soft warning; it's a compiler rejection, meaning the deployment would fail outright. - D: This is a syntax-level compiler constraint, not a governance/security decision requiring CAB escalation.

agentops.question: When promoting a change into the UAT sandbox, which specific bundle-meta.xml transition and metadata action are required?

options.text: Transition the bundle from committed back to draft state to allow business owner edits
Transition bundle-meta.xml from draft to committed state, pinning the `<target>` field to the BotVersion, and assign a versionTag for traceability
Delete the previous BotVersion so only the UAT version remains
Enable a new feature flag on GenAiPlannerBundle exclusively for UAT

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Promotion into UAT specifically requires transitioning bundle-meta.xml to committed state with the target field pinned to the BotVersion, and assigning the versionTag for traceability, before UAT. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Moving from committed back to draft is backwards; UAT and beyond require committed, immutable bundles. - C: Deleting the previous BotVersion removes the fast-rollback safety net, which requires retaining at least two recent versions. - D: There's no UAT-exclusive feature flag mechanism; this action doesn't correspond to any documented step.

agentops.question: A QA engineer wants to verify that a compliance-sensitive action received the exact correct recipient value, but the agent's final conversational text varies in phrasing each run. What is the correct evaluation approach?

options.text: Write a custom evaluation using string\_comparison against the raw conversational response text

Use a JSONPath-based custom evaluation criterion targeting the deterministic action input payload, e.g., extracting `invokedActions[*].function.input.recipient`, rather than the non-deterministic conversational text
Rely solely on the Coherence and Completeness LLM-as-a-Judge metrics
Manually review transcripts after each production run

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Custom evaluations should avoid targeting the non-deterministic final response text for compliance checks; JSONPath custom evaluations against the deterministic action input payload are the recommended approach. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Custom evaluations shouldn't be written against the raw, non-deterministic conversational text. - C: Coherence and Completeness assess response quality, not whether specific structured data was passed correctly to a backend action. - D: Manual transcript review doesn't scale as an automated CI/CD quality gate and isn't the standard mechanism for this need.

agentops.question: A team wants to test whether the agent correctly retains a user's account ID established in turn 1 when referenced again in turn 4, without re-establishing it. What testing capability should they use?

options.text: Apex unit tests with @IsTest(SeeAllData=false)
Deterministic logic tests on `available when` clauses
Multi-turn conversation testing using an injected conversationHistory array to simulate prior turns
Toxicity detection thresholds in the Einstein Trust Layer

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Multi-turn conversation testing, via an injected conversationHistory array, is specifically designed to validate working memory retention across turns, exactly the scenario described. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Apex unit tests validate action implementation logic, not conversational memory across turns. - B: Deterministic logic tests validate guard conditions and variable transitions in isolation, not multi-turn memory retention. - D: Toxicity detection is a Trust Layer content-safety control, unrelated to conversation memory testing.

agentops.question: A CI pipeline needs to run a 1,200-test-case regression suite through the Agentforce Testing Center without triggering Agent Rate Limit Errors. Which approach best respects the documented execution capacity limits? (Choose 2\)

options.text: Run all 1,200 cases in a single job to minimize orchestration overhead
Segment the suite into batches of 20-30 test cases each
Ensure no more than 500 test cases run per job
Schedule all batches to run concurrently within the same hour without regard to job count
Run evaluation suites continuously throughout the development lifecycle rather than as one pre-deployment gate
Disable Einstein Requests tracking to avoid throttling

agentops.explanation: Why correct: There is a maximum of 500 test cases per job, and segmenting large suites into batches of 20-30 cases avoids rate limit collisions — both directly address the 1,200-case suite's capacity risk. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: A single job exceeds the documented 500-test-case-per-job maximum outright. - D: Running many concurrent batches without limit risks exceeding the maximum of 10 concurrent jobs per hour. - E: This is good practice generally, but doesn't by itself solve the batching/rate-limit mechanics being tested here. - F: Einstein Requests tracking cannot be disabled; it's the underlying consumption metric the rate limiter is based on.

agentops.question: During review of a preview session trace, an architect sees a `FunctionStep` entry showing an action was invoked with an unexpected input value. Which testing/debugging capability should be used next to trace the root cause if the action calls backend Apex?

options.text: The Apex Replay Debugger, integrated with the VS Code Agentforce extension, to step through the backend code logic triggered by the action
The Einstein Trust Layer audit log, since it captures Apex execution details
The STDM Message table, since it stores Apex debug logs
Re-run `sf agent validate authoring-bundle`, since it re-executes all actions

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The VS Code Agentforce extension integrates with the Apex Replay Debugger, allowing you to step through traditional Apex code triggered by a probabilistic agent action — the fastest way to diagnose action-level failures. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: Trust Layer audit logs capture prompts, masking, and toxicity data — not Apex execution details. - C: The STDM Message table stores user utterances and raw agent responses, not Apex debug information. - D: `sf agent validate authoring-bundle` performs syntax validation of Agent Script; it does not execute actions or step through Apex logic.

agentops.question: Which LLM-as-a-Judge metric specifically validates that the agent followed the authored instructions of the subagent it routed to, scored as HIGH/LOW/UNCERTAIN rather than pass/fail?

options.text: Topic (Subagent) Classification
Action Sequencing
Instruction Adherence
Conciseness

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The metrics table specifically defines Instruction Adherence as validating whether the agent followed the subagent's authored instructions, using a HIGH/LOW/UNCERTAIN scale, distinct from the pass/fail scoring of other metrics. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Topic Classification checks routing accuracy against expected metadata via exact match, not instruction-following, and isn't scored HIGH/LOW/UNCERTAIN. - B: Action Sequencing validates the order of invoked actions via sequence array match, not adherence to authored instructions. - D: Conciseness is an LLM Judge pass/fail metric about response brevity, not instruction adherence.

agentops.question: A Web-to-Lead form contains adversarial text designed to be retrieved later during an agent's summarization task and override its system instructions. Which defensive control most directly prevents this class of attack, known from the ForcedLeak vulnerability?

options.text: Increasing the toxicity detection threshold in the Einstein Trust Layer
Treating all user-supplied and CRM-stored data as permanently untrusted during LLM grounding, and sanitizing externally-sourced data before it enters the grounding context
Enabling zero data retention with the external LLM provider
Adding more conversation variables to track user identity

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The fundamental defensive principle for indirect prompt injection (as seen in ForcedLeak) is treating all user-supplied data, even CRM-stored data, as untrusted during grounding, combined with sanitizing externally-sourced data before it reaches the agent's context. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Toxicity thresholds catch harmful/toxic content, not instruction-override attempts embedded as seemingly benign text. - C: Zero data retention protects against data persistence with LLM providers; it doesn't prevent the injected instructions from being processed during the current session. - D: Additional conversation variables don't address the untrusted-data grounding problem at all; this is an unrelated mechanism.

agentops.question: An architect needs to pass a verified `isVerified` boolean and `UserEmail` from one action to another without exposing them to the LLM's context window, to reduce the risk of the model leaking or being influenced by these values. Which mechanism should be used?

options.text: Conversation variables set within Agent Script dialog blocks
`attributeMappings` in GenAiPlannerBundle
`ruleExpressions` gating subagent access
Toxicity detection thresholds

agentops.explanation: Why correct: `attributeMappings` in GenAiPlannerBundle is the mechanism for passing sensitive outputs between actions without routing them through the LLM's context window, exactly addressing this need. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Conversation variables set in dialog blocks are part of the visible agent state and can be influenced by or exposed through LLM context, unlike attributeMappings. - C: ruleExpressions gate access to actions/subagents based on boolean conditions; they don't handle secure value propagation between actions. - D: Toxicity thresholds screen content for harmful language; they have no role in secure data propagation.

agentops.question: Which two controls should be validated specifically for a Prompt Template used with customer PII before production go-live? (Choose 2\)

options.text: Data masking compliance — verifying PII in merge fields is masked before leaving the Salesforce trust boundary
Grounding accuracy — verifying RAG retrieval returns correct chunks for given merge field values
The number of subagents referenced by the template
The BotVersion's session timeout setting
The Bot record's channel configuration
Whether the template uses draft or committed bundle state

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Grounding accuracy and data masking compliance are the required validation disciplines for Prompt Templates, separate from agent-level evaluation, especially important when PII is involved. Why each wrong answer fails: - C: Subagent count relates to GenAiPlannerBundle structure, not Prompt Template-specific validation. - D: Session timeout is a BotVersion scaffold setting unrelated to Prompt Template grounding or masking. - E: Channel configuration is a manual post-deployment step, unrelated to PII handling in templates. - F: Bundle state (draft/committed) is a source-control mechanism, not a security validation of the template itself.

agentops.question: Before any agent goes live, which item is explicitly required for agents that retrieve externally-submitted data (such as Web-to-Lead form content)?

options.text: A ForcedLeak-style indirect injection test executed specifically against that agent
A doubled Einstein Requests allowance
Removal of all attributeMappings to simplify the security review
Disabling the Einstein Trust Layer's toxicity detection to reduce false positives

agentops.explanation: Why correct: A ForcedLeak-style indirect injection test is required for any agent that retrieves externally-submitted data, given the documented real-world vulnerability of this pattern. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: Einstein Requests allowance is a capacity/licensing concern, unrelated to security review gates for injection risk. - C: Removing attributeMappings would eliminate the secure PII propagation mechanism, increasing risk rather than reducing it. - D: Disabling toxicity detection removes a security control rather than fulfilling a required gate; this is the opposite of what's required.

agentops.question: At Gate 5 (Staging, before production), which rollback-related item must specifically be verified?

options.text: That a prior BotVersion can be reactivated within the required RTO
That the Bot record's privacy settings match production defaults
That the GenAiPromptTemplate references the correct API version
That the agent user's password has been rotated

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Gate 5's checklist explicitly requires testing the rollback procedure — confirming a prior BotVersion can be reactivated within the required Recovery Time Objective — before proceeding to production. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: Privacy settings alignment isn't listed as a Gate 5 rollback check; it's a general configuration concern, not a rollback-readiness verification. - C: API version checks for Prompt Templates are a deployment-order/compatibility concern, not a Gate 5 rollback item. - D: Password rotation for the agent user isn't part of the documented release gate checklist at all.

agentops.question: A team plans to activate a new BotVersion for a customer-facing external agent on a Friday afternoon with no on-call coverage arranged. Per the activation window guidance, what should happen?

options.text: Proceed as planned; activation timing doesn't matter since rollback is fast
Delay activation; standard guidance advises against activating on a Friday or before a holiday without on-call coverage in place
Activate immediately since Friday afternoons have the lowest customer traffic
Activate only if the evaluation suite pass rate exceeds 95%

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Activation window guidance advises against activating on a Friday or before a holiday unless on-call coverage exists, precisely to ensure the team can respond if the new version misbehaves. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Fast rollback capability doesn't eliminate the need for someone available to execute it; the guidance exists regardless of rollback speed. - C: Traffic volume isn't the stated rationale; the concern is having coverage available to respond to issues, not traffic timing itself. - D: A high evaluation pass rate doesn't substitute for on-call coverage during the highest-risk post-activation window.

agentops.question: Which seasonal release consideration is specifically called out as needing validation 4-6 weeks before each production release window?

options.text: API version shifts affecting GenAiPlannerBundle structure or retrieval
The number of active subagents per agent
The Bot record's default\_agent\_user
The toxicity detection threshold

agentops.explanation: Why correct: API version shifts affecting GenAiPlannerBundle structure or retrieval should be validated in preview sandboxes 4-6 weeks before each production release window. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: Subagent counts aren't tied to seasonal release timing considerations. - C: default\_agent\_user provisioning is a per-environment pre-flight check, not specifically a seasonal-release-timing item. - D: Toxicity thresholds are a Trust Layer configuration validated during security review, not tied to the 4-6 week seasonal release window guidance.

agentops.question: A production incident is traced to the agent's reasoning/routing behavior itself, and the prior BotVersion still exists in the org. What is the preferred rollback option and why?

options.text: Redeploy the prior AiAuthoringBundle from source control and republish, since it captures the fullest prior state
Reactivate the prior BotVersion directly, since it switches users to the prior behavior without redeploying metadata and executes in seconds
Roll back only the underlying Apex class referenced by the agent's actions
Delete the current BotVersion entirely and recreate the agent from scratch

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Reactivating the prior BotVersion is the fastest and preferred rollback path for behavioral/routing issues specifically because it requires no redeployment and executes in seconds, provided the version still exists. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Full redeployment is reserved for cases where the prior BotVersion has been deleted or the issue lies in underlying action implementations — not the fastest option when the version still exists. - C: Apex-only rollback addresses action implementation bugs, not reasoning/routing behavior, which lives in the planner/BotVersion layer. - D: Deleting and recreating the agent is drastic, destroys the fast-rollback safety net, and isn't a documented recovery procedure.

agentops.question: Which precondition must be true at all times in production to guarantee the fast BotVersion rollback path remains available?

options.text: At least the two most recent BotVersions must be retained and not deleted
The GenAiPlannerBundle must be redeployed weekly
The Bot record must have logging disabled
Only one BotVersion may exist in production at any time

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Retaining at least the two most recent BotVersions in production at all times is a precondition for fast rollback. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: Weekly redeployment of GenAiPlannerBundle isn't a documented precondition and would introduce unnecessary deployment risk. - C: Logging settings on the Bot record are unrelated to rollback readiness. - D: Restricting to only one BotVersion would eliminate the ability to reactivate a prior version, directly breaking fast rollback.

agentops.question: After an emergency hotfix is deployed and activated in production, what must happen within 24 hours?

options.text: Nothing further; the hotfix branch can remain isolated indefinitely
Retrieve from production, commit to main, back-propagate to all lower environments, and complete the formal change record
Immediately schedule the next seasonal release upgrade
Delete the hotfix branch to keep the repository clean

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The hotfix process explicitly requires that within 24 hours the fix be retrieved from production, committed to main, back-propagated to lower environments, and formally documented — to prevent divergence and regression on the next regular release. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Leaving the hotfix isolated risks lower environments regressing over the fix on the next normal release, which the 24-hour rule is designed to prevent. - C: Scheduling a seasonal release upgrade has no connection to hotfix reconciliation steps. - D: Deleting the branch before back-propagation would lose the fix's history before it's merged into main and other branches.

agentops.question: A behavioral issue is isolated specifically to an action's Apex implementation (e.g., an incorrect record lookup), not to the agent's reasoning or routing. What is the most targeted rollback approach, and how should its success be confirmed?

options.text: Reactivate the prior BotVersion, since Apex issues are always tied to routing
Redeploy only the affected Apex class from the prior version in source control, then verify via STDM telemetry that the action failure rate drops
Redeploy the entire AiAuthoringBundle and GenAiPlannerBundle together
Disable the affected subagent entirely until the next release

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Apex/Flow rollback is the targeted option for issues isolated to action implementations, with success confirmed by checking that the action failure rate drops in STDM telemetry. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: BotVersion reactivation addresses reasoning/routing issues, not implementation bugs in a specific action's Apex code. - C: Redeploying the full bundle set is unnecessary overhead when the issue is isolated to one Apex class; it also risks introducing unrelated changes. - D: Disabling the subagent removes functionality entirely rather than fixing the specific defect, and isn't the documented remediation.

agentops.question: An operations team notices a sharp, unexplained spike in average Einstein Requests (ER) consumed per session with no corresponding change in traffic. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: A healthy increase in user engagement with the agent
Looping behavior or an inefficient action chain, which is the standard interpretation of unexpected ER consumption spikes
A scheduled monthly behavioral health check running in the background
The Einstein Trust Layer has switched to a different masking algorithm

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Unexpected spikes in average ER consumed per session may indicate looping behavior or an inefficient action chain, making it a key health indicator to monitor. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Increased engagement would more plausibly show up as more sessions, not necessarily higher per-session ER consumption without cause. - C: Scheduled evaluation runs are separate CI/CD activities and would not manifest as a production ER consumption spike per session. - D: Trust Layer masking algorithm changes are not described as affecting per-session ER consumption; this is a fabricated mechanism.

agentops.question: Which STDM table should be queried to reconstruct the exact execution flow of a specific failed interaction, including which subagent was selected and why, and where in the reasoning chain a failure occurred?

options.text: Session (`ssot__AiAgentSession__dlm`)
Participant (`ssot__AiAgentSessionParticipant__dlm`)
Step (`ssot__AiAgentInteractionStep__dlm`)
Message (`ssot__AiAgentInteractionMessage__dlm`)

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The Step table is the most critical diagnostic table, capturing every micro-action of the reasoning engine including subagent selection, action inputs/outputs, and where failures occurred in the chain. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Session captures aggregate session-level metadata and status, not turn-by-turn reasoning detail. - B: Participant tracks who was involved in the interaction (users, contacts, agents), not execution flow details. - D: Message stores the raw utterances and responses per turn, but not the underlying reasoning steps, action inputs, or routing decisions.

agentops.question: What should happen immediately after production go-live, according to standard production monitoring practices?

options.text: Wait 30 days before running any evaluation suite to allow the agent to "settle"
Run the regression evaluation suite against production within 24 hours of first activation and store the output as the production behavioral baseline
Disable STDM telemetry until a full quarter of usage data accumulates
Immediately activate a second BotVersion in parallel for A/B testing

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Establish a behavioral baseline immediately after go-live by running the regression suite against production within 24 hours of first activation, storing that output for future drift comparison. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: A 30-day wait contradicts the explicit 24-hour requirement and would leave the team without a baseline during the highest-risk early window. - C: STDM telemetry should be confirmed flowing as part of go-live checks, not disabled after launch. - D: Parallel BotVersion activation for A/B testing isn't a documented practice; only one BotVersion is active at a time per the metadata model.

agentops.question: A team notices declining Instruction Adherence scores over several weeks with no metadata changes deployed. What is the correct interpretation and response per the continuous improvement guidance?

options.text: Ignore it, since Instruction Adherence is not scored numerically and trends are not meaningful
Treat the declining trend as a change management event requiring an authoring update, since it likely signals ambiguous subagent instructions or an LLM platform shift
Immediately roll back to a prior BotVersion, since any score decline implies a broken deployment
Disable the affected subagent since its instructions are permanently unreliable

agentops.explanation: Why correct: A declining Instruction Adherence trend should be treated as a change management event requiring an authoring update, signaling either ambiguous instructions or a platform-level shift — not necessarily a deployment defect. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Instruction Adherence is scored (HIGH/LOW/UNCERTAIN) and tracked over time specifically to catch this kind of drift; the trend is meaningful. - C: Rolling back addresses deployment-caused regressions, but this scenario has no metadata change, making rollback the wrong tool — an authoring update is needed instead. - D: Disabling the subagent removes functionality rather than addressing the root cause (ambiguous instructions), which can be fixed through authoring.

agentops.question: Which combination of monitoring signals would most strongly suggest an active prompt injection campaign against a production agent? (Choose 2\)

options.text: A steady, unchanged escalation rate
An unexpected spike in Trust Layer toxicity block rate
Anomalous grounding sources appearing in Trust Layer audit logs
A slight decrease in average session duration
Consistent subagent routing accuracy above baseline
Stable Einstein Requests consumption per session

agentops.explanation: Why correct: An unexpected spike in Trust Layer toxicity block rate is a possible indicator of an injection campaign, and reviewing audit logs for anomalous grounding sources is part of standard post-deployment security monitoring. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: A steady escalation rate suggests normal operation, not an attack signal. - D: A slight decrease in session duration alone isn't linked to injection detection. - E: Routing accuracy staying at or above baseline indicates healthy behavior, not an attack indicator. - F: Stable ER consumption is a sign of normal, non-looping behavior, not evidence of an injection campaign.

agentops.question: After a platform auto-conversion from API v64 to v65 format, retrieving a GenAiPlannerBundle throws `UNKNOWN_EXCEPTION` in the Metadata API even though the Salesforce UI shows the bundle without issue. What is the root cause and the most durable fix among the options?

options.text: The org's Einstein Agent license expired during the conversion; renew the license

Orphaned XML references to deprecated or structurally altered actions were left behind by auto-conversion; the UI tolerates them silently but the Metadata API's strict parser treats them as fatal — delete the orphaned GenAiFunction entries in the source sandbox or restore a known-good bundle from source control
The BotVersion needs to be reactivated to force a schema refresh
The retrieval command is missing the `--json` flag

agentops.explanation: Why correct: This symptom is attributed to orphaned XML references left by auto-conversion, tolerated by the UI but rejected by the Metadata API's strict parser; the fix is to delete orphaned GenAiFunction entries or restore a known-good bundle version from source control. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: License expiration produces feature-enablement errors, not an UNKNOWN\_EXCEPTION tied to bundle structure during retrieval. - C: BotVersion reactivation affects which version is live for users; it does not repair corrupted planner bundle XML structure. - D: The `--json` flag controls CLI output formatting only and has no bearing on Metadata API parsing of bundle contents.

agentops.question: An architect is building the action layer for an order-cancellation subagent. The Apex class behind the "CancelOrder" action will sometimes be invoked by the agent multiple times in rapid succession within a single multi-turn conversation. Which testing practice most directly protects against a production failure in this specific scenario?

options.text: Increase the LLM-as-a-Judge Conciseness threshold so the agent produces shorter responses, reducing the chance of repeated invocation
Write Apex unit tests that invoke the action method with bulk/multiple-record inputs, not just a single record, since the agent may call the same action repeatedly across a conversation
Add a ruleExpression gate that limits the action to one invocation per session
Rely on the Testing Center's Action Sequencing metric, since it validates that actions were invoked in the correct order

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Because an LLM-driven agent may invoke the same action repeatedly across turns, Apex unit tests for action implementations must explicitly cover bulk/repeated-invocation behavior, not just single-record happy-path coverage. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Conciseness governs response phrasing quality, not how many times an action is invoked, and doesn't address bulk execution correctness. - C: A ruleExpression gate constrains business logic access conditions; it is a design choice about behavior, not a testing practice that verifies the Apex handles repeated calls correctly. - D: Action Sequencing validates order of invocation via exact-match metadata comparison, not whether the underlying Apex correctly handles being called multiple times.

agentops.question: A Success Architect is reviewing an action implementation's Apex test class and finds it achieves 100% line coverage using a single test method with hardcoded happy-path inputs and no assertions on returned values. Which gap is most critical to close before this action goes into the CI pipeline's Gate 1 check?

options.text: Add System.runAs() tests validating that the agent user's assigned permission set is sufficient for every SOQL query and DML statement the action performs, and add explicit error-path tests and assertions on outputParam values
Nothing further is required, since 100% line coverage satisfies the Apex testing requirement for Agentforce actions
Replace the Apex unit test with an AiEvaluationDefinition custom JSONPath criterion, since evaluation-layer testing supersedes unit testing for agent actions
Add a multi-turn conversation test with an injected conversationHistory array, since that is the correct layer for validating action-level correctness

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Apex unit tests for action implementations must assert on specific outputParam values under varied inputs (not just achieve coverage), explicitly test error conditions like record-not-found or callout timeouts, and use System.runAs() to confirm the agent user's permission set is sufficient — line coverage alone does not validate any of this. Why each wrong answer fails: - B: Line coverage percentage is a code-execution metric, not a correctness or permissions-adequacy check; a test with no meaningful assertions can achieve 100% coverage while proving nothing. - C: JSONPath custom evaluations validate deterministic action inputs passed during agent execution — they are not a substitute for unit-testing the Apex implementation itself and run at a different pipeline stage. - D: Multi-turn conversation testing validates working-memory retention across turns, an agent-reasoning concern, not Apex implementation correctness or permission adequacy.

agentops.question: A QA Engineer wants to verify that an `available when` guard correctly prevents a refund subagent from being reachable until an isIdentityVerified conversation variable is set to true. Which testing approach is purpose-built for this validation, distinct from both Apex unit tests and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation?

options.text: A red-team adversarial test case attempting to bypass the guard via a crafted utterance
A deterministic logic test that verifies the guarded action/subagent is unreachable while the precondition is false and reachable once the specific variable transition occurs
An LLM-as-a-Judge Instruction Adherence score reviewed over a 60-day trend line
An end-to-end test confirming the downstream Flow updated the record's verification status field

agentops.explanation: Why correct: available when guards, ruleExpression conditions, and conversation-variable state transitions execute deterministically and should be tested like a state machine — verifying the guarded element is inaccessible before the precondition and accessible after the specific variable transition. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Red-teaming targets adversarial exploitation attempts via crafted input, not routine verification that a guard's state-machine logic transitions correctly under normal conditions. - C: Instruction Adherence measures whether authored subagent instructions were followed in the model's response, not whether a deterministic boolean guard correctly gated access. - D: End-to-end testing verifies downstream system state changes from an action, which is a different failure class than validating the guard's reachability logic itself.

agentops.question: During UAT, the business owner confirms the agent's conversational responses about a completed refund are coherent and accurate. Two days later, finance reports that several "completed" refunds never actually posted in the ERP system. Which testing gap does this scenario illustrate?

options.text: The evaluation suite's Completeness metric was miscalibrated; this should have been caught by re-tuning the LLM-as-a-Judge scoring threshold
The agent's routing was incorrect; this should have been caught by the Topic Classification metric during the Integration gate

The Testing Center validates the agent's reasoning and conversational output but does not verify downstream system state changes; this gap should have been caught by end-to-end tests confirming the ERP system actually reflected the claimed change
The Einstein Trust Layer failed to mask a sensitive field; this should have been caught by data masking compliance testing

agentops.explanation: Why correct: The Agentforce Testing Center evaluates reasoning and conversational quality but does not confirm that downstream systems actually changed state — end-to-end tests exist specifically to verify that the external API call or ERP update actually executed with the correct effect. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Completeness measures whether a response contains all requested information, not whether a claimed backend transaction actually succeeded in an external system. - B: Topic Classification validates that the utterance routed to the correct subagent, which is unrelated to whether the invoked action's downstream effect actually occurred. - D: Data masking compliance concerns PII leaving the trust boundary; it has no bearing on whether an ERP transaction posted correctly.

agentops.question: A client team has only implemented Apex unit tests and a basic LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation suite for their first Agentforce agent, which retrieves and summarizes externally-submitted Web-to-Lead content. Which two coverage gaps represent the most significant unaddressed risk? (Choose 2)

options.text: Missing security red-team testing, specifically a ForcedLeak-style indirect prompt injection test, since the agent retrieves and processes externally-submitted data
Missing multi-turn conversation testing, since single-shot evaluation utterances cannot reveal working-memory retention failures across turns
Missing Apex governor limit documentation in code comments
Missing a second LLM-as-a-Judge Conciseness pass to further reduce response length
Missing end-to-end testing to verify Apex bulk invocation handles more than 200 records
Missing a duplicate copy of the evaluation suite in a second sandbox for redundancy

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Because this agent retrieves externally-submitted data (Web-to-Lead), it is specifically exposed to the ForcedLeak-style indirect injection pattern, making adversarial red-team testing a required layer; separately, having only Apex tests and basic evaluation leaves multi-turn memory-retention failures completely uncovered. Why each wrong answer fails: - C: Governor limit documentation in comments is a code-quality practice, not a testing-pyramid coverage layer. - D: Additional Conciseness passes tune response brevity scoring; it doesn't address either the injection risk or memory-retention gap. - E: Bulk-record handling is an Apex unit-testing concern already partially covered. - F: Duplicating the same suite in a second sandbox adds redundancy, not new coverage for an unaddressed failure class.

agentops.question: A client is scoping sandbox needs for their first Agentforce project: individual developers need daily iterative Agent Script publishing, QA needs realistic-but-masked data, and Staging needs a full production-equivalent dry run. How should sandbox types be allocated?

options.text: Full Copy sandboxes for all three tiers, since Agentforce evaluation accuracy always requires true production data volume
Developer sandboxes for individual feature work, Partial Copy for QA (and UAT), and Full Copy reserved for Staging only
A single shared Partial Copy sandbox for Developer, QA, and Staging, refreshed nightly to keep costs low
Developer sandboxes for individual feature work, Full Copy for QA to guarantee data realism, and Partial Copy for Staging to reduce refresh cost

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Developer sandboxes suit individual syntax validation and iterative draft-bundle publishing; Partial Copy sandboxes provide the masked, representative data needed for QA/UAT evaluation accuracy at lower cost; Full Copy is reserved for Staging specifically because it requires true production-equivalent data volume and disaster-recovery-procedure validation. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Using Full Copy everywhere is expensive and wasteful for tiers that only need representative masked data. - C: Sharing one sandbox across Developer, QA, and Staging violates the tiered-gate model. - D: This inverts the guidance — Full Copy for QA is unnecessary, while Staging specifically requires Full Copy for production-parity validation.

agentops.question: A Prompt Template uses retrieval-augmented generation grounded by an Einstein Search Retriever, and the agent evaluation suite is passing at 95% in QA. A support ticket reports that the agent gives confident, well-phrased answers that are factually wrong for a specific product line. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The evaluation suite's Coherence metric is too lenient; tightening the LLM-as-a-Judge Coherence threshold will catch factually wrong but well-phrased responses
The RAG retrieval pipeline is not returning the correct knowledge chunks for that product line's merge field values; run grounding accuracy validation with realistic CRM records for that product line
The agent's routing is misclassifying the product line's utterances to the wrong subagent; add more Topic Classification test cases
The Einstein Trust Layer's toxicity threshold is misconfigured for this channel, causing malformed responses

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Agent-level evaluation can pass at a high rate while the underlying RAG grounding is still returning incorrect chunks, producing confident-but-wrong responses — grounding accuracy validation with representative CRM data is a distinct testing discipline. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Coherence measures logical soundness and grammatical correctness, not factual accuracy against retrieved source data. - C: A 95% pass rate with correct routing is consistent with the symptom described; misrouting would typically also degrade Topic Classification scores. - D: Toxicity detection screens for harmful content, not factual accuracy of grounded responses.

agentops.question: A team's STDM telemetry shows a session where the agent misrouted a legitimate billing question to the wrong subagent, causing user frustration and an escalation. The immediate incident is resolved. What should happen next?

options.text: Nothing further is required once the immediate session is resolved and the user's issue is closed

Extract the utterance, expected routing, and any needed conversation history from the STDM tables and add it as a new AiEvaluationDefinition test case within 48 hours, converting the production failure into permanent regression coverage
Lower the Topic Classification threshold in the evaluation suite so similar utterances are scored more leniently going forward
Schedule a CAB review, since any production misrouting incident requires full governance escalation before remediation

agentops.explanation: Why correct: Production sessions where the agent misrouted an utterance should be converted into new evaluation test cases within 48 hours — this converts a one-time production failure into permanent regression coverage that protects against recurrence. Why each wrong answer fails: - A: Resolving the immediate session leaves the underlying routing gap uncovered by the evaluation suite. - C: Lowering the scoring threshold masks the symptom rather than adding coverage that actually detects the misrouting. - D: Misrouting incidents are addressed through the continuous-improvement feedback loop, not automatically escalated to CAB.

agentops.question: A Success Architect is preparing a mid-engagement checkpoint for a client with an Agentforce agent that has been in production for six months. The client asks for a structured way to see where they stand. Which approach best matches documented AgentOps practice?

options.text: Report only the current evaluation suite pass rate, since that single metric is the most comprehensive indicator of overall program health

Summarize maturity across the five dimensions — governance, environment strategy, testing depth, security posture, and monitoring coverage — into a scorecard used to prioritize the highest-impact improvements
Recommend an immediate full CAB review of all deployed agents to reset governance baselines regardless of current state
