Why B fails: A checkbox field polled periodically is a polling-based workaround, not an event-driven Platform Events solution, and it can't inherently support ReplayId-based resumption. Why C fails: A Named Credential manages authentication for outbound HTTP calls; it plays no role in defining or publishing Platform Events. Why D fails: Visualforce with JS polling is a legacy client-side polling technique unrelated to CometD-based Streaming API subscription or replay capability.

options.text: Anypoint Platform is the runtime that executes Mule flows; connectors are pre-built adapters (e.g., Salesforce Connector) that simplify connecting to specific systems; the API Gateway enforces policies (rate limiting, security) on exposed APIs
Anypoint Platform is only a monitoring dashboard with no runtime capability; all logic must run in Salesforce Apex instead
Mule flows can only connect to Salesforce and cannot integrate with any other system
The API Gateway is a Salesforce-native feature that has nothing to do with MuleSoft

pia.explanation: Why A: This accurately reflects MuleSoft's architecture: Anypoint Platform provides both design-time tooling and the Mule runtime executing integration flows, connectors are reusable adapters simplifying system-specific connections, and API Manager/Gateway enforces governance policies on exposed API endpoints. Why B fails: Anypoint Platform includes the actual Mule runtime that executes integration logic; it's far more than a monitoring dashboard, and logic doesn't have to move into Apex. Why C fails: Mule flows and connectors are designed to integrate with a very wide range of systems (ERPs, databases, SaaS apps), not just Salesforce. Why D fails: The API Gateway is a MuleSoft/Anypoint component (part of API Manager) for governing APIs, not a Salesforce-native feature.

options.text: A Custom Object, a Batch Apex job, and a Scheduled Job to refresh it nightly

An External Data Source (configured with the appropriate adapter, e.g., OData 2.0/4.0 or a custom Apex adapter), and External Objects defined against that data source which surface the external records with SOQL-queryable fields, without persisting the data in Salesforce storage
A Named Credential alone, since it fully replaces the need for External Objects
A Platform Event definition that streams the catalog into Salesforce storage

pia.explanation: Why B: Salesforce Connect requires an External Data Source configured with an adapter (standard OData or custom Apex-based) and External Objects defined on top of it, which expose the external data as SOQL-queryable, non-replicated records — the correct component set for this pattern. Why A fails: A Custom Object with nightly Batch Apex refresh is a replication pattern, not Salesforce Connect's virtualization approach, and contradicts "without replication." Why C fails: A Named Credential can support authentication for an External Data Source but doesn't replace the External Data Source/External Object components themselves. Why D fails: Platform Events streaming into storage both misuses events as a persistent store and directly contradicts the "without replication" requirement.

options.text: SF2SF uses Connection objects (established between two orgs) and Subscription/Publish settings per object; a key limitation is that it has constraints around syncing certain complex configurations (e.g., some custom object relationships, validation rule interplay) that may require workarounds or middleware for full fidelity
SF2SF requires no configuration at all and automatically syncs every object and validation rule perfectly
SF2SF only works between a sandbox and a production org, never between two production orgs
SF2SF is implemented entirely via Change Data Capture with no separate feature of its own

pia.explanation: Why A: SF2SF is built on Connection objects between orgs plus per-object publish/subscribe configuration, and it has known limitations in fully replicating complex object relationships or validation-dependent behavior, which is why middleware is sometimes chosen instead for complex fidelity needs. Why B fails: SF2SF requires explicit setup (establishing connections, defining which objects/fields to publish and subscribe) — it is not automatic or zero-configuration. Why C fails: SF2SF can be configured between any two Salesforce orgs, including two production orgs, not just sandbox-to-production. Why D fails: SF2SF is a distinct native feature with its own Connection/Subscription framework; it is not simply an implementation of CDC.

options.text: A Heroku application, a Heroku Postgres database, and the Heroku Connect add-on which manages field-level mappings between Salesforce objects and Postgres tables, keeping them synchronized on a polling cadence
A single Salesforce Connected App with no external database involved at all
A MuleSoft Anypoint runtime deployed inside Heroku's infrastructure
A Platform Event bus that replaces the need for any Postgres database

pia.explanation: Why A: Heroku Connect's architecture centers on a Heroku app backed by a Postgres database, with the Heroku Connect add-on defining object/field mappings and handling the ongoing bidirectional sync between Salesforce and Postgres on a polling cadence. Why B fails: Heroku Connect fundamentally involves an external Postgres database as the replicated data store; there's no external database-free version of this pattern. Why C fails: Heroku Connect is a distinct Heroku add-on/product, not a deployment of the MuleSoft Anypoint runtime. Why D fails: Heroku Connect relies on a Postgres database as its data store; Platform Events are a separate pub/sub mechanism and don't replace the database in this architecture.

options.text: Synchronous REST callouts are strictly better in every scenario because they are simpler to implement

Synchronous REST callouts offer simplicity and immediate feedback but couple Salesforce's transaction to the partner's real-time availability (risking failures during partner downtime); Platform Events decouple the systems, letting the partner consume events whenever it recovers, at the cost of added architectural complexity and eventual (not immediate) consistency
Platform Events guarantee the partner will never miss an update even without implementing any replay logic
There is no meaningful trade-off; both approaches behave identically during partner downtime

pia.explanation: Why B: This captures the real trade-off: synchronous callouts are simple but tightly couple Salesforce's success to the partner's live availability (a real risk given historical downtime), while Platform Events decouple the two systems so the partner can catch up later, at the cost of some added complexity and non-immediate consistency. Why A fails: Simplicity is only one dimension; given the partner's unpredictable downtime, "strictly better in every scenario" ignores the coupling risk synchronous callouts introduce. Why C fails: Platform Events only guarantee no missed updates if the subscriber correctly implements replay/ReplayId logic; this isn't automatic or guaranteed regardless of implementation. Why D fails: The behaviors are materially different during downtime — synchronous callouts fail immediately and visibly, while events queue for later consumption — so claiming no difference is incorrect.

options.text: The Apex callout timeout limit of 120 seconds, meaning a call that takes 3 minutes will time out before the mainframe ever responds
The 50,000 Platform Events per hour limit, since it applies to all synchronous callouts
The 15-character API name limit, since long service names cause failures
The 2 GB heap size limit, since heap size determines callout duration

pia.explanation: Why A: Salesforce enforces a maximum callout timeout of 120 seconds; a mainframe service that can take up to 3 minutes (180 seconds) will exceed this and cause the callout to fail, regardless of retries, unless the design moves to an asynchronous pattern. Why B fails: The Platform Events hourly publish limit is unrelated to synchronous HTTP callout timeouts. Why C fails: API name length limits govern metadata naming conventions, not callout duration or timeout behavior. Why D fails: Heap size governs in-memory object size during Apex execution, not how long an HTTP callout is permitted to wait for a response.

options.text: Ignore the limit since Platform Events publishing is always unlimited for Enterprise Edition orgs

Redesign to reduce event volume (e.g., batching multiple inventory changes into a single event payload, deduplicating rapid successive changes, or filtering to only business-significant changes) to stay within the 50,000/hour limit, or evaluate a higher-capacity event allocation if available for the edition/add-on
Switch entirely to sending 80,000 separate outbound messages per hour instead, since Outbound Messaging has no equivalent limit
Simply increase the number of Salesforce licenses to raise the Platform Events limit automatically

pia.explanation: Why B: Since standard Platform Events publishing has an hourly org limit, the practical response to anticipated volume exceeding it is to reduce the effective event count through batching/deduplication/filtering, or explore an add-on/higher-tier allocation — rather than assuming the limit doesn't apply. Why A fails: Platform Events publishing limits do apply per org based on edition and any purchased add-ons; they are not unlimited by default. Why C fails: Outbound Messaging still consumes processing resources and has its own practical scaling constraints; assuming it has "no equivalent limit" is not a safe architectural assumption, and it doesn't solve an underlying volume problem. Why D fails: Salesforce license count (user licenses) does not directly govern the Platform Events hourly publishing allocation.

options.text: Salesforce Connect fully supports roll-up summary fields and standard cross-object formulas on External Objects identically to native objects, so there is no trade-off

External Objects have limitations on features like roll-up summary fields and certain formula/cross-object capabilities compared to native objects, so if these declarative features are heavily required, full data replication into native custom objects may better meet the functional requirement despite the storage and staleness costs
Full data replication cannot support roll-up summary fields under any circumstances, making Salesforce Connect the only viable option
Both approaches are functionally identical in every respect, so the decision should be based solely on cost

pia.explanation: Why B: External Objects (Salesforce Connect) do not support the full feature parity of native objects; roll-up summaries in particular have well-known restrictions with External Objects, so when those declarative features are essential, replicating the data into native objects (accepting storage cost and staleness) may be the better functional fit. Why A fails: External Objects do not support the full feature parity of native objects; roll-up summaries in particular have well-known restrictions with External Objects. Why C fails: Native custom objects (used in a replication approach) fully support roll-up summary fields; this option incorrectly states the opposite. Why D fails: The two approaches are not functionally identical — they differ meaningfully in supported declarative features, storage cost, and data freshness, all of which matter beyond just cost.

options.text: REST API, since it is always the modern default choice regardless of consumer capability
SOAP API (Enterprise or Partner WSDL), since the partner's environment requires a strongly typed, WSDL-based contract that REST doesn't natively provide
Bulk API 2.0, since it is the best fit for typed contract requirements
GraphQL API, since it offers the most flexible schema definition

pia.explanation: Why B: When a consumer's environment is built around WSDL/strongly-typed SOAP tooling and lacks REST capability, Salesforce's SOAP API (via the Enterprise or Partner WSDL) is the appropriate fit, since it natively provides the typed contract the partner's stack requires. Why A fails: "Always modern default" ignores the explicit stated constraint that the partner's tooling cannot consume REST. Why C fails: Bulk API is designed for high-volume asynchronous data loads, not for satisfying a typed WSDL contract requirement. Why D fails: GraphQL is about flexible querying and reducing over-fetching; it doesn't address a hard requirement for WSDL-based typed contracts.

options.text: Single-record REST API calls, since 15,000 is a manageable volume for individual calls

Bulk API 2.0, since volumes in the thousands (well above the ~2,000 record threshold where Bulk API becomes advantageous) are processed more efficiently asynchronously in bulk than via many individual synchronous calls
Streaming API, since it can insert records directly
Metadata API, since it handles configuration-related bulk changes

pia.explanation: Why B: At volumes like 15,000 records, Bulk API 2.0's asynchronous, chunked processing is significantly more efficient and consumes far fewer API resources than issuing 15,000 individual synchronous REST calls. Why A fails: While technically possible, issuing 15,000 individual calls is inefficient, slow, and unnecessarily consumes the daily API call allocation compared to Bulk API. Why C fails: Streaming API is for event notification/subscription, not for performing record insert operations. Why D fails: Metadata API deploys configuration/metadata components (fields, objects, flows), not data records like Cases.

options.text: Three separate REST API POST calls, one per object, executed sequentially

The Composite API (specifically Composite Graph or a composite request with allOrNone), which can create all three related records in a single API call while supporting all-or-nothing transactional behavior
Bulk API 2.0, since it is designed for exactly this kind of small multi-object transactional request
Streaming API, since events can create multiple records at once

pia.explanation: Why B: The Composite API (particularly Composite Graph) is designed exactly for this: performing multiple related record operations across objects in a single call, with allOrNone-style transactional rollback behavior, minimizing API call count. Why A fails: Three sequential separate calls both consume more API calls than necessary and do not provide atomic all-or-nothing behavior across the three creates. Why C fails: Bulk API 2.0 is designed for large asynchronous bulk loads of a single (or few) object types, not small transactional multi-object graphs needing an immediate synchronous result. Why D fails: Streaming API publishes/subscribes to event notifications; it has no capability to create related records transactionally.

options.text: PushTopic, since it is the most flexible option for custom payloads
Platform Events, since they allow defining custom event objects with app-specific fields independent of any existing SObject, ideal for pure signaling use cases
Generic Streaming, since it supports custom field definitions natively
Change Data Capture, since it supports adding custom fields to change events

pia.explanation: Why B: Platform Events let architects define a completely custom event schema with its own fields, decoupled from any existing SObject — exactly suited to pure business-process signaling that doesn't map to standard/custom object data. Why A fails: PushTopic is SOQL-query-based, tied to changes on existing standard/custom objects, and does not support arbitrary custom field payloads independent of an object. Why C fails: Generic Streaming pushes messages via Apex but is a simpler, older mechanism intended for custom notification without SObject-based structure; Platform Events are the modern, purpose-built, and recommended choice for structured custom event definitions. Why D fails: CDC's payload structure is tied to the actual changed fields of a tracked standard/custom object; you cannot arbitrarily add unrelated custom fields to a CDC event.

options.text: Change Data Capture, since it automatically includes changed-field information in its event payload without requiring custom Apex to compute field-level diffs
A custom trigger comparing Trigger.old and Trigger.new for all 50 fields, then manually building a payload
Outbound Messaging, since it always includes a full diff of changed fields automatically
Salesforce Connect, since External Objects report field-level changes

pia.explanation: Why A: CDC events include changed-field metadata (changedFields) automatically as part of the platform feature, meaning the specific set of fields that changed is available without the team writing custom logic to detect diffs. Why B fails: This is exactly the manual, custom-Apex approach the requirement is trying to avoid; it also doesn't scale well when many fields could change in bulk operations. Why C fails: Outbound Messaging sends a defined field payload configured on the workflow rule; it does not automatically compute or include a "changed fields" diff. Why D fails: Salesforce Connect (External Objects) is for surfacing external data as Salesforce records, unrelated to detecting or reporting changes to Salesforce's own Opportunity fields.

options.text: Metadata API for deploying components (classes, fields, Flows) between orgs, and Tooling API for finer-grained operations like running and monitoring individual Apex test executions
Bulk API for all deployment and testing operations, since it is designed for CI/CD pipelines
REST API SObject Collections for both deployment and test execution
Streaming API for deploying metadata changes in real time

pia.explanation: Why A: Metadata API is the standard tool for deploying metadata components (classes, fields, Flows) across orgs, while the Tooling API provides finer-grained, developer-focused operations like triggering and monitoring individual test runs — using both together fits the described CI/CD needs precisely. Why B fails: Bulk API is designed for high-volume data record operations, not metadata deployment or Apex test execution monitoring. Why C fails: SObject Collections operate on data records via REST, not metadata components or Apex test run management. Why D fails: Streaming API is for event notifications/subscriptions; it is not a metadata deployment mechanism.

options.text: The GraphQL API, since it lets the client specify exactly which fields to retrieve, minimizing over-fetching and payload size for bandwidth-constrained clients
The Bulk API, since it is optimized for minimal payload size on mobile networks
SOAP API, since its XML payloads are more compact than REST/JSON
Metadata API, since it can restrict which fields are queryable

pia.explanation: Why A: The GraphQL API allows the client to declare precisely which fields it needs in the query, directly addressing over-fetching and reducing payload size — ideal for bandwidth-constrained mobile clients displaying a small subset of fields. Why B fails: Bulk API is designed for large asynchronous batch data loads, not for optimizing small, real-time mobile query payloads. Why C fails: SOAP/XML payloads are typically larger, not more compact, than equivalent JSON, and SOAP doesn't offer field-level query shaping like GraphQL. Why D fails: Metadata API manages configuration metadata, not runtime data query shaping for client applications.

options.text: System layer (connects directly to backend systems like Salesforce/ERP, exposing stable APIs over unstable backends), Process layer (orchestrates and applies business logic/transformation across system APIs), Experience layer (tailors APIs for specific consuming channels/apps like mobile or web)
All three layers are identical and exist only for documentation purposes, with no functional difference
The Experience layer connects directly to backend databases, bypassing the System layer entirely
The Process layer is only used for logging and has no orchestration responsibility

pia.explanation: Why A: This is the standard MuleSoft API-led connectivity model: System APIs abstract and stabilize access to backend systems, Process APIs compose/orchestrate business logic across system APIs, and Experience APIs shape data for specific consuming channels — a layered approach that improves reuse and insulates changes. Why B fails: Each layer has a distinct functional purpose (system abstraction, process orchestration, channel-specific shaping); they are not interchangeable or purely documentational. Why C fails: The Experience layer is designed to consume Process/System APIs, not bypass them to hit backend databases directly, which would defeat the purpose of the layered abstraction. Why D fails: The Process layer's core responsibility is orchestration and business logic composition across System APIs, not merely logging.

options.text: Writing a detailed Word document describing the API informally, updated ad hoc as implementation proceeds

Defining the API contract first using OpenAPI Specification (or RAML), enabling API-first design so consuming teams can review, mock, and build against a precise, machine-readable contract before implementation
Skipping documentation entirely and letting teams reverse-engineer the API from Apex source code
Using only inline code comments within the Apex REST resource class as the sole specification

pia.explanation: Why B: API-first design using OpenAPI/RAML produces a precise, machine-readable, reviewable contract that multiple teams can build and mock against before implementation, directly preventing the miscommunication and rework that comes from undocumented or late documentation. Why A fails: An informal, ad hoc document lacks the precision and tooling support (mocking, validation, code generation) that a formal spec provides, and is prone to drifting out of sync. Why C fails: Reverse-engineering from source code requires implementation to exist first, directly contradicting the "before any implementation code is written" requirement, and increases miscommunication risk. Why D fails: Inline code comments are not accessible or reviewable by external consuming teams before implementation and don't provide a structured, tooling-friendly contract.

options.text: A DataWeave (or XSLT) transformation script within the middleware, capable of expressing conditional logic, field mapping, and concatenation between the source XML schema and the target JSON schema
A Salesforce Formula field, since formulas can transform inbound XML before it reaches Salesforce
A Remote Site Setting, since it defines the transformation rules for inbound data
A Permission Set, since it controls how fields are mapped between systems

pia.explanation: Why A: DataWeave (in MuleSoft) or XSLT (in XML-centric tooling) are purpose-built data transformation languages capable of expressing conditional mapping, concatenation, and structural conversion between source and target schemas — exactly the middleware transformation task described. Why B fails: Formula fields operate on data already inside Salesforce records; they cannot transform an inbound XML payload before or as it's being received by Salesforce. Why C fails: Remote Site Settings only allow-list external domains for callouts; they have no data transformation capability. Why D fails: Permission Sets control user access/permissions within Salesforce; they have nothing to do with data format transformation logic.

options.text: Simply making the endpoint URL long and hard to guess, since obscurity alone is a sufficient security control

Verifying an HMAC signature (or digital signature) included in each webhook request, computed by the payment provider using a shared secret, to confirm the payload's authenticity and integrity before processing it
Removing authentication entirely, since webhooks are inherently trusted by design
Requiring only that the request come from any IP address, with no other validation

pia.explanation: Why B: HMAC (or digital signature) verification lets the receiving Apex REST endpoint confirm that a request genuinely originated from the payment provider and wasn't tampered with, using a shared secret to compute and compare signatures — the standard technique for securing inbound webhooks. Why A fails: "Security through obscurity" via an unguessable URL provides no real cryptographic assurance and can be discovered or leaked. Why C fails: Webhooks are not inherently trusted; without verification, anyone who discovers the endpoint URL could forge a malicious payload. Why D fails: IP-based checks alone are weak (IPs can be spoofed or the provider's IP range may be broad/dynamic) and don't verify payload integrity like a signature does.

options.text: Individually hardcoded within each of the ten backend APIs' own codebases, duplicated ten times
An API Gateway (e.g., MuleSoft API Manager) sitting in front of all ten APIs, centrally enforcing rate limiting, API key validation, and threat protection policies consistently across all of them
Nowhere; Salesforce's org-wide daily API limits already provide all necessary rate limiting for every exposed API
Only within Salesforce Named Credentials, since they handle rate limiting for all outbound and inbound calls

pia.explanation: Why B: An API Gateway is specifically designed as a centralized policy enforcement point — applying consistent rate limiting, key management, and security policies across many APIs from one place, avoiding duplicated and inconsistent implementations. Why A fails: Duplicating policy logic across ten codebases is exactly the inconsistency and maintenance burden an API Gateway is meant to eliminate. Why C fails: Salesforce's own daily API limits govern Salesforce-originated API consumption but don't provide governance (like API key management or threat protection) for the ten backend APIs as a set, several of which may not even be Salesforce. Why D fails: Named Credentials manage authentication for Salesforce's own outbound callouts; they are not a centralized gateway mechanism for governing multiple backend APIs' inbound traffic.

options.text: Message queuing (e.g., a durable queue in middleware or an MQ) placed between the two systems, absorbing bursts and feeding the fulfillment system at its sustainable processing rate
Increasing the fulfillment system's Salesforce API daily limit, since that governs its processing throughput
Removing all buffering and having the order system call the fulfillment system directly at full speed, relying on it to drop excess requests
Switching the order system to Bulk API, since Bulk API automatically throttles downstream systems

pia.explanation: Why A: A message queue is the standard technique for absorbing bursty producer throughput and feeding a slower consumer at a sustainable rate, decoupling the two systems' processing speeds without losing messages. Why B fails: Salesforce API daily limits govern Salesforce API call consumption, not the downstream fulfillment system's own processing capacity, which is an unrelated constraint. Why C fails: Calling directly at full speed with no buffering would overwhelm the fulfillment system and cause dropped or failed requests — exactly the problem queuing is meant to prevent. Why D fails: Bulk API governs how Salesforce processes bulk data jobs; it has no mechanism to throttle an unrelated downstream fulfillment system's processing rate.

options.text: CloudHub only, since it is the only Anypoint runtime option available

A hybrid deployment, running Mule runtime on-premise (or in a customer-managed private cloud) for flows handling the residency-restricted data, while still using Anypoint Platform's control plane for centralized management/monitoring across all flows
Fully on-premise with no connection to Anypoint Platform at all, since any cloud connection violates data residency
CloudHub exclusively, ignoring the data residency requirement since Salesforce is also cloud-based

pia.explanation: Why B: A hybrid deployment lets the actual data-processing runtime stay on-premise (satisfying residency requirements) while Anypoint Platform's control plane still provides centralized visibility and management across both on-prem and cloud-deployed flows — reconciling both requirements. Why A fails: CloudHub is not the only runtime option; Mule runtime can also be deployed on-premise or in a customer-managed environment, which is necessary here given the residency constraint. Why C fails: The control plane connection (for monitoring/management) is typically metadata/telemetry, not the actual restricted customer data; a fully disconnected on-prem approach isn't necessary to satisfy residency and would lose the desired centralized visibility. Why D fails: Ignoring a stated hard compliance requirement because "Salesforce is also cloud-based" is a non-sequitur and doesn't address the residency mandate at all.

options.text: Modify the existing endpoint's response structure in place whenever changes are needed, with no versioning, since partners should always just adapt immediately

Include a version indicator in the URI (e.g., /services/apexrest/v1/Orders) or another versioning mechanism, so existing partner integrations on an older version continue working unaffected while a new version is introduced for evolved functionality
Avoid ever changing the API after its first release, permanently freezing all functionality
Require all three partners to redeploy their integration code simultaneously every time any change is made, coordinated manually by phone

pia.explanation: Why B: Explicit API versioning (e.g., in the URI path) is the standard way to let existing consumers keep working against a stable version while new capabilities are introduced under a new version, avoiding breaking changes for partners not yet ready to migrate. Why A fails: In-place breaking changes with no versioning would break all three partners' integrations without warning whenever a change is made. Why C fails: Permanently freezing the API prevents any evolution, which contradicts the stated expectation that the API will need to change over time. Why D fails: Manually coordinating simultaneous redeployment across three partners by phone is operationally fragile and unnecessary when versioning allows independent migration timing.

options.text: Governor limits (e.g., SOQL query and DML limits within the Apex REST method), proper authentication/authorization enforcement (e.g., via Connected App/OAuth scopes), and appropriate HTTP status code handling for success/error responses
Only the URL path structure matters; governor limits do not apply to @RestResource classes
@RestResource classes automatically scale without any governor limit considerations, unlike other Apex code
Authentication is unnecessary for @RestResource endpoints since they are inherently public and safe by default

pia.explanation: Why A: A custom Apex REST API executes within a standard Apex transaction and is subject to the same governor limits (SOQL, DML, CPU time), so the design must account for these, plus proper OAuth-based authentication/authorization and clear HTTP status codes for consumers to handle responses correctly. Why B fails: Governor limits absolutely apply to @RestResource Apex classes just like any other Apex execution context; ignoring them risks runtime exceptions under load. Why C fails: There is no special exemption from governor limits for @RestResource classes — they run in a standard Apex transaction context subject to the same limits. Why D fails: @RestResource endpoints require appropriate authentication (typically OAuth via a Connected App); they are not inherently public or safe without configuration.

options.text: Enterprise WSDL, since it is strongly typed to a specific org's exact schema at generation time, making it ideal for org-agnostic reusable packages
Partner WSDL, since it is loosely typed and works generically across different orgs' schemas without needing regeneration per org, making it suitable for an ISV package deployed broadly
Neither WSDL type works for multi-org ISV scenarios; only REST API can be used
Enterprise WSDL must be regenerated and hardcoded separately into the ISV package for every single customer org before it can be distributed

pia.explanation: Why B: The Partner WSDL is loosely typed and uses generic sObject structures, allowing a single client build to work across many different orgs' schemas without regeneration — exactly suited to an ISV package meant to run generically across varied customer orgs. Why A fails: The Enterprise WSDL is strongly typed to one specific org's schema at the time it's generated, making it a poor fit for a generic package meant to run across many different orgs with different schemas. Why C fails: SOAP API (via Partner WSDL) is a valid and historically common approach for exactly this multi-org generic scenario; REST is not the only option. Why D fails: Regenerating and hardcoding the Enterprise WSDL per customer org is exactly the burden the Partner WSDL is designed to avoid, making this an impractical, non-scalable approach.

options.text: This works fine in all Apex execution contexts with no restriction

This will throw a runtime exception because Apex does not allow callouts after DML statements within the same transaction; the fix is to move the callout to an asynchronous context (e.g., a Queueable Apex enqueued from the trigger, or via Platform Events) executed in a separate transaction
This works fine as long as the callout uses SOAP instead of REST
This works fine only if the Task record is deleted immediately before the callout

pia.explanation: Why B: Salesforce enforces a rule that you cannot make a callout after a DML operation within the same transaction; the standard fix is to defer the callout to an asynchronous context (like Queueable Apex, which runs in its own transaction) so it executes after the DML-containing transaction has committed. Why A fails: This restriction is a real, well-documented governor limit/restriction in Apex — it is not context-independent or unconditionally permitted. Why C fails: The callout-after-DML restriction applies regardless of whether the callout protocol is REST or SOAP; protocol choice doesn't bypass it. Why D fails: Deleting the record doesn't change the fact that a DML statement (the delete itself) occurred before the callout in the same transaction; the restriction would still apply.

options.text: External Services, which registers the API's OpenAPI/Swagger schema and automatically exposes its operations as invocable actions usable directly within Flow
Named Credentials alone, since they alone expose callable Flow actions
Custom Metadata Types, since they can be configured to auto-generate Flow actions
Apex Interfaces, since Flow can invoke any Apex Interface without an implementing class

pia.explanation: Why A: External Services reads a registered OpenAPI (or similar) schema and automatically generates invocable actions for each operation, making them directly usable inside Flow without requiring an Apex developer to hand-write callout logic for each one. Why B fails: Named Credentials manage endpoint/authentication configuration for callouts but do not themselves expose any Flow-invocable actions; they're typically used in conjunction with External Services or Apex. Why C fails: Custom Metadata Types store configuration data; they have no capability to auto-generate Flow-invocable actions from an API schema. Why D fails: An Apex Interface has no implementation on its own; Flow cannot invoke an interface without a concrete class, and this isn't how External Services actually works.

options.text: Three synchronous Apex callouts made directly inline within the same Flow transaction that performed the Opportunity DML

An asynchronous approach — such as publishing a Platform Event from the Flow (or invoking a Queueable Apex action) that is then processed in a separate transaction to make the three outbound calls, avoiding both the callout-after-DML restriction and the risk of the 90-second call impacting the triggering transaction
Synchronous Outbound Messaging triggered directly by the Flow's DML statement within the same transaction
A single Batch Apex job scheduled to run once per year

pia.explanation: Why B: Since the Flow's transaction already contains a DML operation (the Opportunity update) and one downstream call can take up to 90 seconds (risking the callout timeout and violating the callout-after-DML rule), deferring the outbound calls to an asynchronous context via Platform Events or Queueable Apex is the correct way to decouple them safely. Why A fails: Making synchronous callouts inline after the Flow's DML would violate the callout-after-DML restriction, and the 90-second call risks exceeding practical timeout tolerances within that transaction. Why C fails: Outbound Messaging is not something you can force to fire "synchronously within the same DML transaction" in the way described; it is not the correct mechanism to solve this specific timing/restriction problem. Why D fails: A once-per-year scheduled job would introduce enormous delay, completely failing to meet any reasonable near-term notification need tied to an Opportunity update.

options.text: Change Data Capture, since it can be enabled per-object (up to the platform limit) and delivers a consistent event structure (header + changed fields) across all enabled objects without requiring per-field workflow rule configuration
Outbound Messaging, since it requires no per-object configuration at all
Scheduled Apex batch jobs, one per object, running every 5 minutes
Salesforce Connect, since it streams changes for any object without configuration

pia.explanation: Why A: CDC can be enabled on multiple objects (subject to org limits) and delivers a standardized event structure across all of them without needing individual workflow rules per object/field combination, exactly matching the consistency and reduced-configuration requirement. Why B fails: Outbound Messaging does require per-object, per-workflow-rule configuration (and separate field mappings), which is the opposite of the low-configuration, consistent-structure goal described. Why C fails: Five separate scheduled polling jobs reintroduce per-object configuration overhead and polling latency/inefficiency, contrary to the streamlined goal. Why D fails: Salesforce Connect is for virtualizing external data into Salesforce, not for streaming Salesforce's own object changes out to an external subscriber.

options.text: The root cause is a network issue with the external system; the fix is to ask the external system's vendor to increase their server capacity

The root cause is that the trigger design doesn't account for bulk operations — making one callout per record in a large Trigger.new collection can exceed the 100-callout-per-transaction limit; the fix is to redesign for bulk-safety, e.g., batching the records into an async Queueable/Batch job that respects callout limits, or aggregating multiple records into fewer callouts
The root cause is a Salesforce platform bug that only Salesforce Support can fix by raising an internal limit
The root cause is that Contact records cannot be updated in bulk under any circumstances

pia.explanation: Why B: This is the classic bulk-safety failure: code that makes one callout per record works fine for tiny record counts but breaks the 100-callout-per-transaction governor limit at scale; the standard fix is redesigning the trigger to be bulk-safe, deferring to async processing or reducing callout count via aggregation. Why A fails: The described failure is a Salesforce Apex governor limit being exceeded, not a network or external server capacity issue. Why C fails: This is a well-documented, expected governor limit behavior, not a bug, and it is not something Salesforce Support "raises" on request for standard per-transaction callout limits. Why D fails: Bulk Contact updates are entirely normal and well-supported in Salesforce; the issue is specifically with the trigger's non-bulk-safe callout design.

options.text: Use the default or a small scope size (e.g., 50–200) in the Batchable's start/execute method, rather than the maximum 2,000, so each batch execution makes a manageable, throttled number of callouts consistent with the external API's burst tolerance
Always set scope size to the maximum of 2,000 regardless of external system capacity, since larger batches always perform better
Batch Apex cannot make callouts, so this approach is not possible at all
Use a single batch with no scope limit to process all 2 million records in one execution

pia.explanation: Why A: Batchable Apex lets you specify a scope size controlling how many records are processed per execute() invocation; choosing a smaller size appropriate to the external API's burst tolerance prevents overwhelming a fragile downstream system while still processing the full 2 million records across many batches. Why B fails: Maximizing scope size ignores the stated external system constraint and risks overwhelming an API that can only handle small bursts, causing failures. Why C fails: Batch Apex execute() methods can make callouts (when the class implements Database.AllowsCallouts), so this is a valid and common pattern. Why D fails: There's no single-batch-with-no-limit mode; Batch Apex inherently divides work into scoped batches, and attempting to remove scoping isn't how the framework works nor advisable at this volume.

options.text: Nothing; Platform Events guarantee exactly-once delivery so duplicates are impossible

The subscriber must be designed to be idempotent — e.g., using a unique event identifier or business key to detect and safely ignore or safely reprocess duplicate events without causing incorrect duplicate side effects
The subscriber should simply process every event exactly as received, since duplicate processing has no real-world consequences
The publisher, not the subscriber, is solely responsible for guaranteeing no duplicates are ever sent

pia.explanation: Why B: Platform Events use at-least-once delivery, meaning duplicates are possible; subscribers must be designed idempotently (e.g., checking a unique event ID or business key before applying side effects) to avoid incorrect results from reprocessing the same event. Why A fails: Platform Events explicitly provide at-least-once, not exactly-once, delivery — duplicates are an expected possibility that must be handled. Why C fails: Assuming duplicate processing "has no consequences" is unsafe in general — e.g., duplicate order creation or duplicate financial postings would cause real business problems. Why D fails: Given the at-least-once delivery model, the platform does not guarantee the publisher can prevent all duplicates; responsibility for correctness under duplicates falls to the subscriber's idempotent design.

options.text: The subscriber should reconnect and use a stored ReplayId (or -2 for all retained events) to resume streaming from the correct point, replaying any events published during the outage, within the platform's event retention window
Nothing can be done; any events published while the subscriber was offline are permanently and unavoidably lost
The publisher must manually resend every event that occurred during the outage window via a new Apex script
The subscriber should simply reconnect and only receive brand-new events going forward, ignoring the gap entirely

pia.explanation: Why A: The Streaming API's replay mechanism lets a reconnecting subscriber supply a ReplayId (from its last successfully processed event, or -2 to replay all retained events) to resume exactly where it left off, recovering missed events within the platform's retention window. Why B fails: This ignores the entire purpose of the ReplayId/replay mechanism, which exists specifically to prevent this kind of data loss during subscriber outages. Why C fails: Manually resending events via a new script duplicates functionality the platform already provides natively through ReplayId-based resumption, and risks introducing its own errors/duplicates. Why D fails: Ignoring the gap defeats the purpose of reliable event processing and would silently lose two hours of business-relevant events.

options.text: Reduce the number of Mule workers to lower cost, which will proportionally increase throughput

Scale horizontally by increasing the number of Mule workers (or enabling clustering/vCore scaling in CloudHub) so incoming load is distributed across multiple concurrent runtime instances, increasing overall throughput
Switch the flow to process messages strictly one at a time with no concurrency, since serial processing is always faster
Move the flow's logic entirely into a single Salesforce Apex trigger to bypass MuleSoft scaling limits

pia.explanation: Why B: Horizontal scaling — adding more Mule workers or enabling clustering/increased vCore allocation in CloudHub — lets the integration distribute processing load across multiple concurrent runtime instances, directly addressing a throughput bottleneck under peak load. Why A fails: Reducing worker count would decrease available processing capacity, worsening the throughput bottleneck rather than improving it. Why C fails: Serial, non-concurrent processing generally reduces throughput compared to appropriately parallelized processing, especially under high load — this is the opposite of a scaling fix. Why D fails: Moving the entire integration logic into a Salesforce Apex trigger introduces Apex's own governor limits and doesn't solve a MuleSoft throughput scaling problem; it essentially abandons the middleware architecture.

options.text: A custom Apex-based Salesforce Connect adapter (implementing the Connect Framework's Apex classes) to translate calls to/from the proprietary system's native interface, exposed as External Objects
The standard OData 4.0 adapter, since it works with any system regardless of whether it exposes OData
Heroku Connect, since it supports any arbitrary proprietary system format automatically
This scenario cannot be supported by Salesforce Connect under any circumstances

pia.explanation: Why A: When no standard OData interface exists, Salesforce Connect supports building a custom Apex adapter (implementing the appropriate Connect Framework interfaces) to bridge to the proprietary system's native protocol, still exposing the result as queryable External Objects. Why B fails: The standard OData adapter specifically requires the source system to expose an OData-compliant interface; it cannot connect to a proprietary system lacking one. Why C fails: Heroku Connect is specifically built around Postgres-based data synchronization, not a generic connector for any arbitrary proprietary system protocol. Why D fails: This is incorrect — the custom Apex adapter capability exists precisely to support non-standard/proprietary sources that lack a standard adapter.

options.text: Polling interval and field selection are irrelevant since Heroku Connect never consumes Salesforce API calls

More frequent polling intervals and syncing more fields/objects increase how current the replicated data is, but also increase Salesforce API call consumption; the design should balance the business's freshness requirements against the org's available API allocation
Heroku Connect should always be configured to poll as frequently as technically possible, regardless of the business's actual freshness requirements or API budget
Field selection has no effect on API consumption, only polling interval does

pia.explanation: Why B: Heroku Connect's sync mappings consume Salesforce API calls as they poll for changes; more frequent polling and larger field/object scope increase data freshness but also increase API consumption, so the architect must balance these against the org's actual freshness needs and available API budget. Why A fails: Heroku Connect does consume Salesforce API calls as part of its polling-based synchronization mechanism; it is not API-call-free. Why C fails: Maximizing polling frequency without regard to actual business need or API budget risks unnecessarily exhausting the org's daily API allocation for no real benefit. Why D fails: Broader field/object selection in a mapping also affects the volume/frequency of data pulled and thus API consumption, not just the polling interval alone.

options.text: Both are the same type of error and should be handled identically with a simple retry

The timeout is a system error (transient, infrastructure/connectivity-related, often retry-appropriate); the missing-field rejection is an application error (a business/validation failure that a blind retry won't fix, since the payload itself is invalid)
Both are application errors, since they both occur within an "application" context
The timeout is an application error and the missing field is a system error

pia.explanation: Why B: System errors (like network timeouts) stem from infrastructure/connectivity issues and are often transient, making retries appropriate; application errors (like a validation rejection) stem from a problem with the data/business logic itself, where retrying the identical payload will simply fail again. Why A fails: Treating both identically with a blind retry would cause the missing-field case to fail repeatedly without ever fixing the underlying data problem. Why C fails: A network timeout is fundamentally a connectivity/infrastructure issue, not a business validation problem, so classifying it as an application error mischaracterizes its root cause. Why D fails: This reverses the correct classification — a timeout is infrastructure-related (system), and a missing required field is a data/business validation issue (application).

options.text: For both types, silently discard the failed record with no logging or notification

For system errors, implement automatic retry with backoff (and eventual escalation if retries exhaust); for application errors, capture the specific validation failure and route it to a business user/queue for correction rather than blindly retrying the same invalid data
For system errors, immediately notify a human to manually resubmit each request one at a time; for application errors, automatically retry indefinitely
Treat every failure, regardless of type, as unrecoverable and abandon the entire integration permanently

pia.explanation: Why B: This matches each error type to an appropriate strategy: system errors benefit from automated retry/backoff since they're often transient, while application errors need human/business correction of the underlying data since retrying an invalid payload as-is won't succeed. Why A fails: Silently discarding failures with no logging or notification hides problems from the business and prevents any correction or root-cause analysis. Why C fails: This reverses the appropriate strategies — manual intervention makes more sense for application/validation errors, while automated retry fits transient system errors, not vice versa; indefinite retry of bad data will never succeed. Why D fails: Abandoning the entire integration for any single failure is a drastic overreaction that ignores the fact that most integration failures are per-record or per-transaction, not systemic.

options.text: Retry immediately and repeatedly with no delay between attempts, as fast as possible, to resolve the issue before the user notices

Exponential backoff — retrying with progressively longer delays between attempts (e.g., 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) — reduces load on the already-struggling partner service and increases the likelihood that the retry succeeds once the partner recovers
Retry exactly once immediately and never attempt again regardless of outcome
Increase the number of concurrent retry threads to overwhelm the partner service until it responds

pia.explanation: Why B: Exponential backoff spaces out retry attempts with increasing delays, which reduces additional load on an already struggling service and gives it time to recover, improving the odds of eventual success compared to rapid-fire retries. Why A fails: Rapid, undelayed retries add more load to an already overloaded service, worsening the exact problem described in the scenario. Why C fails: A single immediate retry with no further attempts may fail again if the partner hasn't yet recovered, missing the chance for eventual success once load subsides. Why D fails: Increasing concurrent retry threads adds more simultaneous load on a struggling service, the opposite of what's needed to help it recover.

options.text: Always use a plain Insert operation on retry, accepting that some duplicates may occur as an unavoidable cost
Use Upsert operations keyed on a unique External ID field (populated from the source system's unique identifier), so rerunning the batch updates already-created records instead of creating duplicates
Manually query and delete all Account records before every rerun, then reinsert everything from scratch
Disable all validation rules during reruns so duplicate records can be created and cleaned up later

pia.explanation: Why B: Upserting on a unique External ID makes the batch operation idempotent — rerunning it identifies already-created records by their source system key and updates them instead of creating duplicates, safely supporting reruns after partial failure. Why A fails: Plain Insert has no way to recognize previously created records, so rerunning after a partial failure will create duplicate Accounts for rows already processed. Why C fails: Deleting and reinserting everything on every rerun is destructive, risky (loses any interim manual edits), and unnecessarily heavy-handed compared to a targeted upsert. Why D fails: Disabling validation rules doesn't address duplicate detection at all and introduces unrelated risk by bypassing data integrity checks.

options.text: Salesforce Outbound Messaging has no retry mechanism at all; if the first attempt fails, the message is permanently lost

Salesforce automatically retries delivering an unacknowledged outbound message, continuing retry attempts for a period of time (up to 24 hours) before giving up, providing some built-in resilience against transient endpoint issues
Salesforce Outbound Messaging requires the architect to manually write custom Apex retry logic, since there's no built-in retry
Salesforce guarantees an outbound message will always be delivered eventually with no time limit whatsoever

pia.explanation: Why B: Salesforce's Outbound Messaging includes built-in retry behavior for unacknowledged messages, continuing attempts for up to 24 hours before giving up — a meaningful degree of built-in resilience the architect can rely on without custom retry code. Why A fails: Outbound Messaging does have built-in retry logic for unacknowledged messages; it is not a single-attempt, no-retry mechanism. Why C fails: The retry behavior is native/built-in to the Outbound Messaging feature; the architect does not need to write custom Apex to get basic retry behavior. Why D fails: The retry window is bounded (up to 24 hours), not indefinite; after that period, Salesforce stops retrying if the endpoint remains unresponsive.

options.text: Since allOrNone=false was used, the entire job automatically rolls back if even one record fails, so no special handling is needed

Capture and review the per-record error results for the 200 failed records (available in the job's result files), correct or route them for handling (e.g., a re-load after fixing source data), while the 9,800 successful records remain committed
Discard all 10,000 records, including the 9,800 successes, since partial success is not supported by Bulk API
Ignore the 200 failures permanently since Bulk API does not provide any way to identify which specific records failed

pia.explanation: Why B: With allOrNone=false, Bulk API commits successful records independently of failed ones, and provides per-record result/error details so the architect can design a process to review, correct, and reprocess just the failed subset without touching the already-committed successes. Why A fails: allOrNone=false specifically means partial success is allowed — the successful records are NOT rolled back just because some records failed. Why C fails: Bulk API explicitly supports partial success with allOrNone=false; discarding the whole batch would contradict the very setting used. Why D fails: Bulk API result files do report per-record success/failure status and error messages, making it possible to identify exactly which records failed and why.

options.text: Use on-error-continue for the error type where processing should continue after logging, and on-error-propagate for the critical error type that should halt the flow and surface the failure upstream for alerting
Use on-error-propagate for every error type universally, since it is always the safer choice
Use on-error-continue for every error type universally, since it always keeps the flow running regardless of severity
Error handling scopes in Mule flows cannot differentiate behavior by error type

pia.explanation: Why A: Mule's error handling framework allows different error types to be routed to different handlers — on-error-continue lets the flow recover and proceed after logging a non-critical error, while on-error-propagate deliberately stops the flow and surfaces critical failures for alerting, matching the two described needs exactly. Why B fails: Using on-error-propagate universally would halt the flow even for the non-critical error type that should simply be logged and continued past. Why C fails: Using on-error-continue universally would suppress the critical error's propagation, defeating the requirement for it to halt and alert operations immediately. Why D fails: Mule flows explicitly support type-specific error handling (e.g., matching on error type/namespace) precisely so different handlers can apply to different error conditions.

options.text: Halt the entire subscriber permanently the first time any event fails to process

A dead-letter queue pattern — routing the failed event (with error context) to a separate queue/store for later investigation and reprocessing, while the subscriber continues processing subsequent events normally
Silently drop the failed event with no record of it, and continue processing
Reprocess the same malformed event in an infinite retry loop before allowing any further events to be processed

pia.explanation: Why B: A dead-letter queue captures failed messages/events (with enough context to investigate) in a separate location so the main processing pipeline can continue handling subsequent events without getting stuck or losing visibility into the failure. Why A fails: Halting the entire subscriber permanently over a single malformed event would block all subsequent legitimate events, causing unnecessary business impact. Why C fails: Silently dropping the event with no record prevents any investigation or reprocessing, risking undetected data loss. Why D fails: An infinite retry loop on an unprocessable malformed payload will never succeed and will block the subscriber from making progress on later events.

options.text: Leave the Order and successful payment in place with no further action, ignoring the failed shipping step entirely

A compensating transaction (saga pattern step) that, upon detecting the shipping failure, either retries shipping separately or triggers a compensating action (e.g., reversing/refunding the payment or flagging the Order for manual reconciliation), rather than assuming atomicity across the three systems
Roll back the Salesforce Order and the external payment automatically via a native cross-system two-phase commit
Prevent this scenario by making all three systems synchronous, which automatically guarantees atomicity

pia.explanation: Why B: In the absence of true cross-system atomicity, the saga pattern responds to partial failure with an explicit compensating action (like a refund or reconciliation flag) so the overall business state is corrected/handled deliberately rather than left inconsistent. Why A fails: Ignoring the failure leaves an inconsistent state — a paid order with no shipment — which harms the customer experience and financial accuracy. Why C fails: No native two-phase commit exists across Salesforce and two external systems; assuming automatic rollback across all three is not technically achievable this way. Why D fails: Making calls synchronous does not itself provide distributed atomicity; a synchronous chain can still partially fail after an earlier step (payment) has already succeeded.

options.text: OAuth 2.0 Web Server flow, since it involves a browser-based redirect where the user authenticates and explicitly grants consent, issuing tokens scoped to that specific user's context
OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer flow, since it is designed for interactive user consent screens
OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials flow, since it operates in the context of the specific logged-in user
SAML Bearer flow, since it requires no user interaction whatsoever

pia.explanation: Why A: The Web Server flow is specifically designed for scenarios where a user interactively logs in and grants consent via a redirect-based browser flow, resulting in tokens tied to that user's own data access context — precisely what's described. Why B fails: JWT Bearer flow is designed for server-to-server authentication without any interactive user consent screen, the opposite of what's needed here. Why C fails: Client Credentials flow authenticates as a service account/application identity, not as a specific interactively-consenting end user. Why D fails: SAML Bearer flow is used for federated assertion-based authentication, typically without an interactive Salesforce login/consent screen, which doesn't match the explicit user consent requirement.

options.text: A single org-wide Named Credential shared by all users with one fixed service account

A Named Credential configured for per-user (user-specific) authentication, where each user authenticates individually and Salesforce stores/uses each user's own external credentials/tokens for their callouts
Hardcoded credentials embedded directly in Apex, identical for every user
A Named Credential with no authentication configured at all, relying on IP allowlisting only

pia.explanation: Why B: Named Credentials support a per-user (user-specific) authentication mode where each user goes through their own authentication to the external system, and their individual credentials/tokens are used for their own callouts — directly matching the requirement for per-user external access rather than one shared identity. Why A fails: An org-wide Named Credential with one shared account would make every user's calls appear identical to the external system, the opposite of maintaining per-user identity/permissions externally. Why C fails: Hardcoded credentials shared across all users in Apex would similarly erase per-user identity and is a security anti-pattern regardless. Why D fails: IP allowlisting alone provides no user-specific authentication at all; it only restricts by network origin, not by individual user identity.

options.text: Set the OAuth policy to "All users may self-authorize," since this is the most secure setting
Set the OAuth policy to "Admin approved users are pre-authorized," and then explicitly assign only the intended users/profiles/permission sets to the Connected App
Disable the Connected App entirely, since Connected Apps cannot restrict which users can use them
Grant "Modify All Data" to every user so the Connected App works consistently for everyone

pia.explanation: Why B: The "Admin approved users are pre-authorized" policy requires an administrator to explicitly assign specific profiles or permission sets to the Connected App, ensuring only pre-authorized individuals can use it rather than any user with general API access. Why A fails: "All users may self-authorize" allows any user to grant themselves access without admin pre-approval, the opposite of the tightly controlled access the security team wants. Why C fails: Connected Apps explicitly support restricting usage to pre-approved users via this OAuth policy setting; disabling it entirely isn't necessary and removes the integration's functionality altogether. Why D fails: "Modify All Data" is an unrelated, overly broad permission that has nothing to do with which users are authorized to use a specific Connected App, and it violates least privilege.

options.text: Remove all login IP range restrictions from the profile entirely, applying no IP-based control anywhere

Configure the Connected App's IP Relaxation setting to relax IP restrictions specifically for OAuth tokens issued through that Connected App, while leaving other login IP restrictions (e.g., direct username/password login) intact elsewhere
Set the Connected App to require a VPN, which automatically bypasses IP restriction enforcement
There is no way to accommodate a dynamic IP range in Salesforce; the partner must switch to a static IP

pia.explanation: Why B: The Connected App's IP Relaxation setting lets you selectively relax IP enforcement for OAuth tokens issued through that specific Connected App, without having to remove IP restrictions globally from the profile for other login paths. Why A fails: Removing all IP restrictions everywhere is a much broader security reduction than needed; the Connected App-specific relaxation setting exists precisely to avoid this blunt approach. Why C fails: There's no Connected App "require VPN" setting that automatically bypasses IP enforcement; IP Relaxation is the actual mechanism for this scenario. Why D fails: IP Relaxation at the Connected App level is exactly the accommodation mechanism for dynamic/unenumerable partner IP ranges; a static IP requirement isn't the only solution.

options.text: A refresh token policy on the Connected App set to expire the refresh token after a period of inactivity (e.g., "expire refresh token if not used for X days," configured to the desired window)
Refresh tokens in Salesforce never expire under any configuration and this cannot be controlled
Disable OAuth entirely for the Connected App, since that is the only way to expire tokens
Set the Connected App's session timeout value to 90 minutes, which controls refresh token expiration

pia.explanation: Why A: Salesforce Connected Apps support a refresh token policy that can expire the token after a configured period of inactivity, directly addressing the risk of dormant, unused tokens remaining valid indefinitely. Why B fails: Refresh token expiration policies are a configurable Connected App setting; "never expire under any configuration" is factually incorrect. Why C fails: Disabling OAuth entirely removes the integration's functionality altogether rather than selectively managing token lifetime, which isn't necessary given the available policy setting. Why D fails: Session timeout settings govern user session length in the UI context, not the OAuth refresh token's own expiration-on-inactivity policy.

options.text: Salesforce should be configured as the SAML Service Provider (SP), since Salesforce always initiates authentication

Salesforce should be configured as the SAML Identity Provider (IdP), issuing a SAML assertion after the user logs into Salesforce, which the expense tool (acting as the Service Provider) consumes to establish a session without requiring the user to log in again
SAML cannot be used in this direction; only OAuth can enable this kind of delegated login
Salesforce must always be the SAML SP any time it interacts with another SAML-enabled system

pia.explanation: Why B: Since Salesforce is the system where the user first authenticates and the expense tool needs to trust that established identity, Salesforce plays the Identity Provider (IdP) role — issuing the SAML assertion — while the expense tool acts as the Service Provider (SP) consuming it, enabling single sign-on without re-authentication. Why A fails: Salesforce is not the SP in this scenario; it is the source of the authenticated identity being asserted outward, which is the IdP role, not the relying/consuming SP role. Why C fails: SAML delegated/federated login (IdP-initiated SSO) is exactly designed for this cross-application single sign-on scenario; it isn't limited only to OAuth. Why D fails: Salesforce's SAML role (IdP or SP) depends on the specific integration direction; Salesforce can and does act as an IdP for other applications in exactly this kind of scenario, not always as the SP.

options.text: A standard one-way TLS connection where only the partner's server certificate is validated, since this fully satisfies the mutual authentication requirement

Mutual TLS (mTLS): upload/configure a client certificate in Salesforce's certificate keystore, associate it with the outbound Named Credential/HTTP call, so Salesforce presents its own client certificate while also validating the partner's server certificate
Basic authentication with a username and password, which satisfies certificate-based mutual authentication requirements
IP allowlisting alone, since it is functionally equivalent to mutual certificate-based authentication

pia.explanation: Why B: Mutual TLS requires both parties to present certificates; Salesforce supports this by storing a client certificate in its certificate keystore and associating it with the outbound callout (via Named Credential configuration), so Salesforce authenticates itself to the partner via certificate while also validating the partner's server certificate. Why A fails: One-way TLS only validates the server's certificate; it explicitly does not satisfy a mutual (two-way) certificate authentication requirement, which the partner is mandating. Why C fails: Username/password Basic auth is a completely different authentication mechanism and does not involve X.509 certificate-based mutual authentication at all. Why D fails: IP allowlisting is a network-level control unrelated to cryptographic certificate-based mutual authentication; it is not functionally equivalent.

options.text: Shield Platform Encryption has zero impact on SOQL queries, Bulk API, or outbound data visibility for encrypted fields

Filtering (WHERE clause) capability on Shield-encrypted fields is limited depending on the encryption scheme (e.g., deterministic encryption supports exact-match filtering while probabilistic does not support filtering at all), and Bulk API/outbound extracts will return the field's ciphertext or decrypted value depending on the running user's "View Encrypted Data" permission — both must be accounted for in the integration design
Shield Platform Encryption automatically decrypts all fields for any integration user regardless of permissions
Shield Platform Encryption prevents all API access to encrypted fields under every circumstance, making this integration impossible

pia.explanation: Why B: Shield Platform Encryption has real, documented implications: SOQL filtering capability depends on the encryption scheme used (deterministic supports certain exact-match operations, probabilistic does not support filtering), and whether an API caller sees plaintext or ciphertext depends on whether the running user holds the "View Encrypted Data" permission — both are critical design considerations for this integration. Why A fails: Shield Platform Encryption absolutely does affect SOQL filtering capability and what value (encrypted or decrypted) is returned via API/Bulk extracts; "zero impact" is inaccurate. Why C fails: Decryption via API is explicitly gated by the "View Encrypted Data" permission; it is not automatic for every integration user regardless of permission assignment. Why D fails: Encrypted fields remain accessible via API for authorized users/integrations (subject to permission and encryption-scheme constraints); it does not make all API access categorically impossible.

options.text: OAuth 2.0 Device Flow, where the device displays or communicates a short code, the user visits a URL on a separate browser-capable device to enter the code and approve access, and the device then polls for and receives its token — designed exactly for browser-less/limited-input devices
OAuth 2.0 Web Server flow, since the device itself must perform a full browser redirect
SAML Bearer flow, since it eliminates the need for any device-side interaction
Username-password OAuth flow, since it is the most modern and recommended approach for IoT devices

pia.explanation: Why A: The Device Flow is specifically designed for input-constrained, browser-less devices: the device obtains a short code, a human completes the approval on a separate capable device/browser, and the constrained device polls until the token is issued — exactly matching this IoT scanner scenario. Why B fails: The Web Server flow requires the authenticating client itself to perform a browser redirect, which a browser-less device with only a numeric keypad cannot do. Why C fails: SAML Bearer flow involves passing a SAML assertion for authentication, not a code-based device/human split; it doesn't match this specific browser-less approval-by-proxy scenario. Why D fails: The username-password OAuth flow (Resource Owner Password Credentials) is a legacy, discouraged flow due to security concerns (credentials handled by the client), and is not the modern recommended approach for constrained IoT devices — Device Flow is.

options.text: Leave the version hardcoded permanently at 40.0 forever, since Salesforce never actually retires old API versions in practice

Establish a practice of periodically reviewing and updating the API version used by the integration (staying within Salesforce's supported version window) as part of ongoing maintenance, rather than leaving it frozen indefinitely on an aging version
Switch to not specifying any API version at all in any request, since omitting a version guarantees permanent forward compatibility
Rewrite the entire integration in a completely different API (e.g., swap in Bulk API for what was a REST API integration) purely to avoid ever specifying a version number

pia.explanation: Why B: Since Salesforce does periodically retire old API versions, a resilient integration should include a practice of periodically reviewing and bumping the API version used, staying within the supported window, rather than leaving it frozen indefinitely and risking eventual breakage. Why A fails: Salesforce does retire old API versions over time (per its published version support policy), so assuming this will never happen is factually incorrect and risky. Why C fails: Most Salesforce API calls require a version in the URI; omitting it isn't generally how REST/SOAP API versioning works, and it doesn't create some special universal forward compatibility guarantee. Why D fails: Swapping to a completely different API type doesn't eliminate the need to specify and maintain a supported version; Bulk API endpoints are also versioned.

options.text: Hardcode the production URL and settings directly in the Apex class, then manually edit the code before each sandbox deployment

Custom Metadata Types, which can store environment-specific configuration values (endpoint URL, batch size, etc.) as deployable, queryable records that Apex reads at runtime, allowing per-environment values without code changes
Custom Settings only, since Custom Metadata Types cannot be deployed via standard deployment tools
Store the values only as comments in the Apex class documentation, read manually by developers before each deployment

pia.explanation: Why B: Custom Metadata Types are designed exactly for this use case — they store configuration data as metadata records that can be deployed via standard tools (Metadata API/change sets/CI pipelines) and queried by Apex at runtime, letting each environment have its own values without editing code. Why A fails: Hardcoding and manually editing code per environment is exactly the fragile, error-prone practice the requirement is trying to avoid. Why C fails: Custom Metadata Types are in fact deployable via standard deployment tools (Metadata API, packages, change sets) — this is one of their key advantages over Custom Settings, which are more focused on org-specific/hierarchical runtime configuration rather than being metadata deployable in the same way. Why D fails: Comments in Apex are not read or applied automatically by any process; this doesn't provide functional runtime configuration at all.

options.text: Assume the sandbox's Named Credential and Connected App configuration will automatically point to the correct production endpoint and credentials with no changes needed

Explicitly plan to reconfigure (not just deploy as-is) the Named Credential's endpoint URL and authentication details, and the Connected App's settings/consumer keys, for the production environment as part of the promotion process, since these often need environment-specific values
Delete the Connected App and Named Credential entirely in production, since they serve no purpose outside of sandboxes
Rely solely on a full sandbox refresh to automatically carry the correct production values into the org

pia.explanation: Why B: Named Credentials and Connected App settings frequently contain environment-specific values (endpoint URLs, auth provider details, consumer keys/secrets) that must be deliberately reconfigured for production as part of a promotion plan, rather than assuming they'll be correct automatically after a simple deployment. Why A fails: Sandbox configurations typically point to test/mock endpoints and sandbox-specific auth setups; assuming no changes are needed risks the integration pointing at the wrong (or nonexistent) production endpoint. Why C fails: Named Credentials and Connected Apps are exactly the components needed in production to run the live integration; deleting them would break the integration entirely. Why D fails: A sandbox refresh moves data/config from production into a sandbox, not the reverse; it does not "carry" correct production values into anything and is unrelated to a sandbox-to-production promotion of integration settings.

options.text: There is no risk, since Salesforce guarantees all internal serialization behaviors remain byte-for-byte identical forever across every release

Relying on undocumented, non-guaranteed behavior (like incidental field ordering) creates a risk that a future seasonal release could change that behavior and break the integration; the fix is to depend only on documented, guaranteed behavior (e.g., explicitly defining serialization order rather than relying on incidental defaults)
Seasonal releases only affect the Lightning UI and never affect Apex code behavior in any way
This is only a risk for Visualforce pages, not for Apex-based integrations

pia.explanation: Why B: Undocumented incidental behaviors (like a particular default serialization order) are not covered by Salesforce's compatibility guarantees, so a seasonal release could legitimately change them without being considered a "breaking change" from Salesforce's perspective — the resilient fix is to depend only on explicitly documented, guaranteed behavior. Why A fails: Salesforce does not guarantee that every undocumented internal behavior remains identical across releases; only documented, supported behavior carries that guarantee. Why C fails: Seasonal releases can affect platform behavior broadly, including Apex runtime behavior in various ways, not solely the Lightning UI.
